notes: Hard shell skeleton on the outside
Hard shell skeleton on the outside
reason: A fish has a skeleton inside its body; the other four have a hard skeleton on the outside.
explain: Some animals, like crabs, ants, beetles and prawns, wear their skeleton on the outside as a hard shell called an exoskeleton. Fish, like humans, have an endoskeleton: bones inside the body with muscles attached around them. An inside skeleton can grow along with the animal, while animals with an outside skeleton must shed it to grow bigger.
fact: A crab that has just shed its old shell is soft for a few days until its new shell hardens.

notes: A joint; the hand bends here
A joint; the foot bends here
A joint; the leg bends here
Middle of a bone; cannot bend
A joint; the arm bends here
reason: The shin is the middle of a long bone with no joint; the other four are places where the body bends.
explain: Bones are hard and cannot bend. Your body bends only at joints, the places where two bones meet. The wrist, ankle, knee and elbow are all joints. The shin is the front of the shin bone, a single stiff bone, so the leg cannot bend there.
fact: Not every joint moves: the joints between the bones of your skull are fixed.

notes: Protects the skull in a fall
reason: Sunglasses protect the eyes from sunlight; the other four protect bones and joints from knocks in a fall.
explain: When you skate or cycle, a fall can crack bones or hurt joints. A helmet protects the skull and the brain inside it, while pads and guards spread out the force of a hit on the knees, elbows and wrists. Sunglasses are useful too, but they protect the eyes from bright light, not the skeleton from impact.
fact: When people fall, they often put out a hand to catch themselves, which is why wrists are among the most commonly broken bones.

notes: New cells at the root; no muscle
reason: Hair grows when cells at its root divide; the other four are movements made by muscles.
explain: Every movement in your body is made by muscles pulling. Face muscles make a smile, eyelid muscles make a blink, jaw muscles chew, and heart muscle squeezes to pump blood. Hair grows because cells at its root keep dividing and push the hair outward, which does not need a muscle.
fact: You blink around 15 to 20 times a minute, mostly without noticing.

notes: Keeps weight off an injured leg
reason: A thermometer measures temperature; the other four support injured bones or joints.
explain: A broken bone heals best when it is kept still in the right position. A cast or splint holds the bone in place, a sling rests an injured arm against the body, and crutches let a person move without putting weight on an injured leg. A thermometer measures whether someone has a fever.
fact: Many casts today are made of light fibreglass instead of heavy plaster, and come in bright colours.

notes: About 33 small bones in a stack
reason: The upper arm has just one bone; the other four are each made of many bones.
explain: More than half of your 206 bones are in your hands and feet. Many small bones let hands grip and feet flex as you walk. The skull is made of 22 bones joined together, and the spine is a stack of small vertebrae. The upper arm has a single long, strong bone called the humerus.
fact: Some vertebrae at the bottom of the spine join together as you grow, so adults have fewer separate spine bones than babies.

reason: The biceps is in the arm; the other four are leg and hip muscles.
explain: The biggest muscles in your body are in your legs and hips, because they carry your weight and push you forward. The quadriceps straightens the knee, the hamstrings bend it, the calf lifts your heel, and the gluteus maximus straightens your hip when you climb stairs. The biceps bends your elbow.
fact: The gluteus maximus, in your bottom, is the largest muscle in the human body.

notes: Bring food and oxygen to bone
Lie outside bone, attached by tendons
reason: Muscle fibres lie outside the bone; the other four are found inside a living bone.
explain: Bone is living tissue, not a dead stick. It has bone cells that build and repair it, blood vessels that bring food and oxygen, nerves that sense pain, and soft marrow in the middle. Muscles sit outside the bone and pull on it through tendons.
fact: Your whole skeleton slowly rebuilds itself, so most of the bone you have now will be replaced over the next ten years or so.

notes: A working muscle pulls on bone
reason: Muscles cannot push; contracting, relaxing, shortening and pulling are all things muscles do.
explain: A muscle can only pull. It contracts and shortens to pull on a bone, then relaxes and is stretched back. That is why muscles work in pairs: the biceps pulls to bend your elbow, and the triceps pulls to straighten it. Even when you push a door, muscles are pulling on the bones of your arm.
fact: A muscle that bends a joint is paired with one that straightens it; doctors call such a team an antagonistic pair.

notes: Holds it in a comfortable position
Never do this; leave it to doctors
reason: Never try to push a broken bone back; the other four are correct first aid for a suspected fracture.
explain: If someone may have broken a bone, keep the injured part still and supported in the position you found it, and call an adult so they can get medical help. A cold pack wrapped in cloth eases pain and swelling. Pushing the bone back can tear blood vessels and nerves, so only doctors set bones, after an X-ray.

reason: Conjunctivitis affects the eye; the other four affect bones or joints.
explain: Several conditions affect the skeleton. Arthritis makes joints painful and stiff, osteoporosis makes bones thin and easy to break, scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine, and gout happens when sharp crystals build up in a joint, often the big toe. Conjunctivitis is redness and swelling of the thin layer covering the eye.
fact: The word 'arthritis' comes from Greek: 'arthron' means joint and '-itis' means swelling.

notes: One on each side; you have two
reason: You have only one lower jaw bone; the other four come in left-and-right pairs.
explain: Your skeleton is mostly symmetrical, so most bones come in pairs, one on the left and one on the right, like your two kneecaps, thigh bones, collarbones and shoulder blades. A few bones sit on the midline and are single, such as the lower jaw (mandible), the breastbone and each vertebra.
fact: The lower jaw is the largest and strongest bone in the face.

notes: Hard tissue: a fracture of the bone
reason: A cracked shin bone is a bone injury; the other four are soft-tissue injuries.
explain: Sports injuries are often sorted into two groups. Soft-tissue injuries harm muscles, tendons and ligaments, such as a pulled muscle or a twisted ankle. Bone injuries are fractures, where the bone itself cracks or breaks. Both can swell and hurt, so an X-ray is often used to tell them apart.

reason: A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage; the other four have skeletons made of bone.
explain: Most animals with a backbone have skeletons made of hard bone. Sharks and rays are different: their skeletons are made of cartilage, the same firm, bendy tissue found in your nose and ears. Cartilage is lighter than bone, which helps sharks stay up in the water.
fact: Sharks' teeth are not part of their cartilage skeleton; they are constantly replaced, and one shark can lose thousands in its life.

reason: An owl has 14 neck bones; the four mammals each have 7.
explain: Almost all mammals, from mice to giraffes, have exactly seven vertebrae in the neck. A giraffe's neck is long because each vertebra is very long, not because it has more of them. Birds are different: an owl has 14 neck vertebrae, which lets it turn its head much further around than you can.
fact: An owl can turn its head about 270 degrees, three-quarters of a full circle.

notes: Minerals build up over the years
Babies' bones fuse; count falls to 206
Happens at the end of puberty
reason: As you grow, cartilage turns into bone, not the other way round; the other four do happen.
explain: A baby's skeleton has a lot of cartilage, which slowly turns into hard bone as calcium and other minerals are added. Long bones grow at growth plates, bands of cartilage near their ends. At the end of puberty these plates harden into bone and growth in height stops. Some separate bones also join together, which is why adults have fewer bones than babies.
fact: Doctors can estimate a child's age from an X-ray of the hand by looking at how far the growth plates have closed.

notes: Mostly yellow, fatty marrow in adults
reason: In adults the middle of long bones like the shin holds mainly fatty yellow marrow; the other four still have red marrow that makes blood cells.
explain: Bone marrow comes in two kinds. Red marrow makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Yellow marrow is mostly fat. In babies almost all marrow is red, but by adulthood the middle of long bones like the shin turns yellow, and blood cells are made mainly in the hip bones, breastbone, ribs, vertebrae and skull.
fact: When doctors need a sample of marrow from an adult, they usually take it from the hip bone.

clues: Its name means 'three heads', because it starts from three places.
It does much of the work as you rise from the bottom of a push-up.
It sits on the rear of your upper limb and opens your elbow out flat.
explain: The triceps is the large muscle at the back of the upper arm. When it contracts, it pulls on the forearm and straightens the elbow. It works as a pair with the biceps at the front, which bends the elbow. Push-ups and throwing a ball both use the triceps.

clues: Your fingers have several of these, which let them curl up into a fist.
It moves in only one direction and back, like the lid of a box.
The joint in the middle of your leg is the biggest one of this kind.
explain: A hinge joint lets bones move in one plane only, back and forth, like a door on its hinges. The elbow, knee and the joints in your fingers and toes are hinge joints. A ball-and-socket joint, like the shoulder, can move in many directions.

clues: In women it is wider, which helps when a baby is born.
The tops of your thighs fit into it at two deep sockets.
This strong ring at the bottom of your belly holds up your gut and bladder.
explain: The pelvis is a ring of bones at the base of the spine, sometimes called the hip girdle. It carries the weight of the upper body to the legs, gives strong muscles a place to attach, and protects organs like the bladder. The thigh bones fit into its two cup-shaped sockets to form the hip joints.

clues: Doctors check it by looking at how your body lines up from head to toe.
Slumping over a phone for hours is bad for it.
Your teacher reminds you about it when you slouch in your chair.
explain: Posture is the way you hold your body when sitting, standing or moving. Good posture keeps the spine in its natural curves, so muscles and joints are not strained. Slouching for long periods can lead to neck and back aches. Taking breaks and keeping screens at eye level help.

clues: They usually come in a pair and are often made of light metal.
They let someone keep weight off an injured foot while it heals.
A person with a cast on their ankle swings along using one under each shoulder.
explain: Crutches are a pair of sticks that take the body's weight through the arms and hands, so an injured leg or foot can rest while it heals. The padded tops should sit a little below the armpits, and most of the weight goes through the hands. A doctor or physiotherapist shows how to use them safely.

clues: It is one of the most commonly broken bones when people fall on an outstretched hand.
It is long, thin and slightly S-shaped, and you can feel it just under the skin.
It runs sideways across the top of your body, from your breastbone towards your upper arm.
explain: The collarbone, or clavicle, is a long, thin bone that runs from the breastbone to the shoulder blade. It works like a strut that holds the shoulder out to the side, so your arm can swing freely. Because it is thin and near the surface, it often breaks in falls, and usually heals well with a sling.

clues: It keeps an injured limb still and close to the body so it can heal.
It is often a large triangle of fabric tied in a knot.
People with a broken wrist or collarbone often wear one around their shoulders.
explain: A sling is a support, often a triangle of fabric, that holds an injured arm against the body. It keeps the arm still and takes its weight off the injured part, which eases pain and helps healing. Slings are used for broken wrists, collarbones and some shoulder injuries.

clues: Many muscles that move the upper limb attach to this large, triangle-shaped bone.
It glides over your ribs when you swing your arms in circles.
You have two of these on the rear of your upper body, and they stick out a little when you reach behind you.
explain: The shoulder blade, or scapula, is a large triangular bone at the upper back. It is not fixed to the ribs but held in place by muscles, so it can slide around and let the arm move freely. Its shallow socket holds the top of the upper arm bone to form the shoulder joint.

clues: Sprinters sometimes pull this when running very fast.
It runs from the bones you sit on down to the top of the lower leg.
It is a group of three that pulls your heel up towards your bottom.
explain: The hamstrings are a group of three muscles at the back of the thigh. They bend the knee and help straighten the hip when you run or climb. They work as a pair with the quadriceps at the front. Warming up and gentle stretching help lower the chance of a pulled hamstring.

clues: It is the second-longest bone in the body.
Below the thigh, it carries most of your weight, while its thin partner carries much less.
You can feel its sharp front edge just under the skin, where footballers wear guards.
explain: The tibia, or shin bone, is the larger of the two bones in the lower leg and carries most of the body's weight. It runs from the knee to the ankle. Its thin partner, the fibula, sits beside it and mainly gives muscles a place to attach. Only the femur, the thigh bone, is longer.

clues: It is shaped a bit like a short sword, with a small tip at the bottom.
Trained first-aiders press on the lower half of it during CPR.
It sits in the middle of the front of your upper body, joining the curved bones that guard your heart and lungs.
explain: The sternum, or breastbone, is a long bone in the middle of the front of the chest. Most ribs join it through strips of cartilage, which let the rib cage move as you breathe. Together with the ribs, it protects the heart and lungs. Its three parts together look a little like a sword.

clues: In a newborn baby's head, these are still soft gaps that slowly close up.
The bones of your braincase meet at wavy lines of this kind.
This type of joint allows no motion at all.
explain: A fixed joint is where bones meet but cannot move. The bones of the skull fit together at wavy seams called sutures, which lock them tightly to protect the brain. In babies these gaps are still soft, which lets the head change shape a little at birth and grow fast in the first years.

clues: Its rounded top fits a shallow socket to form a ball-and-socket joint.
It is the single long bone above your forearm.
Its name sounds like 'humorous', which is the joke behind the tingle you feel when you knock a nerve near its lower end.
explain: The humerus is the bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder to the elbow. Its rounded top forms the shoulder joint, and its lower end forms the elbow with the radius and ulna. The 'funny bone' is not a bone at all: it is a nerve that runs over the lower end of the humerus, and knocking it makes your arm tingle.

clues: It is made by a thin lining inside the capsule that wraps around movable bone ends.
Like grease in a bicycle chain, it stops surfaces from rubbing and wearing out.
This thick liquid fills the space inside your knee and elbow so they glide smoothly.
explain: Synovial fluid is a thick, clear liquid inside movable joints such as the knee, elbow and shoulder. It is made by the joint's inner lining, and it reduces rubbing between the cartilage-covered bone ends. It also carries nutrients to the cartilage, which has no blood vessels of its own.

clues: Your thumb has two of these, but each of your other digits has three.
Altogether you have 56 of them across your four limbs.
They are the small bones in the digits you use to type, point and wiggle.
explain: Phalanges are the bones of the fingers and toes. Each finger has three, and each thumb and big toe has two, so each hand or foot has 14. Many small bones joined by hinge joints let fingers grip, write and play music. One of these bones is called a phalanx.

clues: Footballers can tear it when they twist on a bent leg with the foot planted.
It is a C-shaped pad, and you have two of them in each of your largest joints.
It sits between the thigh bone and shin bone, soaking up the jolts when you jump.
explain: A meniscus is a C-shaped pad of tough cartilage inside the knee. Each knee has two, one on the inner side and one on the outer side. They spread out the body's weight and absorb the jolt when you land from a jump. A sudden twist with the foot fixed on the ground can tear one, and an MRI scan can show the tear.

clues: Under a microscope, its long fibres show light and dark bands.
It is joined to your skeleton by tendons and pulls on it to move you.
This is the muscle type you control when you choose to wave, kick or smile.
explain: Your body has three types of muscle. Skeletal muscle is attached to bones and moves them when you decide to, so it is called voluntary. Smooth muscle in the walls of the gut and blood vessels, and cardiac muscle in the heart, work without you thinking. Skeletal muscle fibres look striped under a microscope.

scenario: Before a football match, the coach has the team jog slowly and do gentle stretches for ten minutes. Why?
options: It warms muscles and lowers injury risk
answer: It warms muscles and lowers injury risk
optionNotes: A warm-up is light, not tiring
Warm muscles stretch and contract better
explain: A warm-up raises the temperature of your muscles and gets more blood flowing to them. Warm muscles are more flexible and less likely to tear when you suddenly sprint or kick. A short cool-down after exercise, with gentle stretches, helps the body settle back to rest.

scenario: When a boy lifts a heavy bag by bending his elbow, a muscle on the front of his upper arm gets hard and bulges. Which muscle is it?
optionNotes: Front of the upper arm; bends elbow
Back of the upper arm; straightens elbow
explain: When a muscle contracts, it gets shorter and fatter, which is why the biceps bulges when you bend your elbow. The biceps is attached by tendons to the shoulder and the forearm. As it shortens, it pulls the forearm up. The triceps at the back does the opposite job.

scenario: The day after his first long hike, a boy's legs feel sore and stiff. Nothing is swollen and he can walk normally. What will help most?
options: A hard cast on both legs
optionNotes: Muscles need time to recover first
explain: Muscles worked harder than usual often feel sore a day or two later. The soreness comes from tiny strains in the muscle fibres, which repair and grow stronger with rest. Gentle movement, stretching and drinking water help. If pain is severe, there is swelling, or it does not ease, tell an adult and see a doctor.

scenario: When you shake your head to say 'no', the top bone of your spine turns around a small peg on the bone below. What kind of joint is this?
optionNotes: Bends one way, like the elbow
Does not move, like skull bones
Moves in many directions, like the hip
explain: In a pivot joint, one bone turns around another like a wheel around an axle. The top two bones of your neck form a pivot joint that lets your head turn from side to side. Another pivot joint near the elbow lets you turn your palm up and down.

scenario: On a cold winter morning, a girl starts to shiver and her teeth chatter. What are her muscles doing?
optionNotes: Shivering is muscles working, not resting
Muscle does not change into fat
explain: Working muscles release heat as well as making movement. When your body gets cold, your brain makes muscles tighten and relax many times a second. This shivering produces heat to warm you up. It is also why you feel warm after running.

scenario: A child counts the ribs on a model skeleton in the doctor's room. How many pairs of ribs does a human normally have?
optionNotes: 24 ribs in all, 12 on each side
explain: Most people have 12 pairs of ribs, 24 in total, joined at the back to the spine. The top seven pairs join the breastbone at the front through cartilage. The lowest two pairs are called 'floating ribs' because they do not reach the front. Together the ribs form a cage that protects the heart and lungs.

scenario: A boy needs to lift a heavy box of books from the floor. What is the safest way to lift it?
options: Bend at the waist, legs straight
Jerk it up with one hand
optionNotes: Twisting under load hurts the spine
Strong leg muscles do the work
explain: Your leg muscles are much stronger than the muscles of your lower back. Bending your knees, keeping your back straight and holding the load close lets the legs do the lifting and protects the spine. If a box is too heavy, ask an adult to help or carry it together.

scenario: A newborn baby has about 300 bones and cartilage pieces, but an adult has 206 bones. What happens to the rest?
options: Some join together as the child grows
They fall out like baby teeth
answer: Some join together as the child grows
optionNotes: Bones are not lost this way
Separate parts fuse into single bones
explain: Many bones start out as several separate pieces of bone and cartilage. As a child grows, these pieces join, or fuse, into single bones. For example, the skull bones lock together and five spine bones at the base fuse into one bone called the sacrum. That is why adults have fewer, larger bones.

scenario: When a footballer kicks a ball, a large group of muscles on the front of the thigh straightens the knee. Which group is it?
optionNotes: Back of the thigh; bends the knee
explain: The quadriceps is a group of four muscles on the front of the thigh. Their tendon passes over the kneecap and attaches to the shin bone, so when they contract they straighten the knee. The hamstrings at the back of the thigh bend the knee, so the two groups work as a pair.

scenario: A doctor shows a student the small rounded bone at the front of the knee. What is one of its jobs?
options: Protects the front of the knee
Lets the knee twist all the way round
Joins the thigh to the hip
answer: Protects the front of the knee
optionNotes: A bony shield over the joint
The knee is a hinge; it cannot spin
explain: The kneecap, or patella, sits inside the tendon of the quadriceps muscle at the front of the knee. It shields the joint from knocks and works like a pulley, helping the thigh muscles straighten the leg with less effort. Babies are born with a kneecap made of cartilage that slowly turns to bone.

scenario: After six weeks in a cast, a girl's broken arm has healed, but the arm looks thinner and feels weak. Why?
options: The cast removed her bone marrow
Her arm has stopped growing for good
optionNotes: The bone has healed, not vanished
A cast does not affect marrow
Muscles kept still lose size and strength
explain: Muscles stay strong only when they are used. When an arm is kept still in a cast, its muscles get smaller and weaker. After the cast comes off, a physiotherapist gives exercises that slowly rebuild strength and movement, and the arm usually returns to normal within weeks.

scenario: A man lifts a heavy load badly. A soft pad between two bones in his lower spine bulges out and presses on a nerve, sending pain down his leg. Which part has bulged?
optionNotes: Part of the hip joint, not the spine
In the leg, not the spine
At the front of the knee
explain: Between the vertebrae of your spine are discs, flat cushions with a tough outer ring and a softer centre. They absorb jolts and let the spine bend. If a disc bulges, it can press on a nearby nerve, causing pain that travels along that nerve into the leg. This is often called a 'slipped disc', though the disc does not actually slip.

scenario: Astronauts who spend months floating in space, with no weight pressing on their bodies, come back with weaker bones. Why?
options: Bones that carry no weight lose minerals
answer: Bones that carry no weight lose minerals
explain: Bone keeps rebuilding itself, and it builds itself strong where it carries weight and takes impact. In space, the legs, hips and spine carry almost no weight, so the body removes minerals from them and they become weaker. Astronauts exercise about two hours a day to slow this. On Earth, running, jumping and skipping help keep bones strong.

scenario: Your intestines squeeze food along all day and night without you thinking about it. Which type of muscle in their walls does this?
optionNotes: Works by itself in organ walls
Joins muscle to bone; not a muscle
explain: Smooth muscle is found in the walls of hollow organs like the stomach, intestines, bladder and blood vessels. It contracts slowly and steadily without you deciding to, which is why it is called involuntary. In the gut, waves of smooth muscle squeezing push food along.

scenario: Two weeks after a fracture, an X-ray shows a soft lump of new tissue bridging the broken ends. Over the next weeks it hardens into bone. What is this lump called?
optionNotes: Joins bone to bone at joints
New tissue that joins broken bone
explain: After a bone breaks, a blood clot forms around the break. Bone cells then build a soft bridge of new tissue, called a callus, between the broken ends. Over several weeks minerals harden the callus into bone, and over the following months the bone is reshaped to its normal form. A cast keeps the ends lined up while this happens.

scenario: Unlike your other fingers, your thumb can swing across your palm to touch each fingertip. Which type of joint at the base of the thumb, near the wrist, makes this possible?
optionNotes: Two curved surfaces; moves two ways
Allows turning, as in the neck
explain: At the base of the thumb, two bones meet with curved surfaces shaped like a rider sitting in a saddle. This saddle joint lets the thumb move forward and back as well as side to side, so it can touch each fingertip. This ability, called opposition, lets humans grip a pencil or pick up small objects.

reason: A fingernail is made of keratin; the other four contain cartilage.
explain: Cartilage is a firm but bendy tissue. It shapes the tip of your nose and your outer ear, cushions the spaces between the bones of your spine, and covers the ends of bones in joints so they slide smoothly. Fingernails are made of keratin, the same tough protein found in hair.
fact: Before birth, much of the skeleton is cartilage, which slowly turns into bone through childhood.

reason: The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint; the other four are hinge joints.
explain: A hinge joint works like a door hinge: it lets a body part bend and straighten in one direction. Your elbow, knee, fingers and toes all bend this way. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, where the round top of the arm bone sits in a cup, so the arm can swing in a full circle.

notes: You choose when to bend the arm
Works on its own, never rests
You choose when to straighten the arm
You choose when to stand on tiptoe
reason: Heart muscle is involuntary; the others are skeletal muscles you control.
explain: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones and move when you decide to move, so they are called voluntary muscles. Heart muscle, also called cardiac muscle, contracts by itself about 70 times a minute without you thinking about it. It is an involuntary muscle and is found only in the heart.

notes: Protects the bladder and lower organs
reason: Toe bones help you walk and balance; the others mainly protect soft organs.
explain: One big job of the skeleton is protection. The skull is a hard helmet for the brain, the rib cage guards the heart and lungs, the backbone surrounds the spinal cord, and the pelvis shields organs low in the belly. Toe bones are mainly for balance and pushing off when you walk or run.

notes: Pressure on bones makes them stronger
Skin makes vitamin D in sunlight
reason: Lying still all day weakens bones; the other four help build strong bones.
explain: Bone is living tissue that keeps rebuilding itself. It needs calcium to stay hard and vitamin D to absorb that calcium, and your skin makes vitamin D in sunlight. Bones also get stronger when they carry your weight during running, jumping and skipping. When bones are not used, for example in long bed rest, they slowly lose calcium and weaken.
fact: Astronauts in space can lose bone strength because their bones do not carry body weight in low gravity.

notes: Forms the bump below the eye
Bridge at the top of the nose
reason: The clavicle is the collarbone; the other four are skull bones.
explain: The skull is made of many bones. The cranium forms a dome around the brain, and the face bones include the cheekbones, nasal bones and the mandible, or lower jaw. The mandible is the only skull bone that moves freely, which is how you chew and talk. The clavicle, or collarbone, connects the shoulder to the breastbone.

reason: Enamel coats teeth; the other four are parts of a movable joint.
explain: A movable joint such as the knee has several parts. Smooth cartilage covers the bone ends, a tough capsule wraps around the joint, and synovial fluid inside works like oil so the bones glide. Ligaments hold the bones together. Enamel is the hard coating on the outside of teeth.

notes: Skeletal muscle that bends the elbow
Smooth muscle narrows or widens the vessel
reason: The biceps is skeletal (voluntary) muscle; the others are smooth (involuntary) muscle.
explain: Smooth muscle lines hollow organs like the stomach, intestines, bladder and blood vessels. It contracts slowly and on its own, without you deciding to. The biceps is skeletal muscle: it is attached to bones by tendons and moves only when your brain tells it to. Under a microscope, skeletal muscle looks striped and smooth muscle does not.

notes: Fixed joints that do not move
reason: Skull sutures are fixed joints; the others are movable joints.
explain: A joint is any place where two bones meet, but not every joint moves. In the skull, the bones are locked together along wavy lines called sutures, making a strong case for the brain. In a newborn baby these joints are still soft and slightly open, which lets the skull grow along with the brain.
fact: The soft spot on a baby's head is a gap between skull bones that closes by about age two.

notes: Fused bones at the base of the spine
Breastbone in the front of the chest
reason: The sternum is the breastbone; the other four are parts of the spine.
explain: The spine is a column of small bones called vertebrae stacked on top of each other. It has regions: cervical in the neck, thoracic in the upper back where the ribs attach, lumbar in the lower back, and the sacrum at the base. The sternum, or breastbone, is a flat bone at the front of the chest where most ribs join.
fact: Humans and giraffes both have seven neck vertebrae; a giraffe's are just much longer.

notes: Small bone in front of the knee
Bone that holds the lower teeth
reason: The tongue is a muscle; the other four are bones.
explain: Bones are hard because they contain calcium and other minerals. The skull, ribs, kneecap and jawbone are all bones. The tongue has no bone in it at all: it is made of several muscles working together, which is why it can change shape to help you talk, chew and swallow.

notes: Bone pushed out of its joint
Hole in a tooth from decay
reason: A tooth cavity comes from decay; the others are injuries to bones, joints or muscles.
explain: Injuries to the moving parts of the body have different names. A fracture is a broken bone, a sprain is a stretched or torn ligament, a strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon, and a dislocation is when a bone slips out of its joint. A cavity is a hole in a tooth caused by decay from germs and sugar, not by an injury.

reason: The fibula is in the leg; the other four are arm and wrist bones.
explain: Your arm has one bone above the elbow, the humerus, and two below it, the radius and the ulna. The wrist has eight small carpal bones. The leg follows a similar plan: one thigh bone (the femur) and two lower leg bones, the tibia and the thinner fibula.

notes: Bones are the body's calcium bank
Done by the stomach and intestines
reason: Digesting food is not a job of bones; the other four are.
explain: Bones do much more than hold you up. They protect soft organs, give muscles something to pull on, store calcium for the rest of the body, and the soft red marrow inside many bones makes blood cells. Digestion is done by the stomach, intestines and other digestive organs.

notes: Muscle at the front of the upper arm
Muscle at the back of the upper arm
Muscle at the back of the lower leg
Muscle at the front of the thigh
reason: The thigh bone is a bone; the other four are muscles.
explain: Muscles and bones work as a team. Bones form a firm frame, and muscles attached to them by tendons pull on them to make movement. The thigh bone, or femur, is the longest and strongest bone in your body. The muscle on top of it, the quadriceps, straightens your knee when you kick.

reason: Slouching is poor posture; the other four are good posture habits.
explain: Posture is the way you hold your body when you sit, stand or move. Good posture keeps the spine in its natural curves, so muscles and joints are not overworked. Bending the head forward over a phone makes the neck muscles hold up much more strain than usual, which can cause neck and back aches.

notes: Long bone of the upper arm
reason: The scapula is a flat bone; the other four are long bones.
explain: Bones are grouped by shape. Long bones, like the femur, humerus, tibia and radius, are longer than they are wide and act as levers for movement. Flat bones, like the scapula (shoulder blade), skull bones and ribs, are thin and wide, which gives large areas for muscles to attach and protects what lies beneath.

clues: Insects wear theirs on the outside, but yours is on the inside.
It holds you up, protects your organs and gives muscles something to pull on.
In a science lab, a plastic model of this often hangs from a stand.
explain: The skeleton is the full set of bones that supports the body. An adult human skeleton has 206 bones. It holds the body up, protects organs like the brain and heart, and works with muscles to make movement possible. Insects and crabs have an outer skeleton called an exoskeleton instead.

clues: In a newborn baby it has soft spots that close up over time.
Its lower jaw is the only part of it that moves freely.
It is the hard helmet built into you that keeps your thinking organ safe.
explain: The skull is the bony case that protects the brain and gives the face its shape. It is made of about 22 bones. Most of them are locked together by fixed joints called sutures; only the lower jaw moves freely so you can chew and talk.

clues: It rises and falls a little every time you take a breath.
It is made of 12 pairs of curved bones joined to the spine at the back.
This bony shield around your upper body guards the organs that pump blood and breathe air.
explain: The rib cage is made of 12 pairs of ribs, the breastbone in front and the spine at the back. It protects the heart and lungs. It is also flexible: muscles between the ribs lift the cage when you breathe in, making more room for air.

clues: Fish, birds and mammals all have one, but jellyfish and worms do not.
It is made of 33 small bones stacked like a tower, some of them joined together.
The bundle of nerves from your brain runs down through the middle of it, from neck to hips.
explain: The spine is a column of small bones called vertebrae, stacked one on top of another with cushions of cartilage between them. It holds the body upright but can still bend and twist. A tunnel through the vertebrae protects the spinal cord, the bundle of nerves that carries messages between the brain and the body.

clues: Its name means 'two heads' because it is attached at the top in two places.
Its partner on the opposite side is the triceps.
When you lift a heavy bag and show off, this bulges at the front of your upper limb.
explain: The biceps is a skeletal muscle at the front of the upper arm. When it contracts it gets shorter and fatter, pulling the forearm up and bending the elbow. Muscles can only pull, never push, so the triceps on the back of the arm pulls the other way to straighten it.

clues: A doctor usually confirms it with an X-ray picture.
The injured part is kept still in a splint or plaster until it heals.
It is the medical word for when a hard part of your skeleton snaps.
explain: A fracture is a break or crack in a bone. Bone is living tissue, so it can heal: bone cells build new bone across the break over several weeks. Keeping the bone still with a cast or splint lets the two ends join in the right position.

clues: Babies are born with this as soft cartilage that hardens into bone later.
It sits inside a tendon at the front of your thigh muscle.
This small bone shields the front of the place where your thigh meets your shin.
explain: The kneecap, or patella, is a small triangle-shaped bone at the front of the knee. It sits inside the tendon of the thigh muscle and helps that muscle straighten the leg with less effort. It also shields the front of the knee joint from knocks.

clues: Your shoulder has a ball-and-socket type of this.
Some, like those in the skull, do not move at all.
It is any place where two bones meet.
explain: A joint is a place where two or more bones meet. Some joints are fixed, like those in the skull. Others move freely: hinge joints in the elbow and knee bend one way, while ball-and-socket joints in the shoulder and hip let a limb swing in a circle.

clues: You can feel one as a hard cord at the back of your ankle, above the heel.
It is a tough, rope-like band that does not stretch much.
When the meat of your arm or leg pulls, this cord passes the pull on to the skeleton.
explain: A tendon is a strong cord that connects a muscle to a bone. When a muscle contracts, it pulls on the tendon, and the tendon pulls the bone, so the body part moves. A ligament looks similar but connects bone to bone instead.

clues: Footballers sometimes tear the ACL, a famous one inside the knee.
It is a tough, slightly stretchy band.
It holds the skeleton's pieces together where they meet, so they do not slip apart.
explain: A ligament is a strong band of tissue that connects one bone to another at a joint. Ligaments keep joints stable while still letting them move. If a ligament is stretched too far or torn, for example by twisting an ankle, the injury is called a sprain.

clues: Sharks have a skeleton made entirely of it.
It covers the ends of bones so they slide smoothly in a joint.
This firm but flexible tissue shapes the tip of your smelling organ.
explain: Cartilage is a smooth, firm and flexible tissue. It covers the ends of bones in joints so they move without grinding, cushions the spine, and shapes the nose and ears. It has no blood vessels, so it heals much more slowly than bone.
fact: Sharks and rays have no bones; their whole skeleton is cartilage.

clues: It is often treated with rest, a wrapped ice pack and keeping the injured part raised.
It is not a break, but it can hurt just as much.
It happens when the bands holding a joint together are stretched too far or torn.
explain: A sprain is an injury to a ligament, the band that holds bones together at a joint. It usually happens when a joint is bent or twisted too far, often the ankle or wrist. Rest, an ice pack wrapped in cloth, gentle support and raising the limb help the swelling go down. A doctor may take an X-ray to check that no bone is broken.

clues: In adults, much of the active kind is found in flat bones like the hip and breastbone.
It comes in a red type and a yellow, fatty type.
This tissue in the hollow middle of bones makes red cells, white cells and platelets.
explain: Bone marrow is the soft tissue that fills the spaces inside many bones. Red marrow makes all the body's blood cells: red cells, white cells and platelets. Yellow marrow is mostly fat. Children have lots of red marrow, and in adults much of it is replaced by yellow marrow, except in bones like the hip, ribs and breastbone.

clues: Swimmers and runners sometimes get one in the calf after hard exercise.
It usually goes away within a few minutes.
It is a sudden, tight squeeze in part of your body that you cannot relax on purpose.
explain: A cramp is when a muscle suddenly tightens and will not relax for a while. It is common in the calf and can happen after hard exercise or tiredness. Gently stretching and rubbing the muscle usually eases it within minutes. Drinking enough water during sport may help prevent cramps.

clues: Its top is a ball that fits into a socket in the pelvis.
Its lower end forms the upper half of the knee.
It is the biggest and strongest bone in your skeleton, above the knee.
explain: The femur is the thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body. Its rounded top fits into the hip socket to form a ball-and-socket joint, and its lower end forms part of the knee. Its length is roughly a quarter of a person's height.

clues: A special scan that measures bone density helps doctors find it.
Its name means 'porous bone', because the inside of the bone becomes full of larger holes.
It makes bones thin and easy to break, and is most common in grandparents.
explain: Osteoporosis is a condition in which bones lose minerals and become thin and fragile, so they break more easily. It is most common in older adults. Building strong bones in childhood, with calcium, vitamin D and active play, lowers the chance of getting it later in life.

clues: It allows the widest range of movement of any kind of connection between bones.
Your arm can swing in a full circle because of one.
The knob-like end of one bone sits in a hollow of another.
explain: In a ball-and-socket joint, the rounded end of one bone fits into a hollow in another. This lets the limb move forwards, backwards, sideways and in circles. The shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints. The shoulder moves more freely, while the hip has a deeper socket that makes it more stable.

scenario: A boy fell off his bicycle. His wrist is swollen and very painful to move. Which test will show whether a bone is broken?
explain: X-rays pass easily through soft parts like skin and muscle but are blocked by hard bone. So on an X-ray picture, bones show up white and any break appears as a dark line or gap. This helps the doctor decide whether the arm needs a cast.

scenario: During a game, a girl twists her ankle. It is swollen and sore, but she can stand a little. What is the best first thing to do?
options: Rest it, hold an ice pack wrapped in cloth on it, and tell an adult
Keep playing to loosen it up
Put ice straight on bare skin for an hour
answer: Rest it, hold an ice pack wrapped in cloth on it, and tell an adult
explain: A twisted ankle is often a sprain, where the ligaments are stretched or torn. Resting stops further damage, and a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for about 15–20 minutes reduces swelling. Raising the foot also helps. An adult should decide whether a doctor needs to check for a broken bone.

scenario: A child falls from a climbing frame. His forearm looks bent in an odd shape and hurts badly. What should the people around him do first?
options: Ask him to move his fingers fast
Lift him and carry him home quickly
Keep the arm still and supported, and get adult help
answer: Keep the arm still and supported, and get adult help
optionNotes: Can damage nerves and blood vessels
Moving him can worsen the injury
Stops further damage until medical help comes
explain: An arm that looks bent the wrong way may be broken. Moving the broken ends can hurt nearby nerves and blood vessels, so the arm should be kept still and supported, for example with a cushion or folded cloth. An adult should call for medical help. Only a doctor should straighten, or 'set', a broken bone.

scenario: A doctor tells a child that milk, curd, ragi and leafy greens help build hard, strong bones. Which mineral do these foods provide?
optionNotes: Main mineral that makes bones hard
explain: About 99% of the body's calcium is stored in bones and teeth, and it is what makes them hard. Childhood and the teenage years are when bones grow fastest and store the most calcium. Calcium-rich foods, vitamin D from sunlight, and active play together build bones that stay strong in adult life.
fact: Ragi (finger millet) has more calcium than most other grains.

scenario: A student spends hours bending his head down over his phone. Now his neck and upper back often ache. Which change will help most?
options: Lie on the stomach while using the phone
Hold the screen up near eye level and take regular breaks
Bend the head down even further
answer: Hold the screen up near eye level and take regular breaks
optionNotes: Keeps the neck straight and relaxed
Adds more strain to the neck
explain: The head is heavy, and when it tips forward the neck muscles must work much harder to hold it up. Over hours, this strain causes aches. Keeping the screen near eye level keeps the spine in a natural line, and short breaks let the muscles rest and move.

scenario: A child asks the doctor how many bones are in a grown-up's skeleton. What is the correct answer?
explain: A typical adult skeleton has 206 bones. A newborn baby has around 300 bones and bony pieces, many of them partly cartilage. As a child grows, some of these fuse together, such as those in the skull and at the base of the spine, which brings the number down to 206.
fact: More than half of your bones are in your hands and feet.

scenario: A girl's broken forearm is set and wrapped in a hard cast for six weeks. Why does it need a cast?
options: It keeps the bone still so new bone can join the ends correctly
The cast feeds calcium into the bone
The cast keeps germs out of the bone
The cast makes the bone grow longer
answer: It keeps the bone still so new bone can join the ends correctly
optionNotes: Healing needs the ends kept in place
Calcium comes from food, not the cast
Casts do not change bone length
explain: Bone is living tissue that can repair itself. After a break, a soft bridge forms between the broken ends and slowly hardens into new bone over several weeks. If the bone keeps moving, it can heal crooked or slowly, so a cast holds it in the right position while it mends.

scenario: While sprinting, a runner feels a sudden snap at the back of his lower leg, just above the heel. Now he cannot rise onto his toes. Which part is most likely injured?
optionNotes: Links calf muscle to heel bone
explain: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body. It connects the calf muscles to the heel bone, so when the calf contracts, the heel lifts and you rise onto your toes. If this tendon tears, the calf can no longer pull the heel, so standing on tiptoe becomes impossible on that side.

scenario: A grandmother's knees have become painful and stiff over many years. An X-ray shows the gap between her bones has narrowed because the smooth cushion on the bone ends has worn thin. What is this condition called?
optionNotes: Bone pushed out of its joint
explain: Arthritis means swelling and pain in a joint. In the most common kind, osteoarthritis, the cartilage that covers the ends of bones wears thin over many years. Without that smooth cushion, the joint becomes stiff and painful. Gentle exercise, keeping a healthy weight and treatment from a doctor help people manage it.

scenario: A player falls on his outstretched arm. The round top of his upper arm bone has slipped completely out of its shoulder socket. What is this injury called?
optionNotes: Bone pushed out of its joint
explain: A dislocation happens when the bones of a joint are forced out of their normal position. The shoulder dislocates more often than any other large joint because its shallow socket lets it move so freely. A doctor must put the bone back in place, and the arm is then rested in a sling.

scenario: An X-ray of a seven-year-old's forearm shows the bone has bent and cracked on one side only, like a fresh green twig. What type of injury is this?
optionNotes: Partial break in a bendy young bone
explain: Children's bones are softer and more flexible than adults' because they contain more collagen and are still growing. Instead of snapping straight through, a child's bone may bend and crack on one side, like a green twig. This is called a greenstick fracture. It still needs a doctor and usually a cast.

scenario: After an injury, a patient can bend his elbow normally but cannot straighten it against any resistance. Which muscle is most likely not working?
explain: Muscles can only pull, not push, so they work in opposite pairs. The biceps on the front of the upper arm bends the elbow, and the triceps on the back straightens it. If the triceps is not working, the arm can still bend but cannot push or straighten with force.

scenario: A footballer's X-ray shows no broken bones, but the doctor suspects a torn ligament inside his knee. Which scan shows soft tissues like ligaments most clearly?
optionNotes: Good for bones, poor for soft tissue
explain: X-rays show hard bone well but show soft tissues like ligaments, tendons and cartilage poorly. An MRI scan uses a strong magnet and radio waves to make detailed pictures of soft tissues. It does not use X-rays. The patient lies still inside a tunnel-shaped machine while the pictures are taken.

scenario: During a long swim, a boy suddenly feels his calf muscle go tight and hard. He cannot relax it. What should he do first?
options: Get to the side safely, then gently stretch and rub the calf
Swim faster to work it out
answer: Get to the side safely, then gently stretch and rub the calf
optionNotes: Can make it worse and is unsafe
explain: This is a muscle cramp: a sudden, strong tightening that the swimmer cannot relax on purpose. The first step is to get somewhere safe out of deep water. Gently stretching the calf, by pulling the toes towards the shin, and rubbing it usually makes the cramp ease within minutes.

scenario: During a school check-up, a doctor asks a girl to bend forward. One shoulder blade sticks out more, and an X-ray shows her spine curves sideways like an 'S'. What is this condition?
explain: Seen from behind, a healthy spine runs straight down the back. In scoliosis, it curves to one side, often in an S or C shape. It often shows up during the growth spurt around the start of the teenage years. Many cases are mild and only need check-ups, while others are treated with a brace or, rarely, an operation.

scenario: A basketball player twisted her knee and tore a ligament inside it. Her knee now feels wobbly. What is the normal job of a ligament?
options: To carry messages to the brain
To join bone to bone and keep the joint steady
answer: To join bone to bone and keep the joint steady
explain: Ligaments are strong bands that connect bones to other bones at a joint. They let the joint move in the right directions but stop it moving too far. When a ligament inside the knee tears, the bones are not held firmly in place, so the knee feels loose or gives way.

notes: Hypothalamus helps run the body clock
reason: Reading a map is a cerebrum job; the hypothalamus controls the other four.
explain: The hypothalamus is a small area deep in the middle of the brain. It keeps your inner body steady: it senses when you are too hot or cold, and it makes you feel hungry or thirsty when you need food or water. It also helps set your daily sleep-wake rhythm. Reading a map needs thinking and planning, which is done by the cerebrum.
fact: The hypothalamus is only about the size of an almond.

notes: Tests muscle strength from motor nerves
Needs a blood test, not a nerve check
reason: Blood group is found with a blood test; the other four are nerve checks a neurologist does.
explain: A neurologist checks how well the brain, spinal cord and nerves are working, often with simple tests in the clinic. Tapping the knee checks a reflex, walking heel-to-toe checks balance, squeezing fingers checks the nerves that work muscles, and a light touch checks the nerves that carry feeling. Your blood group is about proteins on red blood cells and needs a sample of blood sent to a lab.

notes: Carries sight from eye to brain
Runs from the lower back down the leg
Carries smell from nose to brain
Carries hearing from ear to brain
reason: The sciatic nerve comes from the spinal cord; the other four come straight from the brain.
explain: Most nerves branch out of the spinal cord, but 12 pairs, called cranial nerves, connect directly to the brain. They mainly serve the head and face: seeing, smelling, hearing and moving your face. The sciatic nerve leaves the lower part of the spinal cord and travels down the back of each leg.
fact: The sciatic nerve is the longest and thickest nerve in the body.

notes: Lets the brain sort and store memories
Sends more blood and oxygen to the brain
Robs the brain of rest it needs
reason: Gaming all night harms the brain; the other four keep it healthy.
explain: Your brain stays healthy when you look after the whole body. Sleep lets it store what you learned, exercise pumps more blood and oxygen to it, and learning new things builds fresh connections between nerve cells. Good food gives it steady fuel. Staying up all night leaves you forgetful, slow and grumpy the next day.

reason: An ECG checks the heart; the other four can check the brain or nerves.
explain: Doctors have several ways to check the nervous system. An EEG records the electrical activity of the brain, MRI and CT scans take pictures of the brain, and a reflex test checks if a nerve pathway works. An ECG also records electricity, but from the heart, to check that it is beating in a healthy rhythm.

notes: One arm drifts down when lifted
Usually a sign of a cold
reason: A runny nose is a cold sign; the other four are sudden warning signs of a stroke.
explain: A stroke happens when blood stops flowing to part of the brain, so brain cells there stop getting oxygen. Warning signs come on suddenly: one side of the face droops, one arm goes weak, speech is slurred, or sight suddenly blurs. The FAST rule reminds people to check Face, Arms and Speech, and that it is Time to call an ambulance, because quick treatment saves brain cells. A runny nose is a common sign of a cold.

notes: Doctor for brain and nerve illnesses
Tiny filter unit in the kidney
Chemical that passes nerve signals on
Surgeon who operates on brain or nerves
reason: A nephron belongs to the kidney; the other four are about nerves.
explain: "Neuro" comes from an old Greek word for nerve, so words that start with it are about the nervous system. A neuron is a nerve cell, a neurotransmitter is a chemical that carries signals between neurons, and neurologists and neurosurgeons are doctors who treat the brain and nerves. A nephron is one of about a million tiny filters inside each kidney that clean the blood.

notes: Tiredness makes feelings harder to manage
Attention drops when you are tired
Growth hormone is mostly released in deep sleep
reason: Losing sleep does not speed up growth; the other four are effects of too little sleep.
explain: While you sleep, your brain files away what you learned and clears out waste, and your body releases most of its growth hormone. Without enough sleep, memory gets worse, reactions slow down, moods swing and it is hard to pay attention. Children grow best when they get enough sleep, not less.

notes: An order sent out to muscles
reason: Kicking uses motor neurons carrying orders out; the other four use sensory neurons carrying messages in.
explain: Nerve messages travel in two directions. Sensory neurons carry information in from your senses, such as heat on your skin, a sound or a smell, towards the brain and spinal cord. Motor neurons carry orders out from the brain and spinal cord to muscles, such as the order to kick a ball.

notes: Done by the brain, not the cord
From skin up to the brain
Like pulling away from a hot pan
reason: Memories are stored in the brain; the other four are spinal cord jobs.
explain: The spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerves running down inside your backbone. It is the main highway between the brain and the body: messages about touch travel up it, and orders to move muscles travel down it. It can also handle simple reflexes on its own for speed. Memories are made and stored in the brain, for example with help from the hippocampus.

notes: Bursts of electrical activity cause seizures
Strong headaches that come and go
Airways in the lungs get narrow
reason: Asthma affects the lungs; the other four affect the brain.
explain: Illnesses are often grouped by the body system they affect, which helps decide which doctor to see. Epilepsy, migraine, Parkinson's disease and concussion all affect the brain, so a neurologist usually treats them. Asthma makes the airways in the lungs swell and narrow, so it is a lung condition.

reason: Milk has no caffeine; the other four contain caffeine.
explain: Caffeine is a chemical that acts on the brain and makes you feel more awake. It blocks a natural chemical that builds up during the day to make you sleepy. That is why caffeine drinks late in the day can stop you falling asleep. Children are advised to avoid energy drinks and limit other caffeine drinks.

notes: Low blood sugar can cause a headache
Eye strain can cause a headache
reason: Eating vegetables does not cause headaches; the other four commonly do.
explain: Most everyday headaches have simple causes. Not drinking enough water, going too long without food, poor sleep and staring at screens without breaks can all bring one on. Drinking water, eating regular meals and resting your eyes often help. A headache that is very bad or keeps coming back should be checked by a doctor.

reason: Pumping blood is the heart's job; feelings are made by the brain.
explain: People often say feelings come from the heart, but emotions are actually produced by the brain. Deep areas of the brain react to what happens and create feelings like fear, anger and joy, and the cerebrum helps you understand and control them. Your heart may beat faster when you are scared, but that is because the brain sent it a signal.

notes: Goes straight to smell areas first
reason: Smell signals skip the thalamus at first; the other four senses pass through it.
explain: The thalamus sits in the middle of the brain and works like a sorting office. Signals from your eyes, ears, skin and tongue stop there first and are sent on to the right part of the cerebrum. Smell signals take a different route: they go from the nose to smell areas of the brain first, close to the areas for memory and feelings.
fact: This short route may be one reason a smell can bring back an old memory so quickly.

reason: Balance is controlled by the cerebellum, not the frontal lobe; the other four pairs are correct.
explain: Each half of the cerebrum has four lobes with different main jobs. The frontal lobe at the front plans and makes decisions, the parietal lobe on top handles touch, the temporal lobe near the ears handles hearing, and the occipital lobe at the back handles sight. Balance and smooth movement are mainly the job of the cerebellum, which sits below the back of the cerebrum.

notes: Has its own net of neurons
Dead strands with no living cells
reason: Hair has no neurons; the other four contain nerve cells.
explain: Neurons are not only in the brain and spinal cord. The retina at the back of the eye is made of layers of neurons that start processing what you see. The wall of your gut has hundreds of millions of neurons that control the squeezing that moves food along. The hair you can see is made of dead cells, which is why a haircut does not hurt.

clues: In the cell that runs from your spine to your big toe, this part can be about a metre in length.
It is often wrapped in a fatty coat that makes messages travel faster.
It is the single thin tail that carries a nerve cell's message away from the cell body.
explain: An axon is the long, thin fibre of a neuron that carries its electrical message away from the cell body to the next cell or to a muscle. Each neuron usually has one axon but many dendrites. Many axons are coated in myelin, which lets signals travel much faster.
fact: Signals in some coated axons travel at over 100 metres per second.

clues: Under a microscope, these look like the bare twigs of a bush.
A single nerve cell can have many of these short, spreading fibres around its cell body.
They pick up incoming messages from neighbouring nerve cells and pass them to the cell body.
explain: Dendrites are the short branches around the cell body of a neuron. They collect messages from other neurons, often thousands of them, and pass them to the cell body. If the messages are strong enough, the neuron sends its own signal down its axon. The name comes from the Greek word for tree.

clues: It is a thick band of about 200 million nerve fibres deep in the middle of the brain.
It lets the two sides of the cerebrum share information.
Thanks to it, what one hemisphere learns can quickly reach the other.
explain: The cerebrum is split into a left and a right half, called hemispheres. The corpus callosum is a thick band of nerve fibres that joins them, so the two halves can work as a team. For example, it lets your left hand and right hand coordinate when you clap or tie shoelaces.

clues: An infection of these can cause a stiff neck, fever and a very bad headache.
There are three of them, and a clear fluid flows between two of them.
These thin sheets wrap around the brain and spinal cord, just under the bone.
explain: The meninges are three thin layers that wrap the brain and spinal cord inside the skull and backbone. Cerebrospinal fluid flows between two of the layers and cushions the brain. If germs infect the meninges, the illness is called meningitis, which needs urgent hospital care.

clues: In the brain it forms the outer wrinkly layer, called the cortex, but in the spinal cord it sits in the centre.
It is packed with the main bodies of nerve cells, their short branches and the gaps where they meet.
It looks darker than the fatty, coated wiring that lies beneath it in the brain.
explain: Brain tissue comes in two kinds. Grey matter is made mostly of neuron cell bodies and dendrites, where information is processed. White matter is made of axons coated in fatty myelin, which looks pale and carries signals between areas. In the brain the grey matter is on the outside; in the spinal cord it is in the middle.

clues: Dopamine and serotonin are two examples.
A nerve cell releases these tiny molecules from the end of its axon.
They float across the tiny space between two nerve cells to pass a signal on.
explain: Neurons do not touch each other. When a signal reaches the end of an axon, the neuron releases chemicals called neurotransmitters into the tiny gap, the synapse. They fit into the next neuron like keys in locks and start a new signal. Hormones are also chemical messengers, but they travel in the blood.

clues: It can happen after a serious injury to the cord inside the backbone.
Messages from the brain cannot reach some body parts.
The person cannot control those body parts, such as their legs.
explain: Paralysis means losing the ability to move part of the body. It happens when the nerve pathway between the brain and the muscles is damaged, for example by a spinal cord injury or a stroke. The muscles may be healthy, but they no longer get the orders to work. Many people with paralysis live full, active lives with the right support.

clues: Worry, caffeine or screens late in the evening can all cause it.
A person lies in the dark for hours, wishing they could drift off.
It is the name for trouble dozing off, or waking too early, again and again.
explain: Insomnia means having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, regularly. Stress, caffeine, bright screens and an irregular bedtime are common causes. A regular routine, a dark quiet room and no screens before bed usually help. If it goes on for weeks, a doctor can help find the cause.

clues: It is most common in children and usually stops as they grow up.
The person may get up with their eyes open, but they are not really awake.
Next morning they usually remember nothing about wandering around the house.
explain: Sleepwalking happens during deep sleep, when part of the brain wakes enough to move the body but the parts for awareness and memory stay asleep. It is common in children and usually harmless. Family members can gently guide the person back to bed and keep doors and stairs safe.

clues: It mostly happens during REM, the stage when the eyes move quickly.
Afterwards you might wake with a racing heart, glad it was not real.
It is a frightening story your mind plays while your eyes are shut in bed.
explain: A nightmare is a frightening dream that often wakes you up. Most vivid dreams happen in REM sleep, when the brain is very active while the body stays still. Nightmares are common in children and can come after a stressful day or a scary film. Talking about them with an adult often helps.

clues: It often happens when a lesson or task feels slow or boring.
Your eyes are open, but your thoughts drift far away from where you are.
You might picture yourself scoring a goal or flying, while sitting at your desk.
explain: A daydream is when your attention drifts from the world around you into your own thoughts and pictures, while you are fully awake. Everyone does it. Daydreaming can help with creativity and planning, but it can make you miss things, so it helps to notice when your attention wanders and bring it back.

clues: It works like the body's electrical wiring and control centre.
Its central part sits inside the skull and backbone, and its outer part reaches every finger and toe.
It lets you feel, think, remember and move.
explain: The nervous system is the body's control and messaging network. The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system, which makes decisions. Nerves branching out to the whole body form the peripheral nervous system, which carries messages in from the senses and orders out to the muscles.

clues: Scientists call it the circadian rhythm.
Flying across the world can throw it out of step for a while.
It makes you feel drowsy when it gets dark and alert in the morning, even without an alarm.
explain: Your body clock is a roughly 24-hour rhythm run by a tiny area in the hypothalamus. It uses light from your eyes to stay in step with day and night, and it controls when you feel sleepy and alert. Morning light, regular meals and a fixed bedtime keep it on track.

clues: It often happens after you sit cross-legged or lean on your arm for a long time.
Pressure on the message pathways in a limb causes it.
When you move again, the limb feels fizzy, as if tiny ants are crawling on it.
explain: Pins and needles happens when pressure squeezes a nerve, or the blood supply around it, in an arm or leg. The nerve stops sending normal signals, so the limb feels numb. When the pressure is released, the nerve fires mixed-up signals for a minute, which feel like prickling. If it happens often without a clear reason, a doctor should check it.

clues: It is a learning difference that often runs in families and has nothing to do with how clever someone is.
People with it can have great ideas but find it hard to match sounds to written symbols.
Audiobooks, extra time in exams and patient teaching help pupils with it do well.
explain: Dyslexia is a difference in how the brain processes written language. People with dyslexia find it hard to link letters to sounds, so reading and spelling take more effort. It is not linked to intelligence. With the right teaching and support, people with dyslexia do well in school and work.

clues: The cerebrum is made of two of these, joined by a thick band of fibres.
Each one mainly controls the muscles on the opposite part of the body.
Planet Earth is also split into a northern and a southern one.
explain: Hemisphere means half of a sphere. The cerebrum has a left and a right hemisphere. Each one mainly controls and feels the opposite side of the body, so the left hemisphere moves your right hand. The two halves share information through the corpus callosum.

clues: In a reflex arc, it is the last cell in the chain before the action.
Its long axon carries orders out from the spinal cord.
When it fires, your biceps tightens and your arm bends.
explain: Motor neurons carry orders from the brain and spinal cord out to muscles and glands. Their cell bodies sit in the spinal cord or brain, and their long axons reach the muscles. When a motor neuron fires, the muscle fibres it is connected to contract. Sensory neurons do the opposite job, carrying information in.

scenario: A boy bumps the inner side of his elbow on a table. A strange tingling shoots down to his little finger. People call this spot the 'funny bone'. What did he actually hit?
optionNotes: Would ache, not tingle down the hand
Nerve to the little and ring fingers
explain: The "funny bone" is really the ulnar nerve. At the elbow it runs through a groove just under the skin, with little padding, so a knock squeezes it. The nerve then sends a burst of odd signals that you feel as tingling in your little and ring fingers, because that is the area it serves.
fact: One idea is that the name is a joke: the nerve runs past the humerus bone, which sounds like "humorous".

scenario: A family flies from Delhi to London, where clocks are several hours behind. The first night, a girl is wide awake at 3 am and very sleepy by early evening. What will help her adjust fastest?
options: Keep to Delhi times all trip
Sleep all day, stay up all night
Daylight outdoors and local meal and bed times
answer: Daylight outdoors and local meal and bed times
optionNotes: Keeps her body clock out of step
Light and routine reset the body clock
explain: Her body clock is still set to Delhi time, so it tells her to wake and sleep at the wrong local hours. This is jet lag. Light reaching the eyes is the strongest signal for resetting the body clock, so time outdoors in daylight helps. Eating and going to bed at local times also helps her settle in a few days.

scenario: An 80-year-old grandfather keeps asking the same question and gets lost on his own street, yet remembers his school days clearly. These problems have slowly grown worse over two years. Which condition is most likely?
optionNotes: Slowly damages memory areas of the brain
Follows a knock to the head
explain: Alzheimer's disease slowly damages neurons, often starting in areas such as the hippocampus that store new memories. That is why recent events are forgotten first while old memories last longer. It is not a normal part of growing old. There is no cure yet, but treatment, routines and patient family support help people live well for longer.

scenario: A 70-year-old man has a shaking hand while it rests, slow, stiff movements and very small handwriting. Brain cells that make one chemical messenger have slowly been dying. Which messenger is running low?
optionNotes: Carries oxygen in red blood cells
Helps the brain control smooth movement
explain: These are signs of Parkinson's disease. Deep in the brain, a small group of neurons makes dopamine, a neurotransmitter that helps control smooth movement. When these cells slowly die, movements become shaky, slow and stiff. Medicines that boost dopamine, along with exercise and therapy, help many people stay active.

scenario: A cyclist hit his head in a fall. He was knocked out for a minute and has vomited twice since. The doctor needs a quick picture of his brain to look for bleeding. Which test is usually done first?
optionNotes: Fast X-ray pictures of the brain
explain: After a serious head injury, doctors need to see inside the skull quickly. A CT scan takes X-ray pictures from many angles and a computer builds them into slices of the brain. It takes only a few minutes and clearly shows bleeding or swelling, so the team can decide on treatment fast.

scenario: Just before speaking on stage, a girl's heart pounds, her palms sweat, her mouth feels dry and her breathing speeds up. Which body response is this?
optionNotes: Nerves and adrenaline prepare for action
The body is relaxed and still
explain: When the brain senses a challenge, part of the nervous system and the hormone adrenaline get the body ready to act. The heart beats faster, breathing quickens and digestion slows, so the mouth feels dry. This is the fight-or-flight response. It is normal before a performance, and slow, deep breaths help calm it down.

scenario: A boy practises a new piano tune for 15 minutes every day. After two weeks he can play it smoothly without looking at the notes. What has changed inside his brain?
options: Links between his neurons got stronger
answer: Links between his neurons got stronger
optionNotes: Fingers do not grow that fast
Has nothing to do with skill
explain: Every time you practise, the same group of neurons fires together, and the connections between them grow stronger. The signal travels more easily, so the skill feels automatic. This ability of the brain to change with use is called plasticity. Short, regular practice works better than one long session.

scenario: In a science lesson, one student holds a ruler and drops it without warning. Her partner tries to catch it, and they note how far it fell. What does this test measure?
explain: Reaction time is how long it takes to respond to something. The eyes see the ruler fall, a message travels to the brain, the brain decides, and motor neurons tell the hand muscles to grab. The further the ruler falls, the longer that chain took. Tiredness and distraction make reaction time slower.

scenario: A teenager suddenly has a high fever, a very bad headache and a stiff neck, and bright light hurts his eyes. What should the family do?
options: Rest in a dark room only
optionNotes: These can be signs of meningitis
Helps migraine, but this needs urgent care
explain: Fever, a severe headache, a stiff neck and pain from bright light together can be signs of meningitis, an infection of the meninges around the brain and spinal cord. It needs urgent hospital treatment, which works best when started early. Vaccines protect children against several germs that cause it.

scenario: A man injured his spinal cord in the middle of his back. His arms work normally. Which body parts are most likely to have trouble moving?
optionNotes: Their nerves leave the cord above it
Served by nerves from the brain
Their nerves leave the cord below the injury
Served by nerves from the brain
explain: Nerves leave the spinal cord at every level, from the neck down. Messages from the brain travel down the cord, so an injury blocks messages to parts served by nerves below it. Nerves to the arms leave from the neck, above this injury, so the arms still work. Nerves to the legs leave lower down, so the legs may not move.

scenario: Before filling a tooth, the dentist injects a numbing medicine into the gum. The tooth is drilled, but the girl feels no pain. What has the medicine blocked?
optionNotes: Pain messages cannot reach the brain
She can still hear the drill
explain: Pain is a message carried by nerves to the brain. A local anaesthetic stops nerves in one small area from sending signals for a few hours. The tooth is still being worked on, but the brain never gets the pain message. The rest of the body works normally, and feeling returns as the medicine wears off.
fact: A numb lip is easy to bite by accident, so avoid chewing until the feeling comes back.

scenario: A boy bumped his head at the park. A doctor checked him and sent him home, but his parents must watch him closely for the next day. Which sign means he should go back to hospital at once?
options: A small bruise on his forehead
optionNotes: Common after a bump; usually harmless
Can mean pressure building in the brain
explain: After a head injury, the brain can sometimes bleed or swell slowly, so problems may appear hours later. Warning signs include repeated vomiting, a headache that gets worse, unusual sleepiness, confusion or a fit. Any of these means going straight back to hospital. A small bruise and a normal appetite are reassuring.

scenario: After an injury to the front of his head, a man sees and hears normally, but he struggles to plan his day, makes rash choices and loses his temper easily. Which brain part is most likely affected?
explain: The frontal lobe sits just behind your forehead. It helps you plan, make sensible decisions, focus on goals and control impulses and temper. Damage here can change behaviour even though vision, hearing and movement are fine. The frontal lobe is one of the last brain areas to finish developing, in a person's mid-twenties.

scenario: Tests show a woman's immune system has damaged the fatty coating around some of her nerve fibres. What happens to the signals along those fibres?
options: They slow down or get muddled
They only travel to the brain
answer: They slow down or get muddled
optionNotes: The coating helps speed, so losing it slows signals
Myelin is what speeds them up
explain: The fatty coating is myelin. It works like insulation on a wire and lets signals jump quickly along the axon. In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks myelin by mistake, so signals slow down or get blocked. This can cause tingling, weakness or blurred vision. Treatments can slow the illness and help people stay active.

scenario: For some brain operations, surgeons numb only the scalp and keep the patient awake and talking. The patient feels no pain as the surgeon works on the brain itself. Why?
options: Pain only travels in the legs
Brain tissue has no pain sensors
The patient is too busy talking
answer: Brain tissue has no pain sensors
optionNotes: The skull does not block pain signals
Pain can come from anywhere in the body
It senses the body but not itself
Talking does not stop pain signals
explain: Pain is felt when pain sensors send signals to the brain. The skin, scalp and coverings of the brain have these sensors, but brain tissue itself has none. Surgeons sometimes keep patients awake so they can check that speech and movement are working while they operate. Headaches come from sensors in the coverings, blood vessels and muscles around the brain.

scenario: A girl steps on a drawing pin. In a flash, a message about the sharp point travels from her foot to her spinal cord. Which kind of nerve cell carries it there?
optionNotes: Carries messages in from the senses
Contracts, but does not send messages
explain: Sensory neurons carry information from sense receptors, like pain sensors in the skin, to the spinal cord and brain. In the spinal cord the message is passed on, and motor neurons carry orders back out to the leg muscles to lift the foot. That is why she pulls her foot away before she has even thought about it.
