notes: Thigh bone, the longest bone in the body
Connects the brain to the spinal cord
Part of the brain stem; controls breathing
Largest part of the brain, used for thinking
Back part of the brain, controls balance
reason: The femur is a leg bone; the other four are parts of the brain.
explain: Your brain has three main parts. The cerebrum is the big wrinkly top part that thinks and remembers. The cerebellum sits at the back and keeps you balanced. The brain stem, which includes the medulla, links the brain to the spinal cord and runs automatic jobs like breathing. The femur is the thigh bone in your leg.
fact: An adult brain weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kg, roughly the same as a large bag of sugar.

notes: Fatty coat that speeds up signals
Long wire that sends messages onward
Tiny air sac in the lungs
Control centre of the nerve cell
reason: An alveolus is part of the lungs; the rest are parts of a neuron.
explain: A neuron is a nerve cell built to pass messages. Dendrites are short branches that pick up messages, the cell body keeps the cell alive, and the axon is a long wire that carries the message away. Many axons are wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath, like plastic coating on a wire. An alveolus is a tiny air sac in the lungs where oxygen enters the blood.

items: Pulling hand off a hot pan
notes: Eyes shut fast to protect themselves
You choose to do it and think about it
Hand jerks away before you feel pain
Leg kicks when tapped below the knee
reason: Writing your name is a voluntary action; the others are reflexes.
explain: A reflex is a fast, automatic reaction that you do not have to think about. Reflexes protect you, so the message often takes a shortcut through the spinal cord or brain stem instead of waiting for the thinking part of the brain. Writing your name is a voluntary action: your cerebrum decides to do it and plans each movement.

reason: Solving a sum is done by the cerebrum; the medulla controls the other four.
explain: The medulla is the lowest part of the brain stem. It runs life-support jobs automatically: it sets how fast your heart beats and how fast you breathe, keeps blood pressure steady, and triggers coughing to clear your airway. These carry on even when you are asleep. Solving a sum needs conscious thinking, which happens in the cerebrum.

notes: Bones of the backbone around the spinal cord
Three thin layers wrapping the brain
Hard bony case around the brain
reason: A neuron carries messages; the others protect the brain and spinal cord.
explain: The brain and spinal cord are soft, so the body guards them in layers. The skull and the vertebrae of the backbone form hard bony cases. Inside those, three thin layers called meninges wrap the brain and cord, and cerebrospinal fluid cushions them like water around an egg. Neurons are the cells being protected; they do the job of carrying messages.

notes: Separate part at the back, below
reason: The cerebellum is a separate part of the brain; the other four are lobes of the cerebrum.
explain: The cerebrum is divided into four lobes on each side. The frontal lobe plans and makes decisions, the parietal lobe handles touch, the temporal lobe handles hearing and memory, and the occipital lobe handles sight. The cerebellum is a separate, smaller part tucked under the back of the cerebrum. It coordinates movement and balance.

notes: Daytime exercise helps you sleep deeper
Darkness tells the brain it is night
reason: An energy drink at night makes sleep harder; the others help you sleep well.
explain: Your brain has a body clock that works best with a regular routine. Darkness helps the brain release a sleep signal, while the bright light from screens can delay it. Exercise during the day also helps you sleep more deeply. Energy drinks contain caffeine, which blocks the brain's sleepy signals for hours, so drinking one in the evening makes it hard to fall asleep.
fact: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night.

notes: You choose to move your arm
Happens without any decision from you
reason: Your heartbeat is involuntary; the others are voluntary actions you choose.
explain: Voluntary actions are ones you decide to do. The cerebrum sends a message down nerves to skeletal muscles in your legs, arms, mouth or jaw. Involuntary actions happen on their own. Your heart keeps beating whether you think about it or not, and the brain stem only adjusts its speed.

notes: Common after a hard knock to the head
Not sure where you are or what happened
A skin problem, not a head-injury sign
reason: An itchy rash is not a sign of concussion; the other four are.
explain: A concussion happens when a bump or jolt makes the brain move inside the skull. This can upset how brain cells work for a while. Common signs are headache, confusion, dizziness, feeling sick, and trouble remembering what happened. Anyone with these signs after a head knock should stop playing and be checked by a doctor. A rash is a skin problem.

notes: Pain that pulses, often on one side
Usually from a sprain, not migraine
Called an aura; comes before some migraines
reason: A swollen ankle is not a migraine sign; the other four are.
explain: A migraine is a strong headache that comes in attacks, often with a throbbing pain on one side of the head. Light and sound can feel painful, and many people feel sick. Some people first see flashing or zigzag lights called an aura. A swollen ankle usually comes from a sprain, which is an injury to the ligaments.

notes: Decision-making at the front of the brain
reason: Balance is mainly the cerebellum's job; the rest are mainly cerebrum jobs.
explain: The cerebrum is the largest part of your brain and handles thinking, memory, language and planning. The cerebellum, at the back underneath, takes care of balance and smooth, well-timed movement. When you ride a bike, the cerebellum makes tiny corrections every moment so you do not tip over, without you having to think about it.

notes: Red protein in blood that carries oxygen
Sends the signal away from the cell
reason: Haemoglobin carries oxygen in blood; the rest are part of passing nerve signals.
explain: A nerve signal travels as electricity along the axon. At the end there is a tiny gap called a synapse. The neuron releases chemicals called neurotransmitters, which float across the gap and land on the dendrites of the next neuron, starting a new signal there. Haemoglobin is the red protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen.

notes: Carries the alert to the spinal cord
Not needed for the reflex itself
Connects the two inside the spinal cord
Carries the order to the muscle
reason: The cerebrum is not part of a simple reflex arc; the other four are.
explain: A reflex arc is the shortcut path of a reflex. A receptor in the skin detects danger, a sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord, a relay neuron passes it straight to a motor neuron, and the motor neuron tells a muscle to move. Because the message skips the cerebrum, the reaction is very fast. The cerebrum finds out a moment later, which is when you feel the pain.

notes: Helps blood carry oxygen to the brain
Needed to release energy from food
Waste gas that must be removed
reason: Carbon dioxide is a waste the brain gets rid of; the others are things it needs.
explain: Brain cells work non-stop and use a lot of energy. They need glucose (a sugar) as fuel and oxygen to release the energy from it, both delivered by the blood. Iron from food helps red blood cells carry that oxygen, and the brain is mostly water. Carbon dioxide is the waste gas made when cells use glucose; blood carries it away to the lungs to be breathed out.
fact: The brain is about 2% of your body weight but uses about 20% of your body's energy.

notes: Shallow water can cause head injuries
Raises the risk of a head injury
Helps the seatbelt fit a child safely
Absorbs the force of a fall
reason: Riding on handlebars raises the risk of head injury; the others protect your brain.
explain: Your skull protects your brain, but a hard knock can still injure it. A helmet spreads out and soaks up the force of a fall. Seatbelts and booster seats stop your head hitting the inside of a car. Checking water depth before diving prevents striking your head on the bottom. Sitting on handlebars makes falls more likely, with nothing protecting your head.

notes: Not true; the brain stays busy
Growth and repair happen at night
A stage of sleep with vivid dreams
reason: The brain never switches fully off in sleep; the others really happen during sleep.
explain: Sleep is an active time for the brain. It moves through stages, including REM sleep, when the eyes dart about and most vivid dreams happen. While you sleep, the brain sorts and stores what you learned that day, and the body does repair work. The brain stem also keeps your breathing and heartbeat going all night.

notes: Main message cable down the back
Bundles of fibres reaching every body part
Tough cords joining muscle to bone
Links the brain to the spinal cord
reason: Tendons belong to the muscle system; the others make up the nervous system.
explain: The nervous system is the body's messaging network. The brain and spinal cord form the central part, and nerves branch out from them to every part of the body. All of these are built from neurons. Tendons are tough cords that attach muscles to bones so muscles can pull on them.

clues: Your body has billions of these tiny units, each with a long thin tail called an axon.
They pass electrical signals to one another across tiny gaps.
They are the units that carry information between your senses, your thinking organ and your muscles.
explain: A neuron is a nerve cell, the basic unit of the nervous system. It has branches called dendrites to receive signals, a cell body, and a long axon to send signals on. Neurons pass messages as tiny electrical pulses and use chemicals to cross the gaps between them.
fact: The human brain has about 86 billion neurons.

clues: The signal often takes a shortcut through the spinal cord instead of going up to the cerebrum.
Blinking when a ball flies at your face is one example.
It is the quick action that jerks your hand away from a hot pan before you even feel the pain.
explain: A reflex is an automatic, very quick response to something like heat, a sharp object or a speck flying at your eye. The message travels a short path, often through the spinal cord, so you react before the thinking part of your brain is involved. Reflexes protect the body from harm.

clues: In an adult it is about 45 cm long and about as thick as a finger.
It runs down your back inside a tunnel of stacked vertebrae.
It is the main cable carrying signals between your head and the rest of your body.
explain: The spinal cord is a long bundle of nervous tissue that runs from the brain stem down the back. The vertebrae of the backbone surround and protect it. It carries messages between the brain and the body, and it can also handle some reflexes by itself.

clues: It holds more than half of all the nerve cells in your head, though it is much smaller than the cerebrum.
It sits low down, tucked under the rear of the cerebrum.
It helps you walk steadily, ride a bike and catch a ball without wobbling.
explain: The cerebellum is a smaller part of the brain at the back, under the cerebrum. It coordinates muscles so movements are smooth and well timed, and it keeps your balance. It also helps you learn movement skills like riding a bike or playing an instrument.

clues: It is split into a left half and a right half, joined by a thick bridge of fibres.
Its folded outer layer packs a huge surface into the skull.
This biggest part of the brain lets you think, remember, speak and make decisions.
explain: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain. Its folds pack in a lot of surface, where much of the thinking happens. It handles thought, memory, language, the senses and voluntary movement. The left half mostly controls the right side of the body, and the right half controls the left side.

clues: It is the oldest and lowest part of the brain, shaped a bit like a stalk.
It keeps working all night while you sleep.
It controls automatic life-support jobs like taking in air and keeping your heart pumping at the right speed.
explain: The brain stem connects the brain to the spinal cord. It controls automatic jobs that keep you alive, such as breathing, heart rate, swallowing and waking up. All messages between the brain and body pass through it. The medulla is its lowest section.

clues: Doctors say: when in doubt, sit them out, and see a doctor before playing again.
Signs include confusion, dizziness, feeling sick and forgetting what just happened.
It happens when a hard knock or jolt makes the brain shake inside the skull.
explain: A concussion is a brain injury caused by a knock or jolt that shakes the brain inside the skull. It can cause headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea and memory gaps. Anyone with these signs should stop playing and be checked by a doctor. Most people recover with rest and a slow return to activity.

clues: It often runs in families and can be set off by skipped meals, poor sleep or stress.
During an attack, bright light and loud sounds can feel unbearable, and the person may feel sick.
It is a severe ache on one side of the head, sometimes starting with zigzag lights in the eyes.
explain: A migraine is a strong headache that comes in attacks and can last hours. It often throbs on one side, makes light and noise feel painful, and causes nausea. Some people see flashing lights first, called an aura. Regular meals, good sleep and plenty of water can help prevent attacks, and a doctor can advise on treatment.

clues: Sleep helps your brain lock in what you learned during the day.
There is a short-term kind, like a phone number you just heard, and a long-term kind, like your best friend's birthday.
It is your brain's ability to keep information and bring it back later.
explain: Memory is the brain's ability to take in, keep and bring back information. Short-term memory holds things for a few seconds or minutes. With practice and sleep, some of it moves into long-term memory, which can last for years. A part of the brain called the hippocampus helps form new memories.

clues: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of this every day.
During it, your brain sorts memories and your body does repair work.
You close your eyes, lie down and become unaware of the world until morning.
explain: Sleep is a natural state when the body rests and the brain does important maintenance. The brain sorts and stores memories, clears waste, and the body grows and repairs. Too little sleep makes it harder to concentrate, learn and control your mood.

clues: Learning something new can make these links stronger or create new ones.
Chemical messengers float across this space in a tiny fraction of a second.
It is the very narrow space where one neuron passes its signal to the next.
explain: A synapse is the tiny gap between two neurons. When a signal reaches the end of an axon, the neuron releases chemicals that cross the gap and start a signal in the next neuron. When you practise a skill, the synapses involved become stronger, which is part of how learning works.

clues: It gives some parts of the brain a pale colour, known as white matter.
Signals jump along it from gap to gap, which makes them much quicker.
It wraps around axons like plastic around an electric wire.
explain: Myelin is a fatty layer wrapped around many axons. It works like the plastic covering on a wire, stopping signals from leaking and letting them jump quickly along the axon. Thanks to myelin, some nerve signals travel at more than 100 metres per second. Children's brains keep adding myelin through the teenage years.

clues: Most vivid ones happen during a stage when your eyes dart about under closed lids.
You often forget them within minutes of waking up.
These are the pictures and adventures your mind plays while you are snoozing.
explain: Dreams are images, sounds and stories the brain creates during sleep. The most vivid ones happen in REM sleep, when the eyes move quickly. During REM most body muscles relax, so you do not act out your dreams. Scientists think dreaming may help the brain process memories and feelings.

clues: If one in your leg is pressed for a long time, you may get pins and needles.
It is a bundle of many fibres wrapped together, like a cable of wires.
These thin pathways carry feelings from your skin and orders to your muscles.
explain: A nerve is a bundle of long fibres from many neurons, wrapped together like a cable. Nerves branch out from the brain and spinal cord to every part of the body. Some carry information such as touch and pain inwards, and others carry instructions out to muscles. When a nerve is squashed, its signals get muddled, which you feel as pins and needles.

clues: It is not catching, and many people with it control it well with daily medicine.
Doctors may record electrical activity from the scalp to help diagnose it.
It is a condition where sudden bursts of electrical activity in the brain cause repeated episodes of jerking or blank staring.
explain: Epilepsy is a brain condition in which bursts of electrical activity cause seizures again and again. A seizure might make someone's body jerk, or they may just stare blankly for a few seconds. It is not contagious. Many people with epilepsy take medicine that controls it, and they go to school, play sport and live normal lives.

clues: There is one on each side of the brain, curled deep inside.
Its name comes from a sea creature it looks a bit like.
It helps turn new experiences and facts into things you can still recall years later.
explain: The hippocampus is a curved structure deep in each side of the brain. It helps form new memories and is also used for finding your way around places. Its name comes from the Greek word for seahorse because of its shape. Sleep helps the hippocampus pass new memories to other parts of the brain for long-term keeping.

clues: A doctor can take a small sample from the lower back to test it for infection.
It is clear and bathes the brain and the long cord inside your backbone all the time.
It lets the brain float inside the skull, so knocks are softened.
explain: Cerebrospinal fluid is a clear fluid made inside the brain. It flows around the brain and spinal cord, letting the brain float so it does not press on the skull. This cushions the brain from knocks, and the fluid also carries away waste.

scenario: During a football match, a girl clashes heads with another player. She says she has a headache, feels dizzy and cannot remember the score. What should happen first?
options: Keep playing to see if it passes
Stop playing and get her checked by a doctor
Send her home to sleep alone
answer: Stop playing and get her checked by a doctor
optionNotes: Another knock could make it worse
Does not treat a brain injury
She should be watched by an adult
explain: Headache, dizziness and memory gaps after a head knock are signs of concussion. The safe rule is: when in doubt, sit them out. She should stop playing and be checked by a doctor, with an adult watching her. A second knock before the brain heals can be more serious, so she should only return to sport when a doctor says it is safe.

scenario: The doctor gently taps just below a boy's kneecap with a small rubber hammer, and his leg kicks forward on its own. What is the doctor checking?
optionNotes: Tests nerves and spinal cord together
Needs a blood test, not a hammer
explain: The knee-jerk is a reflex. The tap stretches a tendon, a sensory nerve sends a signal to the spinal cord, and a motor nerve sends one straight back to the thigh muscle, which kicks. If the kick is normal, the doctor knows that path of nerves and spinal cord is working.

scenario: A girl has had several short episodes of staring blankly and not responding. The doctor wants to record her brain's electrical activity using small sensors stuck on her scalp. Which test is this?
explain: Neurons communicate using tiny electrical signals. An EEG (electroencephalogram) picks up these signals through small sensors on the scalp and draws them as wavy lines. It is painless. Unusual bursts in the pattern can help doctors find out whether someone has epilepsy. An ECG looks similar but records the heart instead.

scenario: After an illness affecting the lower back part of his brain, a man walks unsteadily, sways when standing, and his hand shakes when reaching for a cup. His thinking is normal. Which brain part is most likely affected?
optionNotes: Carries signals from eye to brain
explain: The cerebellum sits low at the back of the brain. It fine-tunes every movement so it is smooth and accurate, and it keeps you balanced. When it is damaged, people wobble, sway and their reaching movements become shaky, even though their thinking stays clear.

scenario: An 11-year-old watches videos in bed until midnight and wakes at 6 am. He feels tired and cannot concentrate in class. What is the best advice?
options: Fixed bedtime and screens off an hour before
Catch up on sleep only at weekends
answer: Fixed bedtime and screens off an hour before
optionNotes: Misses learning and does not fix the cause
Gives the brain enough regular sleep
Caffeine is not advised for children
explain: Children of his age need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep. He is getting about 6. Light from screens delays the brain's sleep signal, so switching off an hour before bed helps him fall asleep. A fixed bedtime trains the body clock, and enough sleep improves focus, memory and mood.

scenario: A girl who has been diagnosed with migraine feels an attack starting: a throbbing headache, and light hurts her eyes. Along with any medicine her doctor has prescribed, what helps most right now?
options: Lie down in a quiet, dark room
Go for a run in the sun
answer: Lie down in a quiet, dark room
optionNotes: Reduces light and sound that trigger pain
Bright light and effort can worsen it
Noise and bright screens worsen migraine
explain: During a migraine the brain becomes extra sensitive to light, sound and movement. Resting in a quiet, dark room reduces these and often eases the attack. Drinking water and taking any medicine the doctor has prescribed also helps. Skipping meals, poor sleep and stress are common triggers, so regular routines can prevent attacks.

scenario: A boy touches a hot iron and pulls his hand away in a split second, before he even feels the pain. Which part of the nervous system sent the order to move?
optionNotes: Smooths movement, does not start reflexes
Gets the news a moment later
explain: This is a reflex. The heat signal travels from the skin to the spinal cord, which sends an order straight back to the arm muscles without waiting for the brain. That shortcut saves time and protects the skin. The signal also continues up to the cerebrum, which is why he feels the pain a moment later.

scenario: A grandfather's face suddenly droops on one side, he cannot lift one arm, and his words come out slurred. What should the family do first?
options: Wait a day to see if it improves
Let him lie down and sleep it off
optionNotes: These are signs of a stroke
explain: These are signs of a stroke, when blood supply to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel leaks. Remember FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech trouble, Time to call an ambulance. Brain cells need a steady supply of oxygen, so fast hospital treatment protects as much of the brain as possible.

scenario: At school, a classmate suddenly falls to the floor and her arms and legs start jerking. A teacher is on the way. What should you do to help?
options: Move hard objects away and cushion her head
Splash cold water on her face
Hold her arms and legs down firmly
answer: Move hard objects away and cushion her head
optionNotes: Can break teeth or block breathing
Keeps her safe until it stops
Can hurt her; the jerking cannot be stopped
explain: This is a seizure. You cannot stop it, so the goal is to keep the person safe: move hard or sharp things away, put something soft under the head, and note the time. Never hold them down or put anything in their mouth. When the jerking stops, an adult can roll them onto their side. An ambulance is needed if it lasts more than 5 minutes or it is their first seizure.

scenario: A man falls from a ladder and lands on his back. He is awake but says he cannot feel his legs. He is not in any other danger. What should people nearby do?
options: Keep him still and call an ambulance
Rub his legs to bring back feeling
Help him stand up to test his legs
answer: Keep him still and call an ambulance
optionNotes: Protects the spinal cord until help arrives
Does not help a spinal injury
Moving may harm the spinal cord more
explain: Losing feeling in the legs after a fall can mean the spinal cord is injured. The spinal cord carries messages between the brain and body, and moving the person could damage it further. Unless there is danger like fire or traffic, keep the person still, keep them calm and call an ambulance. Paramedics have special equipment to move them safely.

scenario: After a nerve injury in his arm, a man can feel a light touch on his fingers, but he cannot move them. His muscles are healthy. Which nerve cells are not passing their signals?
optionNotes: Cover the body, not nerve signals
Working, since he can feel touch
Carry orders from spinal cord to muscles
explain: Nerves contain two main kinds of neurons. Sensory neurons carry information such as touch from the body to the spinal cord and brain. Motor neurons carry orders the other way, from the spinal cord to muscles. Since he can feel touch but cannot move his healthy muscles, the motor signals are the ones being blocked.

scenario: A student stays up all night before every test, reading her notes once. She forgets most of it by the next week. What advice will help her memory most?
options: Read the notes once very quickly
Only study with loud music on
Study in short sessions over several days and sleep well
answer: Study in short sessions over several days and sleep well
optionNotes: Repetition and sleep build lasting memories
explain: Memories become strong when the brain meets the same information several times, with gaps in between. Each time, the links between neurons get stronger. Sleep also matters: while you sleep, the brain moves new learning into long-term memory. Skipping sleep before a test makes it harder to learn and to remember.

scenario: After an injury to the back of her head, a woman has trouble seeing clearly. The eye doctor says her eyes are completely healthy. Which part of the brain is most likely affected?
optionNotes: At the sides; hearing and memory
At the back; makes sense of what eyes see
At the front; planning and decisions
explain: Your eyes collect light, but you actually see with your brain. Signals travel from the eyes along the optic nerves to the occipital lobe at the back of the cerebrum, which turns them into images. If this area is injured, a person can have healthy eyes but still have trouble seeing.

scenario: A boy skipped breakfast and lunch. By afternoon he feels shaky and cannot concentrate on his work. Which fuel is his brain running low on?
optionNotes: Sugar that is the brain's main fuel
Helps fight infections and heal cuts
explain: Brain cells use a lot of energy and depend mostly on glucose, a sugar that comes from digested food and travels in the blood. When you go a long time without eating, blood glucose drops, and the brain cannot work as well. Regular meals with whole grains, fruit and protein keep a steady supply.

scenario: Even when you are fast asleep, you keep breathing and your heart keeps beating. Which part of the brain controls these automatic jobs?
optionNotes: Runs breathing and heart rate automatically
explain: The brain stem links the brain to the spinal cord. It controls life-support jobs automatically, including breathing, heart rate and swallowing, so they continue while you sleep. You can choose to hold your breath for a short while using your cerebrum, but the brain stem soon makes you breathe again.

scenario: A scan shows a woman has had a small stroke on the left side of her brain. Which side of her body is most likely to feel weak?
optionNotes: Not how brain control is arranged
Controlled by the right side of the brain
Weakness usually affects one side of the body
explain: Most nerve pathways between the brain and body cross over in the brain stem. So the left half of the brain controls movement and feeling on the right side of the body, and the right half controls the left side. Damage on one side of the brain usually causes weakness on the opposite side of the body.

notes: Lens you look into at the top
Flat platform where the slide sits
Reflects light up through the slide
reason: A test tube holds liquids; the other four are parts of a light microscope.
explain: A light microscope works by shining light up through a thin sample. The mirror sends light upward, the stage holds the slide, and two lenses (the objective and the eyepiece) make the image bigger. A test tube is useful lab glassware, but it is not part of a microscope.
fact: Many school microscopes have three objective lenses on a turning wheel, so you can switch between low and high power.

notes: Oxygen passes through it into the cell
Waste like carbon dioxide leaves through it
Job of ribosomes, not the membrane
reason: Making proteins is the job of ribosomes; the other four are jobs of the cell membrane.
explain: The cell membrane is a thin, flexible layer around every cell. It holds the contents in and works like a gatekeeper, letting useful things such as oxygen and food in and sending waste out. Proteins are built by tiny parts called ribosomes, which sit inside the cell.
fact: The cell membrane is so thin that thousands of them stacked together would still be thinner than a sheet of paper.

notes: Tiny grain with no membrane around it
A small bag with a membrane
reason: A ribosome has no membrane around it; the other four are wrapped in membranes.
explain: Many parts inside a cell are wrapped in their own thin membrane, like rooms with walls. The nucleus, mitochondria, lysosomes and the Golgi body all have these walls. Ribosomes are tiny grains with no membrane, which is why even bacteria, with no 'rooms' at all, still have them.
fact: A single busy cell can contain millions of ribosomes.

notes: Small green plant; makes its own food
A fungus; absorbs food from its surroundings
reason: A mushroom is a fungus that cannot make its own food; the other four are plants that make food using sunlight.
explain: Plants have cells with chloroplasts, the green parts that use sunlight to make food. Grass, tulsi, mango trees and moss are all plants. A mushroom is a fungus. Its cells have no chloroplasts, so it takes in food from rotting leaves, wood or soil around it.
fact: The mushroom you see is only a small part of the fungus; most of it is a web of fine threads hidden underground.

notes: A section of DNA with one instruction
The full set of an organism's DNA
reason: An antibody is a germ-fighting protein; the other four are words for genetic material.
explain: DNA is the molecule that stores a cell's instructions. A gene is one section of DNA, a chromosome is a long coiled bundle of DNA, and the genome is the complete set of DNA in an organism. An antibody is a protein made by white blood cells to fight germs, so it belongs to the immune system.
fact: The human genome has about 20,000 genes that carry instructions for making proteins.

notes: Holds only 23 chromosomes, half the usual
reason: An egg cell has 23 chromosomes; the other body cells have 46.
explain: Most human body cells carry 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs. Egg cells and sperm cells carry only one chromosome from each pair, so they have 23. When an egg and sperm join, the new cell has 23 + 23 = 46 again, half from each parent.
fact: The human egg cell is one of the largest cells in the body, roughly the size of a full stop.

notes: Waste gas the cell gives out
Taken in for many cell jobs
reason: Carbon dioxide is a waste the cell gives out; the other four are things a body cell takes in.
explain: Your body cells take in glucose and oxygen and use them in respiration to release energy. They also take in amino acids to build proteins and minerals for many small jobs. Respiration leaves carbon dioxide as waste, which the blood carries to the lungs to be breathed out.
fact: Plant cells do the opposite during the day: they take in carbon dioxide to make food and give out oxygen.

notes: Pulled by gravity, not spreading out
Oxygen moves from lungs to blood
Colour spreads out from the tea bag
reason: A ball rolls because of gravity; the other four are examples of diffusion.
explain: Diffusion is when tiny particles spread from a place where there are many of them to a place where there are few. Perfume, ink and tea colour all spread out this way without anyone stirring them. Oxygen gets into your blood, and then into your cells, by diffusion too. A rolling ball moves because gravity pulls it, which is a different thing.
fact: Diffusion is faster when things are warm, which is why tea colour spreads faster in hot water than in cold.

notes: Crawls by pushing out its body
Crawls through tissue to chase germs
Fixed in place by its cell wall
reason: An onion cell cannot move by itself; the other four cells move on their own.
explain: Some cells can move themselves. An amoeba crawls by pushing out parts of its body, a paramecium beats thousands of tiny hairs, a sperm lashes a long tail, and some white blood cells crawl out of blood vessels to reach germs. An onion cell is a plant cell, held in place by its firm cell wall inside the onion.
fact: Sperm cells are among the smallest cells in the human body, while egg cells are among the largest.

notes: Smaller than a typical body cell
Made of many cells, so bigger
Short stretch of DNA in a cell
reason: A tissue is made of many cells, so it is bigger than one cell; the other four are smaller than a cell.
explain: Living things are organised in levels. Inside a cell are smaller parts like the nucleus, ribosomes and genes. Above the cell come tissues, which are groups of similar cells working together. A virus is not a cell at all and is usually far smaller than a human cell.
fact: Most viruses are so small that they can only be seen with an electron microscope.

notes: Ice does this; not a life process
reason: Melting happens to non-living things like ice; the other four are life processes.
explain: All living things, from one-celled amoebas to elephants, carry out life processes. They grow, reproduce, release energy from food through respiration, and get rid of waste through excretion. These happen inside cells. Melting is a change that happens to non-living materials such as ice or wax when they are heated.
fact: Even a single bacterium carries out all these life processes inside one tiny cell.

notes: Part inside a cell; builds proteins
Part inside a cell; stores things
Part inside a cell; releases energy
A whole cell, not a part
Part inside a cell; controls it
reason: A cheek cell is a whole cell; the other four are parts found inside cells.
explain: The small working parts inside a cell are called organelles, which means 'little organs'. The nucleus controls the cell, mitochondria release energy, ribosomes build proteins and vacuoles store things. A cheek cell is a whole cell that contains organelles like these.
fact: Your cheek lining constantly sheds old cells and replaces them, which is why a gentle scrape collects so many.

notes: Divide often to replace worn skin
Most never divide after early life
Divide often; replaced every few days
Divide to make new blood cells
Divide quickly so hair keeps growing
reason: Most brain nerve cells do not divide after early life; the other four keep dividing.
explain: Cells that wear out quickly are replaced by cell division. Skin, gut lining, hair root and bone marrow cells divide all the time. Most nerve cells in the brain stop dividing early in life, so the ones you have now need to last for many years. This is one reason protecting your head with a helmet matters.
fact: The cells lining your gut are replaced every few days because food and digestive juices wear them down.

reason: Making sperm cells needs meiosis; the other four use mitosis.
explain: Cells divide in two ways. Mitosis makes two new cells that are exact copies of the old one, which is how you grow, heal and replace worn cells. Meiosis is used only to make egg and sperm cells. It halves the number of chromosomes from 46 to 23, so that a fertilised egg ends up with 46.
fact: Meiosis also shuffles genes, which is one reason brothers and sisters do not look exactly alike.

notes: Cotton swab picks up cheek cells
reason: Distilled water has no cells and so no DNA; the other four contain cells with DNA.
explain: DNA is kept inside the nucleus of cells. So anything that contains cells, like a hair with its root, saliva with cheek cells, blood with white cells, or a cotton swab rubbed inside the cheek, also contains DNA. Distilled water is pure water with no cells in it, so it has no DNA.
fact: A hair cut from the end has almost no usable DNA; the root is the part that holds living cells.

items: All life is made of cells
New cells come from old cells
Cell is the unit of life
notes: False; cells only come from cells
True; each cell lives and works
reason: Cells do not form from dust; the other four are true ideas from cell theory.
explain: Cell theory is one of the big ideas of biology. It says all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells come only from cells that already exist, by division. People once believed living things could appear from mud or dust, but careful experiments showed this does not happen.
fact: Cell theory was put together in the 1830s to 1850s by Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow.

notes: Brown stain used on onion peel
Blue stain used on cheek cells
Red stain used on plant cells
Pink stain used in medical labs
reason: Salt water adds no colour; the other four are stains for colouring cells.
explain: Many cell parts are almost see-through, so scientists add stains, which are coloured chemicals that soak into certain parts. Iodine, methylene blue, safranin and eosin each colour different parts, making the nucleus and other structures easy to see. Salt water is clear, so it cannot make anything show up.
fact: Hospital labs often use two stains together, one for the nucleus and one for the rest of the cell, to spot problems in tissue samples.

clues: Robert Hooke gave it its name in 1665 after looking at thin slices of cork.
Your body has trillions of these, and most can only be seen with a microscope.
An amoeba is made of just one of these, while you are made of many.
explain: The cell is the smallest part of a living thing that is itself alive. Some living things, like an amoeba, are a single cell, while a human is made of trillions. Groups of cells make tissues, and tissues make organs. Robert Hooke named them 'cells' because the boxes he saw in cork reminded him of small rooms.

clues: Bacteria and fungi have one too, but your own cells do not.
It is made of a tough material that also makes up paper and cotton.
Onion peel cells have this thick, firm layer around the membrane, giving them a fixed box shape.
explain: The cell wall is a firm layer around the outside of plant cells, outside the cell membrane. In plants it is made of cellulose, the same material as cotton and paper. It gives the cell a fixed shape and stops it bursting when it fills with water. Animal cells have no cell wall, which is why they can change shape.

clues: It is the top level: cells make tissues, tissues make organs, organs make systems, and systems make this.
It means any whole, separate creature that can grow and reproduce on its own.
A mango tree, a cat and an amoeba are each one of these.
explain: An organism is a complete living thing. It can be as small as one cell, like a bacterium, or made of trillions of cells, like a human or a tree. In large organisms, cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form organ systems that keep the whole organism alive.

clues: It has a single curved piece of glass held in a frame, usually with a handle.
Holding it over an ant makes the ant look several times larger.
In stories, a famous investigator carries one to study clues up close.
explain: A magnifying glass is a single curved lens that bends light so objects look larger, usually a few times their real size. That is enough to see an insect's legs but not individual cells. A microscope uses two or more lenses together to magnify hundreds of times, which is what you need to see cells.

clues: It is lowered gently at an angle so that no air bubbles get trapped.
It keeps the sample flat and stops it from drying out.
This small, see-through piece is placed on top of the sample before you look through the microscope.
explain: A cover slip is a very thin square of glass placed over a sample on a microscope slide. It flattens the sample into an even layer, keeps it moist and protects the lens. Lowering it slowly at an angle pushes air out, because bubbles can look like cells and confuse you.

clues: It usually has one big storage sac full of watery sap in its middle.
Its firm box made of cellulose gives it a neat, brick-like shape.
You find it in onion peel, tulsi and mango trees, and many of them can make food from sunlight.
explain: Plant cells have three things animal cells do not: a cell wall made of cellulose, chloroplasts that make food using sunlight, and a large central vacuole filled with sap. They also share parts with animal cells, such as the nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and mitochondria. Onion peel cells have no chloroplasts because they grow underground.

clues: The opposite word describes elephants, trees and you.
A creature described by this word must feed, move and reproduce with a body that is just a lone tiny unit.
Amoeba, paramecium and bacteria are described by this word.
explain: Unicellular means made of just one cell. In a unicellular organism, that one cell must do every job: take in food, release energy, get rid of waste, move and reproduce. Multicellular organisms like humans share these jobs among many specialised cells. 'Uni' means one, as in unicorn or uniform.

clues: Plant roots take in moisture from the soil mainly by this process.
Sprinkle salt on cucumber slices and liquid seeps out of them because of it.
Raisins soaked overnight swell up because of it.
explain: Osmosis is the movement of water through a membrane that lets water pass but holds back bigger particles like sugar and salt. Water moves from the side where it is more plentiful to the side where there is more dissolved stuff. A raisin is full of sugar, so water moves into it and it swells. Salt on cucumber pulls water out the same way.

clues: Gregor Mendel's experiments with pea plants were the first careful study of this.
It explains why a puppy grows into a dog like its mother and father, never a kitten.
It is the passing of features like eye colour from a mother and father to their children.
explain: Heredity is the passing of features from parents to their young through genes. Each child gets half its genes from the mother and half from the father, carried in the egg and sperm. This is why children often look like their parents, and why living things always produce young of their own kind.

clues: Gardeners make these when they grow a whole new rose bush from a cut piece of stem.
It is a living thing with exactly the same DNA as the one it came from.
In 1996, scientists in Scotland made a famous lamb this way, using a body cell from an adult.
explain: A clone is a living thing with the same DNA as the one it came from. Many plants make clones naturally, and gardeners make them from cuttings. Bacteria make clones every time they divide. In 1996, scientists made Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell.

clues: Without it, many parts of a cell look almost see-through under a microscope.
Safranin, often used on onion peel, is one kind.
A drop of it makes the nucleus show up dark and clear.
explain: A stain is a coloured chemical added to a sample on a slide. Different parts of a cell soak up the stain by different amounts, so the nucleus or the cell wall stands out. Without a stain, most cells are pale and hard to see under a light microscope.

clues: This English thinker also studied springs, and a law about stretching is named after him.
He wrote a famous book called Micrographia, full of drawings of tiny things.
He looked at thin slices of oak bark through his microscope and named the little boxes he saw after small rooms.
explain: Robert Hooke was an English scientist who, in 1665, looked at thin slices of cork through his microscope. He saw many small empty boxes and called them 'cells' because they reminded him of small rooms. Those were the walls of dead plant cells. His book Micrographia showed people a hidden world of tiny things for the first time.

clues: Its cells sit tightly side by side, like tiles on a floor.
It forms the inner surface of your mouth, stomach and gut.
The cells you gently scrape from inside your cheek belong to this type.
explain: Epithelium is a tissue made of tightly packed cells that covers surfaces and lines spaces in the body. It forms the outer layer of skin and lines the mouth, stomach, gut and blood vessels. Because the cells fit closely together, epithelium works like a protective barrier, keeping germs out and controlling what passes through.

clues: White blood cells have many of these to break down germs they swallow.
It is a tiny bag inside animal cells, holding strong chemicals that break things apart.
It is often called the cell's clean-up crew, breaking down worn-out parts.
explain: A lysosome is a small bag inside animal cells filled with enzymes, which are chemicals that break big molecules into small ones. It breaks down worn-out cell parts so their materials can be reused, and destroys germs that a cell has swallowed. Its membrane keeps the strong enzymes from damaging the rest of the cell.

clues: It is named after an Italian scientist, Camillo, who described it in nerve cells in 1898.
Under an electron microscope it looks like a stack of flat pouches, like a pile of pancakes.
It takes proteins made in the cell, wraps them in tiny bubbles and sends them where they are needed.
explain: The Golgi body, also called the Golgi apparatus, is a stack of flat membrane pouches inside the cell. It receives proteins and other materials, finishes them off, and packs them into tiny bubbles called vesicles. These are sent to other parts of the cell or out of it, a little like a post office sorting parcels.

clues: In humans, it happens only in the testes and the ovaries.
It ends with four new cells, each with a different mix of genes.
It makes cells with 23 chromosomes instead of 46, so that when two such cells join, the result has 46.
explain: Meiosis is a special kind of cell division used to make egg and sperm cells. It halves the number of chromosomes, from 46 to 23, and shuffles the genes. When an egg and sperm join at fertilisation, the new cell has 46 chromosomes again. Mitosis, the everyday kind of division, makes exact copies with 46.

clues: Euglena and many bacteria move using one of these.
It is a long, thin thread that sticks out from a cell and lashes back and forth.
The male cell that joins an egg uses one to travel towards it.
explain: A flagellum is a long, thin, whip-like thread that sticks out of some cells and moves them through liquid. Sperm cells, euglena and many bacteria use flagella. Cilia are similar but much shorter and come in large numbers, like the hairs that cover a paramecium. The plural of flagellum is flagella.

scenario: A student puts an onion peel slide under a microscope, but the picture looks blurry. What should she do?
optionNotes: Moves the lens to the sharp distance
Moves the sample and spills it
explain: A lens gives a sharp picture only when it is at the right distance from the sample. The focus knob moves the stage or lens up and down to find that distance. Start with the low-power lens and turn the knob slowly until the cells look clear.

scenario: A curious child asks the doctor what an ant, a banyan tree and her own body are all built from. What is the smallest living unit they share?
optionNotes: Smallest unit of every living thing
Made of tissues, so not smallest
Trees and ants have no bones
explain: Every living thing is made of one or more cells, and the cell is the smallest unit that is alive. Cells group into tissues, and tissues form organs. An ant, a tree and a child look very different, but all are built from cells.

scenario: Under a microscope, cells from a leaf are full of small green dots. What do these green parts do?
optionNotes: Job of white blood cells in animals
explain: The green dots are chloroplasts. They contain chlorophyll, a green substance that captures sunlight. Chloroplasts use that energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water, a process called photosynthesis. This sugar feeds the plant and, through food chains, nearly every animal.

scenario: A geneticist explains that the instructions for building and running your body are stored inside almost every cell. In which part of the cell are they kept?
explain: The nucleus is the control centre of the cell. It holds DNA, packed into chromosomes, which carries the instructions for making proteins and running the cell. Almost every body cell has a full set of these instructions. Mature red blood cells are an exception, as they lose their nucleus.

scenario: The mouth, stomach and intestines work together as a team to break down food. What is a team of organs like this called?
optionNotes: Several organs doing one big job
A small part inside a cell
explain: The body is organised in levels: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs that work on the same big job form an organ system. The mouth, stomach and intestines belong to the digestive system. Other organ systems include the circulatory system and the nervous system.

scenario: A neurologist shows a picture of nerve cells. They are very long and have many thin branches at their ends. What is their main job?
optionNotes: Long shape reaches far; branches connect
explain: In the body, a cell's shape often matches its job. Nerve cells are long so they can carry electrical messages over large distances, such as from your spine to your toes. Their branches connect with many other cells, so messages can be passed on quickly.

scenario: A scientist studies the thin, flexible layer around a cheek cell. It lets food and oxygen in and lets waste out. What is this layer?
optionNotes: Animal cells like cheek cells lack one
Flexible layer that controls entry and exit
explain: Every cell is wrapped in a cell membrane. It is thin and flexible and lets only certain substances in and out, so it is called 'selectively permeable'. Plant cells also have a firm cell wall outside the membrane, but animal cells such as cheek cells do not.

scenario: A student is told to peel the thinnest possible layer of onion skin for her slide. Why must it be so thin?
options: So light can pass through it
So it fits in the eyepiece
answer: So light can pass through it
optionNotes: Not the reason; living or not, thick layers block light
Thick layers block light and overlap
Smell does not affect the view
The sample goes on the stage, not the eyepiece
explain: A school microscope shines light up through the sample. If the sample is thick, light cannot get through and many layers of cells pile on top of each other, so you see a dark blur. A layer one cell thick lets light through and shows each cell clearly.

scenario: A single cell in a dish divides into two. Each new cell divides again, and then again. How many cells are there after three rounds of division?
optionNotes: That would be adding, not doubling
That counts the rounds, not the cells
explain: In cell division one cell becomes two, so the number doubles each round: 1, 2, 4, 8. Doubling grows numbers very fast. After 20 rounds, one cell would become over a million cells, which is how a single fertilised egg can grow into a body with trillions of cells.

scenario: A microscope's eyepiece lens magnifies 10 times and its objective lens magnifies 40 times. How many times bigger does the cell look?
optionNotes: Adds the numbers instead of multiplying
explain: In a microscope, the objective lens makes a bigger image, and the eyepiece makes that image bigger again. So the two magnifications multiply: 10 × 40 = 400. At 400 times, a cheek cell looks large enough for you to see its nucleus clearly.

scenario: On the underside of a leaf, a student sees pairs of bean-shaped cells around tiny holes. What is the job of these paired cells?
explain: These are guard cells, and the holes are called stomata. When guard cells fill with water, they bend apart and the hole opens to let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out. When they lose water, they close the hole so the plant does not dry out.

scenario: A brother and sister have the same mother and father, yet they look quite different. Why?
options: Each got a different mix of genes
Only one got genes from their mother
answer: Each got a different mix of genes
optionNotes: Food affects health, not eye colour
Each egg and sperm carries a different mix
Cell number does not set looks
Every child gets genes from both parents
explain: Each child gets half their genes from their mother and half from their father. But every egg and every sperm carries a different shuffled half, so each child gets a different combination. Only identical twins, who come from one fertilised egg, share the same genes.

scenario: A potted plant is not watered for days, and its leaves droop. Inside its cells, which part has shrunk the most?
optionNotes: Stays firm and keeps its shape
Does not store the cell's water
Its water store empties, so the cell goes soft
Make food; not the water store
explain: A plant cell's large vacuole is a sac full of watery sap. When it is full, it presses outward against the cell wall and keeps the cell firm, like air in a tyre. When the plant runs short of water, the vacuoles shrink, cells go soft and the leaves droop. Watering refills them.

scenario: Some cells in the pancreas make large amounts of proteins to send out. Under an electron microscope, they are packed with tiny dots that build proteins. What are these dots?
optionNotes: Found in plant cells; make sugar
explain: Ribosomes are tiny structures that build proteins by joining amino acids in the order set by the cell's DNA. Cells that make a lot of protein, such as pancreas cells that make digestive enzymes and insulin, are crowded with ribosomes. A cell's parts often show what job it does.

scenario: Under an electron microscope, a bacterium and a human cheek cell are compared. The cheek cell has a part that the bacterium does not. Which part?
optionNotes: Bacteria keep DNA loose, with no nucleus
explain: Bacteria are simple cells. Their DNA floats in the cytoplasm instead of sitting inside a nucleus wrapped in a membrane. Human, animal, plant and fungus cells all have a true nucleus. Both kinds of cell have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes.

scenario: A skin cell and a nerve cell from the same person carry exactly the same DNA, yet they look and work very differently. Why?
options: Each uses a different set of its genes
answer: Each uses a different set of its genes
optionNotes: The question says the DNA is the same
Genes are switched on or off by cell type
Nerve cells carry a full set of genes
explain: Almost every cell in your body has the same full set of genes, like the same recipe book. But each cell type only uses the recipes it needs. Nerve cells switch on genes for carrying messages, and skin cells switch on genes for making tough keratin. This is how one fertilised egg gives rise to hundreds of different cell types.

notes: Stiff outer layer of plant cells
Thin skin that controls what enters
reason: Animal cells have no cell wall; the other four are found in animal cells.
explain: Animal cells, like the ones in your body, have a nucleus, a cell membrane, cytoplasm and mitochondria. Plant cells have all of these too, plus a stiff cell wall outside the membrane. The cell wall is made of a tough material called cellulose, which helps plants stand upright without bones.
fact: Cotton and paper are made mostly of cellulose from old plant cell walls.

notes: A fungus that grows on damp ground
Green plant that grows in lawns
reason: A pebble is non-living and not made of cells; the rest are living things made of cells.
explain: Every living thing is made of one or more cells. The cell is the smallest unit that can carry out life jobs like taking in food, growing and making more of itself. A pebble is made of minerals, not cells, so it cannot grow, feed or reproduce.

notes: Single cell big enough to hold
reason: An ostrich egg is a single cell you can see without a microscope; the others need a microscope.
explain: Most cells are far too small to see with your eyes, so we need a microscope. They are measured in micrometres, and a thousand micrometres fit in one millimetre. An unfertilised ostrich egg is a rare exception: it is one single cell, filled with stored food, and it is the largest single cell known.
fact: About 130 red blood cells lined up side by side would stretch roughly one millimetre.

notes: Whole living thing in one cell
reason: An amoeba is unicellular (one cell); the others are multicellular.
explain: Some living things are made of just one cell. They are called unicellular, and that one cell must eat, move and reproduce by itself. Multicellular living things, like trees, cats and you, are made of many cells that share the work, with different cells doing different jobs.

reason: A root hair cell is a plant cell; the others are human cells.
explain: Your body has about 200 kinds of cells, each shaped for its job. Nerve cells are long to carry messages, and muscle cells are long and stretchy so they can shorten. Root hair cells belong to plants: they have a long thin finger that reaches into the soil to soak up water.

notes: Organ that processes food and chemicals
reason: A neuron is one cell; the other four are whole organs.
explain: The body is built in levels. Cells group into tissues, tissues group into organs, and organs work together as organ systems. A neuron is a single nerve cell, the lowest level. The heart, liver, stomach and brain are organs, each made of several tissues working together.

reason: A scar comes from an injury during life; the others are inherited through genes.
explain: Inherited traits are passed from parents to children through genes, which are instructions stored in DNA. Eye colour, blood group, natural hair colour and earlobe shape all come from these instructions. A scar forms when skin repairs a wound, so it is not in your genes and cannot be passed on to your children.

reason: Uracil is found in RNA, not DNA; the other four are the four DNA bases.
explain: DNA is written in a code of four chemical 'letters' called bases: A (adenine), T (thymine), G (guanine) and C (cytosine). A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C, which holds the two strands of DNA together. Cells copy parts of DNA into a related molecule called RNA, which uses U (uracil) in place of T.
fact: If the DNA in one of your cells were stretched out, it would be about 2 metres long.

reason: Xylem is a plant tissue; the other four are the main animal tissue types.
explain: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing the same job. Animals have four main tissue types: muscle (movement), nerve (signals), epithelial (covering and lining) and connective (support, like bone and blood). Xylem is a plant tissue made of tubes that carry water from the roots up to the leaves.

notes: Short sections of DNA with instructions
Small dense spot that builds ribosomes
reason: The cell membrane wraps the whole cell; the other four are found inside the nucleus.
explain: The nucleus is the control centre of the cell. Inside it, long DNA molecules are wound into chromosomes, and sections of DNA called genes carry instructions. The nucleolus is a dense spot that helps build ribosomes. The cell membrane is outside the nucleus: it wraps the whole cell and decides what goes in and out.

reason: Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus; the others do.
explain: Most body cells keep a nucleus all their life. Red blood cells push their nucleus out as they mature, which leaves more room for haemoglobin, the substance that carries oxygen. Without a nucleus they cannot repair themselves, so each one lasts only about 120 days before it is replaced.

notes: Green single cell with a whip-like tail
Not a cell; needs a host cell
reason: A virus is not a cell; the other four are living things made of one cell.
explain: A virus is much smaller than a cell and is just genetic material inside a protein coat. It has no cytoplasm or membrane of its own and cannot grow or copy itself alone. It must enter a living cell and use that cell's machinery to make new viruses. Yeast, amoeba, paramecium and euglena are each a complete living thing made of one cell.

reason: The stomach is a single organ; the others are organ systems.
explain: An organ system is a team of organs that work together for one big job. The digestive system includes the mouth, stomach, intestines and liver. The stomach on its own is one organ, one member of that team. Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, and organs make organ systems.

notes: Protein that makes skin stretchy and strong
reason: Glucose is a sugar; the other four are proteins.
explain: Genes are instructions for making proteins. Small parts in the cell called ribosomes read a copy of a gene and join building blocks called amino acids in the right order to make a protein. Keratin, haemoglobin, collagen and the enzyme amylase are all proteins built this way. Glucose is a sugar, not a protein, and is not made directly from a gene.

notes: Said all animals are made of cells
Said all plants are made of cells
reason: Newton studied gravity and motion; the others are known for discovering and explaining cells.
explain: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at thin slices of cork and saw tiny boxes he called 'cells'. Anton van Leeuwenhoek built strong lenses and was the first to see living microbes. Schleiden and Schwann later concluded that all plants and animals are made of cells, which became part of the cell theory. Isaac Newton is famous for gravity and light, not cells.

reason: The mouth lining is epithelial tissue; the other four are connective tissues.
explain: Connective tissue supports, joins or carries things around the body, and its cells sit in a material called matrix. In bone the matrix is hard, in cartilage it is bendy, and in blood it is a liquid called plasma. Epithelial tissue is different: its cells are packed tightly into sheets that cover surfaces, like your skin or the inside of your mouth.

notes: Coloured dye that shows cell parts
Thin glass laid over the sample
Adds drops of water or stain
reason: A stethoscope is for listening to the body; the others are used to prepare a microscope slide.
explain: To look at cells, you place a thin sample on a glass slide, add a drop of water or stain with a dropper, and gently lower a thin cover slip on top. The stain colours parts like the nucleus so they are easier to see. A stethoscope is a doctor's tool for listening to sounds inside the body, not for looking at cells.

clues: Red blood cells lose this part as they mature, but most other body cells keep it.
This round part holds the chromosomes and is wrapped in its own membrane.
It is often called the cell's boss because it gives instructions to the rest of the cell.
explain: The nucleus is the control centre of most cells. It holds DNA, the instructions for building and running the cell, wrapped up in chromosomes. A membrane around the nucleus keeps the DNA safe while still letting messages pass in and out.

clues: Robert Hooke used an early one in 1665 to look at cork.
You put a glass slide on its stage and turn a knob to focus.
This tool makes tiny things like cells look big enough to see.
explain: A microscope uses lenses to make tiny objects look much bigger. A school light microscope can magnify about 400 times, enough to see cells and their nucleus. Without microscopes, nobody would have discovered that living things are made of cells.

clues: Blood, bone and fat are all examples of this.
It is the level of the body that sits between a single unit of life and a whole heart or liver.
It is a team of similar building blocks that all do the same job.
explain: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together on one job. Muscle tissue contracts, nerve tissue carries signals, and epithelial tissue covers surfaces. Different tissues then join to form organs, like the stomach or heart.

clues: Police can compare it from a single hair root to identify a person.
It is a very long molecule shaped like a twisted ladder.
It holds the instructions you inherited from your parents.
explain: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the molecule that stores the instructions for building and running a living thing. It looks like a twisted ladder, and the order of its chemical 'letters' spells out the instructions. You get half your DNA from your mother and half from your father.
fact: About 99.9% of the DNA of any two people is the same.

clues: Animal cells do not have this part, but many plant cells do.
It contains a pigment called chlorophyll.
This part of a plant cell uses light energy to make food from water and carbon dioxide.
explain: Chloroplasts are small green parts found in leaf cells and other green parts of plants. They hold chlorophyll, which captures light energy. Using that energy, the plant turns water and carbon dioxide into sugar for food and gives out oxygen. This process is called photosynthesis.

clues: The skin is the largest one in your body.
It is built from different layers of cells that share one big job.
The liver, stomach and brain are each an example of this.
explain: An organ is a body part made of different tissues that work together on a big job. The stomach, for example, has muscle tissue to churn food, epithelial tissue to line it, and nerve tissue to control it. Several organs together form an organ system.
fact: The skin of an adult weighs about 4 kilograms and is the body's largest organ.

clues: It has no fixed shape and keeps changing its outline.
It wraps around tiny bits of food to swallow them.
This tiny creature moves by pushing out finger-like bulges of its body.
explain: An amoeba is a living thing made of just one cell. It moves by pushing out bulges called pseudopodia, which means 'false feet', and flowing into them. To eat, it surrounds a food particle with these bulges and takes it inside. When it grows big enough, it splits in two to make new amoebae.

clues: Many chemical reactions of the cell take place here.
Mitochondria and ribosomes float in it.
It fills the space between the outer membrane and the nucleus.
explain: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like material that fills a cell, between the cell membrane and the nucleus. It is mostly water with dissolved food, salts and other chemicals. The cell's small working parts, called organelles, sit in it, and many of the cell's reactions happen there.

clues: Muscle cells have large numbers of these tiny bean-shaped parts.
They have their own small piece of DNA, passed down only from your mother.
They use oxygen to release the power stored in food.
explain: Mitochondria are small bean-shaped parts inside cells. They use oxygen to break down food such as glucose and release energy the cell can use. This process is called cellular respiration. Busy cells, like muscle and heart cells, have many mitochondria because they need lots of energy.

clues: They become easy to see under a microscope just before a cell divides.
Half of yours came from your mother and half from your father.
These thread-like bundles in the nucleus are made of tightly coiled genetic material.
explain: Chromosomes are thread-like structures in the nucleus made of DNA wrapped tightly around proteins. Human body cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: one of each pair from your mother and one from your father. Packing DNA this way lets a very long molecule fit inside a tiny nucleus.

clues: It is so thin that you cannot see its structure even with a school microscope.
It lets oxygen and water through but keeps many other substances out.
Both plant and animal cells have this thin wrapper; in plants it sits just inside a stiffer covering.
explain: The cell membrane is a very thin, flexible layer around every cell. It is 'selectively permeable', which means it lets some substances in and out while blocking others. This keeps the inside of the cell stable. In plant cells, a stiff cell wall sits outside the membrane.

clues: When a plant does not get enough to drink, this part shrinks and the plant droops.
In plant cells it can fill most of the inside of the cell.
It is a bag filled with cell sap that helps keep plant cells firm.
explain: A vacuole is a membrane bag inside a cell that stores water, food and waste. Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole full of cell sap. When it is full it presses outward and keeps the cell firm, which keeps the plant upright. Animal cells have only small vacuoles, or none.

clues: Scientists have counted about 20,000 of these in a human.
Each one is a short section of a chromosome.
It is one instruction that helps decide things like your eye colour.
explain: A gene is a section of DNA that carries the instructions for making one protein or controlling one feature. Genes come in pairs, one from each parent, which is why children look a bit like both. Humans have about 20,000 genes spread across 46 chromosomes.

clues: It is how a cut on your knee gets new skin.
Before it begins, the cell makes a full duplicate set of chromosomes.
This process turns one body cell into a pair of identical cells.
explain: Mitosis is the way a body cell divides to make two new cells that are exact copies of it. First the cell copies all its chromosomes, then it shares them equally between the two new cells. Mitosis lets you grow, heals cuts, and replaces old cells such as skin cells.

clues: It is one of the smallest parts of a cell and has no membrane around it.
Thousands of them sit in the cytoplasm or stick to a folded network of tubes.
It reads a copy of a gene and links small units together in the right order.
explain: Ribosomes are tiny structures that make proteins. They read a message copied from a gene and join amino acids in the exact order that message says. Every living cell, even a bacterium, has ribosomes, because every cell needs proteins to survive.

clues: Too much ultraviolet light from the sun can cause these in skin cells.
Most of them are harmless, a few cause problems, and a few can be useful.
It happens when a letter in the genetic code is copied wrongly or damaged.
explain: A mutation is a change in the DNA code. It can happen when a cell copies its DNA and makes a small slip, or when things like strong sunlight damage DNA. Cells have repair systems that fix most of these changes. Over many generations, some mutations give living things new features, which is part of how species change.

clues: It is why the smell of food cooking reaches you in another room.
Oxygen gets into your cells this way without the cell spending energy.
Substances drift from where there is a lot of them to where there is little.
explain: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a place where they are crowded to a place where they are fewer, until they are evenly spread. It needs no energy from the cell. Oxygen diffuses into cells because there is more of it outside, and carbon dioxide diffuses out because there is more of it inside.

scenario: A doctor gently scrapes the inside of a patient's cheek with a clean wooden stick and smears the cells onto a glass slide. Which tool should be used to look at the cells?
optionNotes: Listens to heart and lung sounds
explain: Cheek cells are far too small to see with your eyes, so a pathologist uses a microscope. Its lenses magnify the cells hundreds of times. Looking at cells this way helps doctors find out whether cells are healthy or not.

scenario: A child scrapes her knee. A week later the wound has closed with new skin. Where did the new skin come from?
options: Healthy skin cells nearby divided to make new cells
Skin cells travelled from the face
answer: Healthy skin cells nearby divided to make new cells
optionNotes: A plaster only covers and protects
A clot only seals the wound for a while
Skin cells do not travel around the body
explain: New cells only come from existing cells. When skin is damaged, healthy skin cells at the edges of the wound divide again and again by mitosis, and the new cells fill the gap. The blood clot and scab only protect the wound while this repair happens underneath.

scenario: A girl has her mother's curly hair and her father's brown eyes. What in her cells carries the instructions for these features?
optionNotes: Makes up most of the cell
explain: Genes are sections of DNA that hold instructions for features like hair type and eye colour. A child gets one set of genes from the mother and one from the father. That mix is why children often have some features from each parent.

scenario: A student looks at a thin onion peel under a microscope. She sees brick-shaped cells, each with a thick, firm outer layer. Which part gives these cells their fixed shape?
explain: Onion cells are plant cells, so they have a cell wall outside the cell membrane. The cell wall is made of cellulose and is stiff, which gives each cell a fixed, box-like shape. Animal cells have no cell wall, so cells like cheek cells have rounder, irregular shapes.

scenario: A drop of pond water under the microscope shows a single cell shaped like a slipper. It is covered in tiny hairs that beat together to make it swim. What is it?
optionNotes: Too small for a school microscope
explain: Paramecium is a one-celled organism that lives in ponds. Its surface is covered in tiny hairs called cilia, which beat like oars to push it through water and sweep food into its mouth-like groove. An amoeba, by contrast, has no fixed shape and crawls using bulges of its body.

scenario: The heart is made of muscle tissue, nerve tissue and connective tissue working together to pump blood. What level of body organisation is the heart?
explain: Living things are built in levels: cells, then tissues, then organs, then organ systems. The heart is an organ because it is made of several different tissues that work together for one job. The heart joins with blood vessels and blood to form the circulatory system.

scenario: Under the microscope, a student's cheek cells look almost see-through, and she cannot spot the nucleus. What should she add to the slide?
options: Nothing; cheek cells have no nucleus
A drop of stain such as methylene blue
answer: A drop of stain such as methylene blue
optionNotes: Cheek cells do have a nucleus
Colours cell parts so they show
explain: Most cells are nearly colourless, so their parts are hard to see. A stain is a dye that soaks into some cell parts more than others. Methylene blue colours the nucleus darker blue, so it stands out clearly against the rest of the cell. Plant cells such as onion peel are often stained with iodine.

scenario: Two babies are born and tests show they have exactly the same DNA. What explains this?
options: They were born on the same day
They grew from one fertilised egg that split in two
They grew from two separate eggs
answer: They grew from one fertilised egg that split in two
explain: Identical twins form when one fertilised egg divides into two separate embryos early on. Because they started as the same cell, they share the same DNA. Non-identical twins come from two different eggs, each fertilised by a different sperm, so their DNA is as different as that of ordinary brothers and sisters.

scenario: An egg cell always carries an X chromosome. A sperm cell carries either an X or a Y. What decides whether a baby is a boy or a girl?
options: Whether the egg carries X or Y
Whether the sperm carries X or Y
The month the baby is born
answer: Whether the sperm carries X or Y
optionNotes: XX makes a girl, XY a boy
Birth month does not decide this
explain: Humans have one pair of sex chromosomes. Girls usually have XX and boys usually have XY. The egg always gives an X, so the baby's sex depends on the sperm: a sperm with an X makes XX (a girl), and a sperm with a Y makes XY (a boy).

scenario: A pathologist compares muscle cells from an athlete's leg with fat cells. The muscle cells are packed with one kind of tiny part. Which part helps them release lots of energy?
explain: Muscles need a lot of energy to contract. Mitochondria release this energy by breaking down food using oxygen, a process called respiration. Cells that work hard, like muscle cells, have many more mitochondria than less active cells. Regular exercise can increase the number of mitochondria in muscle cells.

scenario: In a lab, red blood cells are placed in pure water. Water flows in until the cells swell and burst. Why does the water move in?
options: Water moves through the membrane to where water is less concentrated
answer: Water moves through the membrane to where water is less concentrated
optionNotes: Red blood cells have no nucleus
explain: This movement is called osmosis. Water moves across a membrane from where there is more water (pure water) to where there is less water (the salty inside of the cell). Animal cells have no cell wall, so they swell until they burst. That is why fluids put into a patient's vein are mixed to match the saltiness of blood.

scenario: A geneticist counts the chromosomes in the nucleus of a normal human skin cell. How many does she find?
optionNotes: Found in egg and sperm cells
explain: Normal human body cells have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs. Egg and sperm cells have only 23, one from each pair. When an egg and sperm join, the new cell has 46 again, half from each parent.

scenario: A scientist needs to see the shape of a virus, which is about a hundred times smaller than a typical body cell. Which instrument should she use?
optionNotes: Uses electrons; magnifies over a million times
Good for cells, too weak for viruses
explain: A light microscope uses light and can show objects down to about the size of bacteria. Viruses are smaller than that. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light, so it can show far tinier objects, including viruses and the inside parts of cells.

scenario: Your body replaces millions of blood cells every second. Special cells in the bone marrow can turn into red cells, white cells or platelets. What are these cells called?
explain: Stem cells are cells that have not yet chosen a job. When they divide, some new cells stay as stem cells and others mature into specialised cells. Blood stem cells in bone marrow keep making new red cells, white cells and platelets throughout life. Doctors can use donated stem cells to treat some blood diseases.
