scenario: Gregor Mendel crossed tall pea plants with short pea plants. All the young plants grew tall. What word describes the 'tall' version of the gene?
optionNotes: Shows up even with one copy
Hidden when paired with a stronger version
explain: Each plant gets two copies of a gene, one from each parent. A dominant version shows its effect even if only one copy is present. The young plants each had one 'tall' copy and one 'short' copy, and only the dominant tall version showed. The short version is called recessive; it shows only when a plant has two copies of it.
fact: Mendel studied about 28,000 pea plants in a monastery garden in the 1850s and 1860s.

scenario: Investigators find a single hair, with its root, at a scene. To check whose hair it is, what should the lab compare with samples from suspects?
optionNotes: Many people share it, and dye changes it
explain: Every person's DNA is slightly different, except for identical twins. Cells in a hair root contain DNA, so a lab can read parts of it and compare the pattern with samples from suspects. This method is called DNA fingerprinting, and it was first developed in 1984.

notes: Two, one each side of the spine
Two, one each side of the heart
Only one, low in the belly
Two, one each side of the nose
Two, one each side of the head
reason: You have only one bladder; the other organs come in pairs.
explain: Many organs come in pairs: two kidneys, two lungs, two eyes and two ears. Having two gives a backup, which is why a person can live well with one healthy kidney. The bladder is a single stretchy bag low in the belly. Both kidneys send urine down to this one bladder, which stores it.

notes: Holding urine for hours is not good
Too much salt makes kidneys work harder
Adds sugar, not a kidney-friendly habit
reason: Sugary drinks every day do not help the kidneys; the other four are kidney-friendly habits.
explain: Your kidneys filter all your blood many times a day. Drinking enough water keeps urine flowing, and going to the toilet when you feel the urge helps keep the urinary tract healthy. Less salt and regular activity help keep blood pressure normal, which protects the kidneys' tiny filters. Plain water is a better everyday drink than sugary ones.

notes: Hard tissue that holds you up
Red fluid pumped by the heart
reason: Bone is a hard, solid tissue; the other four are body fluids.
explain: Your body has several fluids that move things around or carry waste out. Blood carries oxygen and food, lymph drains extra fluid from tissues, urine carries waste from the kidneys, and sweat cools the skin. All of them are mostly water. Bone is a solid tissue hardened with calcium.

notes: Exercise makes you sweat a lot
A high temperature loses extra water
reason: Reading in a cool room does not make you lose much extra water; the other four do.
explain: You need extra water whenever your body is losing more than usual. Heat and exercise make you sweat, fever raises water loss through skin and breath, and diarrhoea carries water out with loose stools. If this water is not replaced, you can become dehydrated. Sitting quietly somewhere cool uses much less.

reason: The uterus is a reproductive organ; the other four belong to the urinary system.
explain: These words sound alike, but they mean different things. Urea is a waste, urine is the liquid that carries it, ureters carry urine from kidneys to bladder, and the urethra carries it out of the body. The uterus is part of the female reproductive system; it is where a baby grows before birth.

notes: Extra salt raises calcium in urine
Keeps urine dilute; lowers the risk
Less water is left for urine
reason: Drinking plenty of water lowers the risk of kidney stones; the other four raise it.
explain: Kidney stones form when minerals in urine become so concentrated that they make crystals, which slowly grow. Not drinking enough, sweating a lot and eating a lot of salt all make urine more concentrated or richer in minerals. Some families are more likely to get stones too. Drinking plenty of water keeps urine dilute, so crystals are less likely to form.

notes: Turned into urea by the liver
reason: Oxygen is something cells need; the other four are wastes the body must get rid of.
explain: Cells make waste as they work. Using food for energy makes carbon dioxide, which you breathe out. Breaking down protein makes ammonia, which the liver turns into urea for the kidneys to remove. Muscles make creatinine. Oxygen is the opposite: your cells need a steady supply of it to release energy from food.

notes: White cells wait there to fight germs
reason: Making urine is the kidneys' job; the other four are jobs of the spleen.
explain: The spleen is a soft organ in the upper left of the belly, behind the ribs. It filters blood: it removes old red blood cells and traps germs. It also holds white blood cells that fight infection and keeps a reserve of some blood cells. People can live without a spleen, but they may catch some infections more easily.

notes: Wrong: the bladder only stores urine
Sent out with bile into the gut
reason: The bladder stores urine but does not make it; the other four pairs are correct.
explain: Several organs help remove waste. The lungs breathe out carbon dioxide, the kidneys make urine to carry urea away, the skin loses salts in sweat, and the liver sends pigments from old red blood cells out in bile. The bladder only stores urine that the kidneys have already made, until you go to the toilet.

notes: Taken back as the body needs
reason: Creatinine is a waste left in the urine; the kidneys take the other four back into the blood.
explain: Kidney filters push water and many small molecules out of the blood, both useful and waste. The tubules then take the useful ones back into the blood: glucose, amino acids, needed salts and most of the water. This is called reabsorption. Wastes such as creatinine are left behind and leave the body in urine.

notes: Tells the brain when to go
reason: Filtering blood is the kidneys' job; the other four are things the bladder does.
explain: The bladder is a stretchy, muscular bag that holds urine. As it fills, its walls stretch and nerves tell your brain it is time to find a toilet. When you go, its muscle walls squeeze and push urine out through the urethra. The kidneys do the filtering and make the urine in the first place.

notes: May be a sign of diabetes
May mean a stone or infection
White cells and germs show up
reason: A urine test cannot show a broken bone; it can find the other four.
explain: A urine test is quick and painless, and it tells doctors a lot. Healthy urine has almost no sugar, protein or blood. Finding them can point to problems such as diabetes, leaky kidney filters, a stone or an infection. A broken bone is checked with an X-ray picture instead.

notes: Extra water comes out as urine
Water leaves as sweat, so less urine
Body sends more blood to the core
reason: Sweating a lot makes you pass less urine; the other four tend to make you pass more.
explain: Your kidneys balance water. When you take in extra water from drinks or watery foods, they make more urine to remove it. In the cold, the body sends more blood to its core, and the kidneys respond by making more urine. When you sweat a lot, water is already leaving through the skin, so the kidneys save water and make less urine.

notes: Clusters at the tops of the legs
Dead tissue with no lymph nodes
reason: Fingernails have no lymph nodes; the other places have clusters of them.
explain: Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped lumps that filter lymph, the fluid drained from your tissues. They sit in clusters along lymph vessels, with large groups in the neck, armpits, groin and belly. White blood cells inside them trap germs. Fingernails are made of hard, non-living keratin and have no lymph nodes.

notes: Takes cleaned blood away from the kidney
Main vein returning to the heart
reason: The ureter carries urine; the other four are blood vessels.
explain: Blood reaches each kidney through a renal artery that branches off the aorta, the body's biggest artery. After filtering, cleaner blood leaves through a renal vein and flows into the vena cava, the large vein that returns blood to the heart. The ureter is a different kind of tube: it carries urine from the kidney down to the bladder.

notes: Extra fluid builds up in tissues
Clears the nose; not a kidney sign
reason: Sneezing is not a sign of kidney trouble; the other four can be.
explain: When kidneys are not working well, water and salt can build up, causing puffiness around the eyes and ankles and raising blood pressure. Damaged filters may let protein leak into urine, which can make it foamy, and a person may pass much less urine. A doctor checks these signs with urine and blood tests. Sneezing is the nose clearing out dust or germs.

notes: Useful things taken back into blood
Tubule adds extra wastes to the fluid
Ducts gather urine from many nephrons
reason: Emulsification happens in digestion; the other four are steps in making urine in the kidney.
explain: Each nephron makes urine in steps. Filtration pushes fluid out of the blood in the glomerulus. Reabsorption takes useful things back into the blood. Secretion moves some extra wastes from the blood into the tubule. Collecting ducts then gather the finished urine. Emulsification is a digestion word: bile breaking fat into tiny droplets.

clues: More than half of your body weight is made of this.
It makes up about 95% of urine and nearly all of sweat.
It falls as rain and comes out of the tap, and it is the best choice when you are hot after playing.
explain: Water makes up more than half of your body. It carries nutrients in blood, carries waste out in urine, and cools you as sweat. You lose water all day through urine, sweat and breath, so you need to replace it. Plain water does this without adding sugar.

clues: Urea, carbon dioxide and creatinine are all examples of this.
Cells make it as a leftover while they work, and it can harm you if it builds up.
Kidneys, lungs and skin all help get rid of this from your body.
explain: Your cells are always working, and like any factory they make leftovers. These wastes include carbon dioxide from releasing energy and urea from breaking down protein. If they built up they would harm you, so the lungs, kidneys, skin and liver work together to remove them. Removing body waste is called excretion.

clues: In the kidneys, this happens in tiny balls of blood vessels inside each nephron.
Small things like water, salt and urea are pushed through, while blood cells stay behind.
When you make tea, you pour it through a mesh so the leaves stay back; this works the same way.
explain: Filtration lets small things pass through a barrier while holding big things back. In the kidney, blood pressure pushes water, salts, glucose and urea out of tiny capillaries in the glomerulus. Blood cells and most proteins are too big to pass, so they stay in the blood. This is the first step in making urine.

clues: It is common in young children and usually stops on its own as they grow.
It is nobody's fault, and a doctor can suggest simple ways to help.
It happens when the bladder empties while a child is dozing and the brain does not wake them in time.
explain: Bedwetting happens when the bladder empties during sleep. The brain and bladder take time to learn to work together at night, and some children take longer than others. It is common, often runs in families, and usually stops with age. Going to the toilet before bed helps, and a doctor can help if it continues.

clues: It can follow years of very high blood pressure or diabetes that is not well controlled.
Urea and creatinine build up in the blood, and the person may feel tired, itchy and puffy.
Both bean-shaped filters can no longer clean the blood well enough, so a machine or a donated organ is needed.
explain: Kidney failure means the kidneys can no longer filter the blood well enough to keep a person healthy. Wastes, extra water and salts build up, causing tiredness, itching and swelling. Long-term high blood pressure and diabetes are common causes. Treatment is dialysis, which cleans the blood with a machine, or a kidney transplant.

clues: Hundreds of these bean-shaped lumps sit along a network of thin vessels that drain fluid from your tissues.
They act like checkpoints, packed with white blood cells that trap and fight invaders.
When you have a sore throat, a doctor may feel for tender, puffed-up ones under your jaw.
explain: Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped structures along the lymph vessels. Lymph, the fluid drained from tissues, passes through them before returning to the blood. White blood cells inside the nodes catch and destroy germs. When they are busy fighting an infection, they can become larger and tender.

clues: People who have this take medicines every day so their body accepts the gift.
It can free a person whose kidneys have failed from needing dialysis.
A medical team places a healthy bean-shaped organ from another person into the patient's body.
explain: In a kidney transplant, a healthy kidney from another person is placed in someone whose own kidneys have failed. One working kidney can do the job of two. The patient takes daily medicines to stop the immune system from attacking the kidney. A living family member can donate one kidney and stay healthy with the other.

clues: Many newborn babies get a mild form of it in their first week, and it usually clears up.
It happens when a pigment from old red blood cells builds up because it is not cleared fast enough.
A person with it can look golden or lemon-coloured, which a doctor checks in daylight.
explain: When old red blood cells are broken down, a yellow pigment called bilirubin is made. The liver normally clears it into bile. If too much is made, or the liver cannot clear it fast enough, it builds up and turns the skin and the whites of the eyes yellow. This is jaundice; it is a sign, and doctors look for the cause.

clues: It is a medical emergency, so an ambulance should be called straight away.
The body's cooling system fails, and the person may become confused and stop sweating.
It can strike after hard exercise or long hours outside on a scorching day if the body overheats.
explain: Heatstroke happens when the body gets so hot that it can no longer cool itself. Body temperature rises very high, and the person may become confused, stop sweating or faint. It is an emergency: call for help and cool the person down while waiting. Drinking water, resting in shade and avoiding hard exercise in the hottest hours help prevent it.

clues: Some bacteria, mushrooms and plants make these.
The body breaks them down or removes them, mostly in a large organ on the right of the belly and in the kidneys.
It is a substance that can damage the body even in small amounts, like the venom of a cobra.
explain: A toxin is a poisonous substance made by a living thing, such as certain bacteria, plants or snakes. The liver changes many harmful substances into safer forms, and the kidneys then remove them in urine. Some toxins are too strong for this, which is why doctors use treatments such as antivenom.

clues: Its parts include two tubes called ureters and one called the urethra.
This body system cleans your blood and removes liquid waste.
It includes two bean-shaped filters and a stretchy bag that holds liquid until you go to the toilet.
explain: The urinary system is made of two kidneys, two ureters, the bladder and the urethra. The kidneys filter blood and make urine, the ureters carry it down, the bladder stores it, and the urethra carries it out. Together they remove waste and keep the right amount of water and salt in your body.

clues: The fluid it collects goes straight on into a long, twisting tubule.
It is found in the outer layer of the kidney, at the start of each tiny unit.
This hollow, double-walled pouch wraps around a ball of capillaries and catches the fluid pushed out of them.
explain: Each nephron begins with a Bowman's capsule, a cup-shaped pouch wrapped around a ball of capillaries called the glomerulus. Blood pressure pushes fluid out of the capillaries, and the capsule catches it. The fluid then flows into the tubule, where useful things are taken back into the blood.
fact: It is named after William Bowman, an English surgeon who described it in 1842.

clues: Without this step, you would lose about 180 litres of fluid a day as urine.
Glucose, amino acids, useful salts and most of the water are rescued this way.
After the first filtering, this step moves the good stuff from the kidney's tiny tubes into the blood again.
explain: Kidney filtration is not choosy, so useful things leave the blood along with waste. Reabsorption fixes that. As the fluid flows along each tubule, cells in the wall move glucose, amino acids, needed salts and about 99% of the water into the blood again. What is left becomes urine.

clues: It can be a sign that the kidneys or heart are not working well.
It happens when extra liquid leaks out of blood vessels and collects in the tissues.
If you press a thumb on the affected skin, a small dent may stay for a few seconds.
explain: Oedema is swelling caused by extra fluid trapped in the body's tissues. Normally the lymph vessels and kidneys keep fluid in balance. If the kidneys cannot remove enough salt and water, or the heart pumps weakly, fluid collects, often in the feet, ankles or around the eyes. Doctors treat the cause.

clues: Your body has several of these, including one at the bottom of the food pipe.
One sits where the bladder meets the urethra, and you learn to control it as a toddler.
It works like a drawstring on a bag, tightening to keep an opening shut until it is time to let go.
explain: A sphincter is a ring of muscle that closes an opening. Sphincters at the base of the bladder keep urine in until you decide to go. Toilet training is a child learning to control one of them. Others sit at the bottom of the oesophagus and at the stomach exit, controlling when food passes.

clues: These dissolved minerals carry tiny electric charges that help nerves and muscles work.
You lose some of them in sweat and in diarrhoea, which is why ORS contains them.
The kidneys keep their levels in the blood just right by removing extras in urine.
explain: Electrolytes are minerals such as sodium, potassium and chloride that dissolve in body fluids and carry tiny electric charges. Nerves and muscles, including the heart, need the right amounts to work. You lose them in sweat, vomit and diarrhoea. The kidneys keep their levels balanced by keeping or removing them as needed.

clues: Nurses use a sterile, thin, soft one, and only when there is a medical need.
It is used when someone cannot pass urine on their own, for example after an operation.
This hollow, bendy line is gently passed up the urethra so urine can flow out into a bag.
explain: A urinary catheter is a thin, soft, hollow tube that a nurse or doctor passes up the urethra into the bladder. It lets urine flow out into a bag when a person cannot pass urine themselves, for example after an operation. It is kept clean and is removed as soon as it is no longer needed, to lower the chance of infection.

scenario: Seven-year-old Dev is dry all day but sometimes wets the bed at night. He feels embarrassed. What should his doctor tell the family first?
options: He is doing it on purpose
It is common and usually stops
answer: It is common and usually stops
optionNotes: Not true; he cannot control it in sleep
He needs water; just less near bedtime
Many children his age still wet the bed
explain: Bedwetting is common at this age, and many seven-year-olds still wet the bed sometimes. The bladder and brain are still learning to work together at night. It is not anyone's fault. Going to the toilet before bed and drinking more earlier in the day help, and a doctor can suggest more if it continues.

scenario: On a normal school day, which drink is the best everyday choice to keep Mira's body well supplied with water?
optionNotes: Sugar and caffeine; not for children
Sugar adds energy you may not need
explain: Plain water replaces the water your body loses through urine, sweat and breath without adding sugar. Sugary drinks add a lot of energy and harm teeth, and energy drinks contain caffeine, which is not advised for children. Milk and water-rich fruit also count, but water is the best everyday drink.

scenario: At a summer fair, a woman becomes confused. Her skin feels very hot and dry, and she has stopped sweating. What should be done first?
options: Call for help and cool her
Let her rest in the sun
Ask her to walk it off
answer: Call for help and cool her
optionNotes: Adds heat, the opposite of what she needs
explain: Confusion with very hot skin points to heatstroke, when the body can no longer cool itself. It is an emergency. Call for help straight away, move her to shade, and cool her with cool water and fanning while waiting. Children should get an adult to do this.

scenario: A boy's face and ankles are puffy. A urine test shows a lot of protein, which makes his urine foamy. Which part of his urinary system is most likely letting protein leak through?
explain: Healthy kidney filters, the glomeruli, let water and waste through but hold back large proteins. If the filters become leaky, protein escapes into the urine and can make it foamy. With less protein in the blood, fluid seeps into tissues and causes puffiness. A nephrologist, a kidney specialist, can treat this.

scenario: On a cool, rainy day, Kabir drinks many glasses of water. He goes to the toilet often, and his urine is pale and clear. What does this show?
options: His kidneys are removing extra water
answer: His kidneys are removing extra water
optionNotes: A normal bladder fills faster with more urine
Normal response to drinking a lot
explain: Your kidneys keep the amount of water in your body steady. When you drink more than you need, they let more water out, so you make lots of pale, watery urine. This is a sign the kidneys are doing their job well. When you are short of water, they do the opposite and make less, darker urine.

scenario: Ritu had a kidney stone last year. Her nephrologist tells her to drink plenty of water every day. How does this help?
options: Keeps urine dilute so crystals don't form
answer: Keeps urine dilute so crystals don't form
optionNotes: More water, fewer minerals per drop
Kidneys make more urine, not less
explain: Kidney stones grow from minerals that form crystals when urine is very concentrated. Drinking plenty of water makes more urine with the minerals spread out, so crystals are less likely to form and small ones can be washed out. Doctors often suggest drinking enough to keep urine pale all day.

scenario: A doctor explains that many medicines leave the body within hours. First, one large organ changes them into forms the kidneys can easily remove. Which organ is this?
optionNotes: Filters old blood cells and germs
Changes many chemicals into removable forms
explain: The liver is the body's main chemical-processing organ. It changes many medicines and other substances into forms that dissolve easily in water. The kidneys can then filter them into urine, or the liver sends some out in bile. This is one reason doctors set doses carefully and adjust them when the liver or kidneys are unwell.

scenario: The morning after eating a big plate of beetroot, Sam notices his urine is pinkish-red. He has no pain and feels well. What is the most likely cause?
optionNotes: Beetroot pigment can pass into urine
Needs heat and a very high temperature
Would be an emergency with pain
explain: Beetroot contains a strong red pigment, and in some people part of it passes into the urine unchanged. This is harmless and fades within a day or two. Red or pink urine without eating beetroot or similar foods, or with pain, should be checked by a doctor, because it can mean blood in the urine.

scenario: Mr Rao's kidneys have failed, and he goes to hospital for dialysis three times a week. Which treatment could let him stop dialysis?
optionNotes: Treat bacterial infections, not failed kidneys
Checks the problem; does not treat it
A working kidney does the filtering
Failed kidneys cannot remove extra water
explain: Dialysis uses a machine to clean the blood when kidneys have failed. A kidney transplant places a healthy kidney from a donor into the patient, and one working kidney is enough. After a successful transplant, the person no longer needs dialysis but takes daily medicines so the body accepts the new kidney.

scenario: Fluid leaks out of tiny blood vessels into your tissues every day. Lymph vessels collect this extra fluid, called lymph. Where does the lymph finally go?
options: Out of the body as urine
Out through the skin as sweat
optionNotes: Urine is made by the kidneys
Joins large veins near the neck
Lymph does not go to the stomach
explain: Every day some fluid seeps out of capillaries into the spaces around cells. Lymph vessels collect it, pass it through lymph nodes where germs are filtered out, and empty it into large veins near the neck. Without this drainage, fluid would build up and tissues would swell.

scenario: Each day the kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid out of the blood, yet a person passes only about 1.5 litres of urine. What happens to the rest?
options: It is taken back into the blood
It stays stored in the bladder
answer: It is taken back into the blood
optionNotes: About 99% is reabsorbed by the tubules
Sweat is much less than this
The bladder holds only about half a litre
Bile is made by the liver
explain: Kidney filters push a large amount of fluid out of the blood, both waste and useful things. As this fluid flows through the tubules, about 99% of the water, plus glucose and needed salts, is taken back into the blood. Only the leftover water and waste become urine. This lets the kidneys clean blood thoroughly without drying you out.

scenario: After PE on a hot day, Leela's dark blue T-shirt dries with white, crusty marks under the arms and on the back. What are the marks?
optionNotes: Sugar is not lost in sweat
Bone does not leave the body
Dye does not form crusty marks
explain: Sweat is mostly water with some salt dissolved in it. When sweat dries on cloth, the water evaporates and the salt is left as white marks. This is why people who sweat a lot for a long time need to replace salt as well as water.

scenario: A man with long-term kidney failure feels tired and looks pale. His blood test shows too few red blood cells. His nephrologist says this is linked to his kidneys. Why?
optionNotes: Red cells are too big to filter
Urine colour does not affect blood
Water does not destroy red cells
explain: Healthy kidneys make a hormone called erythropoietin, which tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells. Failing kidneys make less of it, so fewer red cells are made and the person becomes tired and pale. Doctors can give this hormone as an injection to help.

scenario: Ali is healthy, but he notices that his first urine in the morning is darker yellow than later in the day. What is the most likely reason?
options: No drinks overnight, so it is concentrated
answer: No drinks overnight, so it is concentrated
optionNotes: Kidneys save water while you sleep
explain: You go many hours without drinking while you sleep. During that time the kidneys save water, so the urine they make is more concentrated and darker. Once you drink in the morning, urine becomes paler again. Dark urine all day long is a sign to drink more.

scenario: After an operation that removed several lymph nodes from her armpit, a woman's arm on that side slowly becomes swollen with fluid. What is the most likely reason?
options: Lymph from the arm cannot drain well
answer: Lymph from the arm cannot drain well
optionNotes: Would cause swelling in many places
Fewer nodes means a blocked drainage route
explain: Lymph from the arm drains through lymph vessels and nodes in the armpit before returning to the blood. If many of those nodes are removed, the fluid has fewer routes out, so it can collect in the arm and cause swelling. Doctors and physiotherapists can help with special massage, exercises and sleeves.

scenario: Red blood cells wear out after about four months. One organ in the upper left of the belly, behind the ribs, removes many of these old cells from the blood. Which organ?
optionNotes: Stores urine, low in the belly
Digests food; does not filter blood
Filters out old red blood cells
explain: Red blood cells last about 120 days. As they age, they become less flexible, and the spleen catches and breaks them down as blood flows through it. The iron is recycled to make new cells, and the rest is turned into a pigment the liver removes. The liver also helps with this clean-up.

reason: The stomach is a digestive organ; the rest make up the urinary system.
explain: The urinary system cleans your blood and removes liquid waste. Kidneys filter the blood and make urine, ureters carry it down, the bladder stores it, and the urethra lets it out. The stomach is part of the digestive system and works on food, not urine.

notes: Remove urea and extra water as urine
Sweats out water, salts, a little urea
Turns harmful wastes into ones that can be removed
Tastes and moves food; removes no waste
reason: The tongue does not help remove the body's waste; the other four do.
explain: Excretion means getting rid of waste made by your own cells. Kidneys remove urea in urine, lungs breathe out carbon dioxide, and skin loses salts and a little urea in sweat. The liver changes harmful substances such as ammonia into safer ones that the kidneys can then remove. The tongue helps with taste and swallowing.

notes: Should stay in blood; too big to filter
Removed to keep salt levels balanced
reason: Red blood cells should not be in normal urine; the others normally are.
explain: Kidney filters let water and small molecules through but hold back big things like blood cells and most proteins. So normal urine contains water, urea, extra salts and creatinine, a waste made by muscles. Blood in urine is a sign something is wrong, such as an infection or a kidney stone, and should be checked by a doctor.

notes: Kidneys saving water: sign of dehydration
Can happen when fluid is low
reason: Pale urine means you have enough water; the others are signs of dehydration.
explain: When you lose more water than you drink, your kidneys hold back water and make a small amount of dark, concentrated urine. You may also get a dry mouth, headache or dizziness. Pale straw-coloured urine shows the kidneys have enough water to work with.

notes: Very little water, lots of salt
reason: Salty chips add almost no water and make you thirsty; the others help you stay hydrated.
explain: You get water from drinks and from watery foods like fruit and soup. Salty, dry snacks give almost no water, and the extra salt makes your body need more water to flush it out through the kidneys. That is why salty food makes you thirsty.

notes: Knot of capillaries where filtering starts
Tiny air sac in the lungs
Cup that catches the filtered liquid
Twisting tube that takes back useful things
reason: An alveolus is an air sac in the lungs; the others are parts of a nephron.
explain: A nephron is a tiny filtering unit in the kidney. Blood is filtered in the glomerulus, and the liquid is caught by Bowman's capsule. As it flows along the tubule, useful things like glucose, salts and most water are taken back into the blood. What is left drains into a collecting duct as urine.

reason: The gall bladder is a digestive organ; the rest are part of the lymphatic system.
explain: The lymphatic system is a network of thin vessels and small organs. It drains extra fluid from your tissues and returns it to the blood, filtering it on the way. Lymph nodes, tonsils, the spleen and the thymus all hold white blood cells that fight germs. The gall bladder stores bile and belongs to the digestive system.

reason: Making bile is a liver job; the others are kidney jobs.
explain: Kidneys do more than make urine. By deciding how much water and salt to let go, they keep the amount of water and the salt level in your blood steady. If you drink a lot, they make more urine; if you are low on water, they make less. Bile is made by the liver to help digest fat.

items: Recycles iron from old red cells
notes: Liver job: makes a poison safer
Liver job: clears chemicals from blood
Liver job: saves iron for new cells
Liver job: some waste leaves in poop
reason: Storing urine is the bladder's job; the others are cleaning jobs of the liver.
explain: The liver is the body's chemical cleaning plant. It changes ammonia, a poisonous waste from protein, into urea, which the kidneys remove. It breaks down medicines and other chemicals, recycles iron from worn-out red blood cells, and sends some wastes out in bile, which leaves the body with poop. Urine is stored in the bladder.

notes: Water vapour lost in each breath
Makes you sweat and lose water
reason: Drinking juice adds water; the others make the body lose water.
explain: Your body loses water in several ways: urine, sweat, breath and a little in poop. Hot weather and exercise raise sweat losses a lot. To stay balanced, you need to take in as much as you lose, mostly from drinks and watery foods.

notes: Filters old cells and germs from blood
reason: The heart pumps but does not filter; the others act as filters.
explain: Your body has several filters. Kidneys filter waste from blood, lymph nodes trap germs from lymph, the spleen removes worn-out red blood cells and germs from blood, and tonsils catch germs entering the throat. The heart is a pump that moves blood to all these places; it does not filter anything.

notes: Keeps you out of direct sun
Lets sweat dry and heat escape
reason: A thick jacket traps heat; the others help the body stay cool on a hot day.
explain: Your body keeps its inside temperature close to 37 °C. On hot days, sweat glands release sweat, and as it evaporates it carries heat away from your skin. You can help by resting in shade, wearing loose light clothes and drinking water to replace what you sweat out.

notes: Thin tube that carries urine onward
Holds food for a few hours
reason: The ureter only carries urine; the others are stretchy stores that hold something for a while.
explain: Some organs act as storage bags so your body can release things at the right time. The bladder holds urine, the gall bladder holds bile until a meal arrives, the stomach holds food while it churns, and the rectum holds poop. The ureter is a thin tube that moves urine from the kidney to the bladder; it does not store it.

notes: Less salt for kidneys to remove
reason: A plaster cast treats broken bones; the others are care for kidney failure.
explain: When kidneys fail, waste and water build up in the blood. Dialysis uses a machine and filter to clean the blood instead. A kidney transplant gives the patient a working kidney from a donor. Eating less salt and controlling how much fluid they drink reduces the load while the kidneys cannot do their job.

notes: Lymph job: returns fluid to blood
Lymph job: special vessels in villi
Heart job; lymph has no pump
reason: Pumping blood is the heart's job; the others are jobs of the lymphatic system.
explain: Some liquid leaks out of tiny blood vessels and bathes your cells. The lymphatic system collects this extra fluid, filters it through lymph nodes, and returns it to the blood. It also carries digested fats from the intestine and holds many white blood cells. Lymph has no heart; body movements squeeze it along.

items: Make a hormone for red blood cells
Keep blood from getting too acidic
notes: Kidney job: tells bone marrow to make more
Kidney job: helps bones get calcium
Kidney job: adjusts salt and water
reason: Insulin comes from the pancreas; the other four are extra jobs of the kidneys.
explain: Besides making urine, kidneys have other jobs. They release a hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells, turn vitamin D into its active form, help control blood pressure, and remove extra acid. This is why people with failing kidneys can become anaemic and have weak bones. Insulin is made by the pancreas.

items: About the size of a fist
Near the back, below the ribs
In the chest beside the heart
answer: In the chest beside the heart
notes: True: curved like a kidney bean
True: one on each side of the spine
True: partly protected by lower ribs
False: kidneys are in the back of the belly
reason: Kidneys are not in the chest; the other four statements about kidneys are true.
explain: Most people have two kidneys, each shaped like a bean and roughly the size of a fist. They sit at the back of the belly, one on each side of the spine, partly protected by the lowest ribs. The heart and lungs are higher up, in the chest.
fact: The right kidney usually sits a little lower than the left, because the liver is above it.

clues: Most people have two, one on each side of the spine, just below the ribs at the back.
Each one contains about a million tiny cleaning units called nephrons.
These organs take waste and extra water out of what the heart pumps, making the yellow liquid you flush away.
explain: Kidneys are your body's main cleaners. All your blood passes through them many times a day. They filter out urea, extra salts and extra water to make urine, while keeping useful things like glucose and blood cells in the blood.
fact: Your kidneys filter about 180 litres of liquid from your blood each day, but return almost all of it, leaving about 1.5 litres of urine.

clues: In an adult it can hold about half a litre.
Its stretchy muscle wall sends signals to your brain as it fills up.
Two thin tubes bring liquid waste into this bag from the kidneys.
explain: The bladder is a stretchy, muscular bag low in your belly. It collects urine from the kidneys so you do not have to go all the time. As it fills, nerves tell your brain, and you feel the urge to go. A ring of muscle stays tight until you decide to release it.

clues: About 95 out of every 100 parts of it are water.
It carries urea and extra salts out of the body.
It gets darker and stronger-smelling when you have not drunk enough.
explain: Urine is the liquid waste made by your kidneys. It is mostly water, with urea, salts and other wastes dissolved in it. Its colour is a quick guide: pale straw means you are well hydrated, while dark yellow means you need to drink more.

clues: Long play in hot sun, vomiting or diarrhoea can cause it.
Signs include headache, tiredness and dark urine.
It happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in.
explain: About 60% of your body weight is water, and every cell needs it. When you lose more fluid than you take in, through sweat, vomiting or diarrhoea, you become dehydrated. Your kidneys respond by making less, darker urine. Drinking water, or ORS after vomiting or diarrhoea, puts the fluid back.

clues: A part of your brain notices when your blood becomes too salty.
It is your body's alarm that fluid is running low.
Your mouth feels sticky and you really want a glass of something.
explain: Thirst is a feeling your brain creates when your blood gets too concentrated, meaning too much salt for the amount of water. At the same time, the brain signals the kidneys to save water. Both help bring your water level back to normal. In hot weather, drink before you feel very thirsty.

clues: Not drinking enough fluid for a long time raises the chance of getting one.
Minerals in liquid waste clump together into a hard lump.
When it moves down the tube towards the bladder it causes very bad cramps in the side and back.
explain: When urine is very concentrated, minerals in it can form crystals that grow into hard lumps called kidney stones. Small ones may pass out on their own; as they squeeze down the thin ureter they can cause severe pain. Drinking enough water keeps urine dilute and lowers the chance of stones forming.

clues: You have two of these, each about 25 to 30 centimetres long in an adult.
Muscles in their walls squeeze liquid waste downward in small spurts.
Each one links a bean-shaped cleaning organ to the storage bag in your lower belly.
explain: Each kidney has one ureter, a narrow muscular tube that carries urine down to the bladder. Its walls squeeze in waves, so urine moves even when you are lying down. Do not confuse it with the urethra: there are two ureters but only one urethra, which carries urine out of the body.

clues: You have only one of these, and it is much shorter in girls than in boys.
A ring of muscle around its start lets you choose when to go to the toilet.
It is the last passage liquid waste travels through before it leaves the body.
explain: The urethra is the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. Muscles around it stay closed until you choose to go. Because it is shorter in girls, germs can reach the bladder more easily, which is why girls get bladder infections more often and should wipe from front to back.

clues: Each one has a cup-shaped end wrapped around a knot of tiny blood vessels.
A long, twisting tube follows, where useful things are taken back into the blood.
Each of your two bean-shaped cleaning organs is packed with these tiny working parts.
explain: A nephron is the kidney's tiny filtering unit, and each kidney has about a million of them. Blood is filtered at one end, then the liquid flows along a twisting tubule. On the way, useful things such as glucose, salts and most of the water are taken back into the blood. What remains becomes urine.

clues: It is made when the body breaks down extra amino acids.
It is made from ammonia, which is poisonous, so the body changes it into this safer substance.
Your kidneys remove it from the blood, and a little leaves in sweat too.
explain: When your body uses protein, it produces ammonia, which is poisonous. The liver quickly turns ammonia into urea, which is much less harmful. Urea travels in the blood to the kidneys, which remove it in urine. It is the main waste in urine after water.

clues: Many patients need this about three times a week, for around four hours each time.
Their own filtering organs have failed, so this treatment does the job instead.
A tube carries the patient's red body fluid through an artificial filter and back again.
explain: Dialysis is a treatment for people whose kidneys have stopped working. Their blood is pumped through a machine with a special filter that removes waste and extra water, then returned to the body. It keeps the patient healthy but does not cure the kidneys, so many patients wait for a kidney transplant.

clues: No heart pumps this; your muscles squeeze it along when you move.
It travels in its own set of thin vessels, separate from arteries and veins.
It drains back into the blood after passing through small bean-shaped stations that trap invaders.
explain: Some of the liquid part of blood leaks out of capillaries to bathe your cells. Most goes back, but the extra is collected by lymph vessels and is then called lymph. It passes through lymph nodes, where white blood cells catch germs, and then rejoins the blood near the heart.

clues: Breathing out carbon dioxide is one example of it.
Sweating out salts and urea is another example.
It is the name for getting rid of harmful leftovers made by your own cells.
explain: Your cells make waste as they work, such as carbon dioxide and urea. Excretion is the removal of these wastes from the body. Kidneys, lungs, skin and liver all take part. Getting rid of undigested food as poop is usually called egestion, because that food was never part of your cells.

clues: Blood pressure here is high, which pushes water and small molecules out.
It sits inside a cup called Bowman's capsule.
It is a tiny knot of thin blood vessels where cleaning the blood begins in each kidney unit.
explain: The glomerulus is a tight knot of tiny blood vessels at the start of each nephron. Blood enters under high pressure, so water, salts, glucose and urea are squeezed out into Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass and stay in the blood.

clues: Fish release it straight into the water around them.
It forms when the body breaks down amino acids from extra protein.
This harmful chemical is quickly changed into a safer substance so the kidneys can remove it.
explain: Protein contains nitrogen. When the body breaks down extra amino acids, the nitrogen ends up in ammonia, which is poisonous even in small amounts. Fish can release it directly into the water. Humans cannot, so the liver turns it into urea, which is safer to carry in the blood until the kidneys remove it.

clues: Each minute, about one-fifth of everything your main pump sends out flows through this pair.
Each one branches straight off the aorta, the body's largest main pipe.
It carries waste-filled supply into the bean-shaped cleaning organs.
explain: 'Renal' means to do with the kidneys. Each renal artery carries blood from the aorta into a kidney to be cleaned. The kidneys get about a fifth of the blood the heart pumps, far more than their size suggests, because cleaning blood is their job. Cleaned blood leaves through the renal vein.

clues: Your body's movers make it at a steady rate every day as they use energy.
Doctors measure its level in a sample from a vein to check how well the filtering organs work.
If the filtering organs slow down, this substance builds up instead of leaving in urine.
explain: Creatinine is a waste made by muscles at a fairly steady rate. Healthy kidneys remove it from the blood into urine. Because its production is steady, a high creatinine level in a blood test is a sign the kidneys are not filtering well, and doctors use it to check kidney health.

scenario: Arjun played football for two hours in the afternoon sun and drank almost nothing. Now he has a headache, a dry mouth and dark yellow urine. What is the most likely problem?
optionNotes: Causes sharp pain in side or back
Lost more water than he drank
Reaction to a food, often with rash
Would follow an injury, with swelling
explain: Playing in the heat makes you sweat a lot. If you do not drink, your body runs low on water. The kidneys save water by making a small amount of dark urine, and a dry mouth and headache follow. Resting in shade and sipping water usually helps; tell an adult if he feels very unwell.

scenario: A man has sudden, severe pain that comes in waves from his back and side down towards his groin. His urine looks pink. What is the most likely cause?
optionNotes: Burning pain in the upper belly
Pain settles in the lower right belly
Would be in the leg, not the back
Stone scraping down the ureter; blood in urine
explain: A kidney stone is a hard lump of minerals that forms when urine is concentrated. As it moves down the narrow ureter, the muscles squeeze around it and cause waves of pain from the back to the groin. It can scrape the lining, so a little blood colours the urine pink. Drinking enough water helps prevent stones.

scenario: A doctor wants a quick, painless first check on how a child's kidneys are working. Which test should come first?
optionNotes: Shows what the kidneys are letting through
explain: Urine is made by the kidneys, so it shows what they are doing. A urine test can find things that should not be there, such as blood, protein or sugar. It needs only a small sample collected in a clean cup, so it is a common first test before a blood test or scan.

scenario: Priya's aunt wants to donate a kidney to her brother, whose kidneys have failed. She asks how many kidneys a person needs to live a healthy life. What is the answer?
optionNotes: Without any kidney, waste builds up
One healthy kidney can do the work of two
Most people have two, but one is enough
People normally have two, not three
explain: Most people are born with two kidneys, but one healthy kidney can do enough filtering for the whole body. After a donation, the remaining kidney grows a little and takes on more work. This is why living people can safely donate a kidney after doctors check they are healthy.

scenario: A girl often holds her urine for long hours at school. Now she feels burning when she passes urine and needs to go very often. What is the most likely problem?
optionNotes: Slow, hard poop; no burning urine
Loose, watery poop; no burning urine
Germs in the bladder or urethra
explain: A urinary tract infection happens when germs get into the urethra and bladder. Urine left sitting for long gives germs time to grow, which irritates the lining and causes burning and frequent urges. A doctor may test the urine and prescribe medicine. Drinking enough water and going to the toilet when you need to help prevent it.

scenario: A pathologist tests a healthy child's urine sample. Which substance makes up most of it?
optionNotes: Main waste, but only a small part
Should not be in healthy urine
explain: Urine is about 95% water. Wastes such as urea and extra salts are dissolved in that water, which is how the kidneys carry them out of the body. This is why you need to drink enough: the kidneys need water to wash wastes away. Blood in urine is a sign to see a doctor.

scenario: During a cricket match on a very hot day, a boy feels dizzy, weak and sweaty, with a headache. He is awake and talking. What should be done first?
options: Move him to a cool, shady place and give sips of water
Let him keep playing to finish the match
Wrap him in a warm blanket
Give him a cup of hot tea
answer: Move him to a cool, shady place and give sips of water
optionNotes: Cools the body and replaces lost fluid
More heat and sweating makes it worse
explain: These are signs of heat exhaustion: the body has lost a lot of water and salt through sweat and is struggling to cool down. Move him out of the sun, loosen tight clothes, cool his skin with a damp cloth and give small sips of water or ORS. An adult should stay with him and get medical help if he does not improve or becomes confused.

scenario: A blood test shows a patient has high levels of urea and creatinine in her blood. Which organs are most likely not working well?
optionNotes: Should remove urea and creatinine into urine
explain: Urea comes from breaking down protein, and creatinine comes from working muscles. Healthy kidneys keep both at low levels by moving them into urine. If they build up in the blood, it suggests the kidneys are not filtering well. A nephrologist, a kidney doctor, would then look for the cause.

scenario: A doctor wants a painless picture of a child's kidneys that uses sound waves and no radiation. Which test is this?
optionNotes: Sound echoes build a live picture
explain: An ultrasound sends very high-pitched sound, too high for us to hear, into the body. The sound bounces off organs, and a computer turns the echoes into a picture. It uses no radiation, so it is safe for children and is the same kind of scan used to see babies before birth. It can show the size of the kidneys and stones or blockages.

scenario: In class, a student asks a kidney doctor how big a kidney is. Which comparison is closest?
optionNotes: About 10 to 12 cm long in an adult
explain: Each adult kidney is about 10 to 12 cm long, roughly the size of a fist. Even though kidneys are small, they receive about a fifth of all the blood the heart pumps each minute. That huge blood flow lets them clean all your blood many times every day.

scenario: Tara has a sore throat. The doctor feels small, tender lumps on both sides of her neck, below the jaw. These lumps usually go down when the infection clears. What are they?
optionNotes: Single gland at the front of the neck
Not linked to a throat infection
Swell in mumps, near the ears
explain: Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped filters along lymph vessels. When germs are nearby, white blood cells in the nodes multiply to fight them, so the nodes swell and feel tender. Once the infection clears, they shrink back. Lumps that stay large for weeks should be checked by a doctor.

scenario: A bodybuilder eats far more protein than his body needs. The extra amino acids are broken down. Which waste will his kidneys have to remove more of?
optionNotes: Made by the liver for digestion
Useful fuel, kept in the blood
Made from the nitrogen in extra protein
explain: The body cannot store extra protein. The amino acids are broken down, and the nitrogen in them becomes ammonia, which the liver turns into urea. More protein eaten means more urea in the blood for the kidneys to remove, and the body needs more water to flush it out.

scenario: After drinking two big glasses of water, Neha feels a strong urge to go to the toilet. Which organ is stretching and sending signals to her brain?
optionNotes: Makes urine but does not store it
explain: Kidneys make urine all the time, and it drips down the ureters into the bladder. The bladder's muscular wall stretches as it fills. Nerves in the wall send messages to the brain, which you feel as the urge to go. A ring of muscle keeps urine in until you reach a toilet.

scenario: A patient's skin and the whites of his eyes have turned yellow. His doctor explains that a yellow waste from old red blood cells is building up because one organ is not clearing it. Which organ?
optionNotes: Clears the yellow pigment into bile
Mainly removes urea; not the main exit for this pigment
explain: When old red blood cells are broken down, a yellow pigment called bilirubin is made. The liver normally collects it and sends it out in bile. If the liver is unwell or bile cannot flow, bilirubin builds up and turns skin and eyes yellow. This is called jaundice, and a doctor needs to find the cause.
fact: Many newborn babies get mild jaundice for a few days because their liver is still getting up to speed.

scenario: A school poster shows a urine colour chart. Which colour shows a person is drinking about the right amount?
optionNotes: Badly dehydrated or unwell: see a doctor
Very concentrated: drink more; see a doctor if it stays
explain: Urine gets its yellow colour from a pigment the body makes when it recycles old red blood cells. With plenty of water, the pigment is diluted and urine looks pale straw yellow. With too little water, the kidneys save water and urine gets darker. Red or brown urine needs a doctor's check.

scenario: On a hot day, Kiran sweats a lot and notices he goes to the toilet much less often than usual. What is the best explanation?
options: All his urine is coming out as sweat
optionNotes: They take back more water into the blood
The bladder only stores what it receives
Blockage causes pain, not a hot-day pattern
Sweat and urine are made in different places
explain: When you lose water as sweat, your brain releases a hormone that tells the kidneys to take back more water from the tubules into the blood. Less urine is made, and it is darker. This keeps your body's water level steady. Drinking more water on hot days lets the kidneys return to normal.

notes: Indian gooseberry, very rich in vitamin C
Grain with almost no vitamin C
Citrus fruit rich in vitamin C
Fruit with lots of vitamin C
Sour citrus fruit with vitamin C
reason: White rice has almost no vitamin C; the other four are good sources of it.
explain: Vitamin C keeps gums healthy and helps cuts heal. Your body cannot store much of it, so you need some most days from fresh fruit and vegetables. Amla, guava, orange and lemon are all rich in it. White rice gives energy from starch but almost no vitamin C.
fact: Gram for gram, amla and guava have more vitamin C than oranges.

notes: Dairy food made by helpful bacteria
Dairy food made by curdling milk
reason: Potato is a starchy vegetable; the other four are dairy foods rich in calcium.
explain: Dairy foods come from milk, and they are a rich source of calcium. Calcium is the mineral that makes bones and teeth hard and strong. Potato is a vegetable that mostly gives starch for energy and has very little calcium.
fact: About 99% of the calcium in your body is stored in your bones and teeth.

notes: Leafy vegetable, very low in fat
Nuts that are about half fat
reason: Spinach is very low in fat; the other four are rich sources of fat.
explain: Fats are an energy-rich nutrient. They also help your body take in vitamins A, D, E and K. Ghee, butter, oil and groundnuts are all high in fat, so small amounts go a long way. Spinach is a leafy vegetable that gives vitamins, minerals and fibre but almost no fat.

notes: Hard outer coat of a tooth
Soft flap hanging at the back of the throat
Soft centre with nerves and blood vessels
Part of a tooth above the gum
reason: The uvula hangs at the back of the mouth; the other four are parts of a tooth.
explain: A tooth has layers. Hard enamel covers the crown, the part you can see. Under it is dentine, and in the centre is the pulp, which holds nerves and blood vessels. The uvula is the small soft flap that dangles at the back of your mouth; it helps close off the nose when you swallow.
fact: Enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, harder than bone.

notes: Dissolves food so taste buds detect it
Starts in the stomach, not the mouth
reason: Saliva does not digest protein; the other four are jobs saliva does.
explain: Saliva is the watery juice made by glands around your mouth. It wets and softens food, dissolves bits of it so your taste buds can detect flavour, and makes food slippery to swallow. It also contains amylase, an enzyme that starts breaking starch into sugar. Protein digestion begins later, in the stomach, with the enzyme pepsin.

notes: Done mainly by the small intestine
Gut bacteria make some vitamin K
reason: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine; the other four happen in the large intestine.
explain: By the time food reaches the large intestine, most nutrients have already been absorbed through the villi of the small intestine. The large intestine takes back water and some salts, so the leftovers become firm stool. It is also home to trillions of helpful bacteria, some of which make vitamin K.

notes: Roasted, rich in protein and fibre
Fresh fruit with vitamins and fibre
Fried in oil; high in fat
reason: The samosa is deep-fried and high in fat; the other four are roasted, boiled or fresh snacks.
explain: How food is cooked changes how healthy it is. Deep-frying soaks food in oil, which adds a lot of fat and energy without adding vitamins or fibre. Roasted, boiled, sprouted or fresh snacks keep more of their nutrients and fibre. A samosa is fine now and then, but the other four are better everyday snacks.

notes: Neck gland that makes a hormone
Makes bile for the small intestine
Sends digestive juice to the small intestine
Make juice in the stomach wall
reason: The thyroid releases a hormone into the blood; the other four send digestive juices into the gut.
explain: Digestive glands make juices that pour into the food tube: saliva into the mouth, gastric juice into the stomach, and bile and pancreatic juice into the small intestine. The thyroid gland in your neck sends its hormone straight into the blood instead. That hormone controls how fast your body uses energy, and has no direct part in digesting food.

notes: Bean very rich in plant protein
Seeds rich in protein and fat
reason: Egg is an animal protein; the other four are protein foods from plants.
explain: Protein builds and repairs muscles, skin and other tissues. You can get it from animals (eggs, milk, fish, meat) or from plants. Dal, chickpeas, soya and peanuts all belong to the bean and pea family, called legumes, which are some of the richest plant sources of protein. Vegetarians often get much of their protein from them.

items: Lying down after a big meal
answer: Lying down after a big meal
notes: Gives enzymes smaller pieces to work on
Keeps food moving through the gut
reason: Lying down straight after a big meal can cause acid trouble; the other four help digestion.
explain: Good habits help your digestive system do its job. Chewing well breaks food into small pieces, fibre and water keep things moving and soft, and moving your body helps the gut muscles work. Lying flat right after a large meal makes it easier for stomach acid to flow back up the food pipe, causing a burning feeling.

reason: Cucumber gives very little vitamin A; the other four are rich in the orange pigment the body turns into vitamin A.
explain: Many orange and yellow foods contain beta-carotene, the pigment that gives them their colour. Your body turns beta-carotene into vitamin A, which you need to see in dim light and to keep skin healthy. Carrot, mango, papaya and pumpkin are rich in it. Cucumber is mostly water and gives very little.

notes: Pouch where the large intestine begins
Longest part of the large intestine
First part of the small intestine
Last short passage to the outside
reason: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine; the other four are parts of the large intestine.
explain: The small intestine has three parts, and the duodenum comes first, just after the stomach. Bile and pancreatic juice pour into it. The large intestine starts with a pouch called the caecum (where the appendix is attached), runs on as the colon, and ends with the rectum and the anal canal.
fact: Duodenum comes from a Latin phrase meaning 'twelve fingers', roughly its length in finger-widths.

notes: Cells using nutrients to build and work
reason: Inhalation is a step in breathing; the other four are steps of nutrition.
explain: Nutrition in humans happens in steps. Ingestion is taking food in, digestion breaks it into small molecules, absorption moves those into the blood, and assimilation is when cells use them for energy, growth and repair. The last step, egestion, removes undigested waste. Inhalation means breathing in, which belongs to the breathing system.

notes: Too little food energy and protein
reason: Chickenpox is caused by a virus; the other four are deficiency diseases caused by poor diet.
explain: A deficiency disease happens when the diet lacks a nutrient for a long time. Kwashiorkor and marasmus come from too little protein and food energy, rickets from too little vitamin D, and scurvy from too little vitamin C. They cannot spread from person to person, and the right food helps prevent them. Chickenpox is an infection caused by a virus and can spread.

notes: Needed in small amounts for health
A gas we breathe in, not eat
reason: Oxygen is a gas taken in by the lungs; the other four are nutrients we get from food.
explain: Nutrients are substances in food that the body needs. The main groups are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals, plus water and fibre. You need oxygen too, but you get it by breathing, not eating. Your cells use that oxygen to release energy from the nutrients in food.

notes: Holds water and makes stool soft
Takes up space in the stomach
reason: Building muscle is a job of protein; the other four are things fibre does.
explain: Fibre is the part of plant food your body cannot digest. It still has jobs: it soaks up water and adds bulk so stool moves easily, it feeds the helpful bacteria in your large intestine, and it fills you up. Building and repairing muscle is the job of protein.

notes: Holds a meal for a few hours
Muscle walls mix food with juice
Acid kills many germs in food
reason: Bile is made by the liver; the other four are jobs of the stomach.
explain: The stomach is a stretchy, muscular bag. It holds a meal for a few hours, churns it with gastric juice, and uses strong acid to kill many germs. Its enzyme pepsin starts breaking down protein. Bile is made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and used in the small intestine.

clues: Strong muscle walls in this J-shaped organ squeeze and mix food for a few hours.
It sits in the upper left of your tummy, just below the ribs, at the bottom of the food pipe.
Swallowed food lands here and is mashed into a thick soup before moving on to the small intestine.
explain: The stomach is a stretchy, muscular organ between the oesophagus and the small intestine. Its walls squeeze to mix food with gastric juice, which contains acid and the enzyme pepsin. After a few hours the food has become a thick liquid that moves on in small amounts.
fact: An adult's stomach can stretch to hold about 1 to 1.5 litres of food and drink.

clues: Bile and pancreatic juice pour into the first part of this organ.
Most digestion finishes here, and digested food passes through its walls into the blood.
This coiled tube fills much of your belly. It is about 6 metres in an adult but narrower than the 'large' one.
explain: The small intestine is the coiled tube after the stomach. Juices from the liver and pancreas finish digesting food here. Its inner wall is covered with tiny villi that pass nutrients into the blood. It is called 'small' because it is narrow, even though it is the longest part of the gut.

clues: Trillions of tiny helpful microbes live inside this part of the gut.
Leftover food that could not be digested moves slowly through it while liquid is soaked up from the mush.
This wide tube, about 1.5 metres in an adult, frames the coiled small intestine and ends at the rectum.
explain: The large intestine is the last main part of the gut. It is wider but shorter than the small intestine. It takes water and some salts back from undigested leftovers, so waste becomes firm stool. Helpful bacteria living there break down some fibre and make a little vitamin K.

clues: This small pear-shaped pouch is tucked under a large organ on the right side of the belly.
Between meals it holds a green-yellow juice and makes it stronger by removing some of its water.
When you eat an oily meal, it squeezes and sends its juice into the small intestine to help break up fat.
explain: The gall bladder is a small pouch under the liver. The liver makes bile all the time, and the gall bladder keeps it ready between meals. When fatty food arrives in the small intestine, the gall bladder squeezes bile out through a tube. Bile breaks fat into tiny droplets so enzymes can digest it faster.

clues: An adult has eight of these, four in the upper jaw and four in the lower.
They have thin, flat, sharp edges, a bit like a chisel.
When you take the first snap out of an apple, these teeth in the middle of your smile do the work.
explain: Incisors are the flat, sharp-edged teeth at the front of your mouth. They slice food into pieces small enough to chew. Behind them, canines grip and tear, and premolars and molars crush and grind. Each type of tooth has a shape that matches its job.

clues: Adults have four of these, one on each side of the upper and lower jaw.
They have the longest roots of all your teeth and a single sharp tip.
They sit at the corners of your mouth, next to the flat front teeth, and help grip and rip food.
explain: Canines are the pointed teeth at the corners of your mouth, between the incisors and premolars. Their sharp tip helps grip and tear tougher food. Their long roots hold them firmly in the jaw. Meat-eating animals have much larger canines than humans do.

clues: Children with this deficiency condition may grow slowly and have weak, aching legs.
It happens when the body cannot get enough calcium into the growing skeleton.
Children who rarely go out in the sun and get little milk may develop legs that bow outward.
explain: Rickets is a deficiency disease in children whose bones stay soft and can bend. It is usually caused by too little vitamin D, which the body needs to absorb calcium from food. Skin makes vitamin D in sunlight, and milk, eggs and fish also provide it. Playing outdoors and eating these foods helps prevent rickets.

clues: This deficiency disease can cause weak muscles, swollen legs and tingling or numb feet.
It was common long ago where people ate mainly polished grain with the outer bran removed.
It is caused by too little of the very first B vitamin.
explain: Beriberi is caused by too little vitamin B1, also called thiamine. The body needs B1 to turn food into energy, especially in nerves and muscles. Polishing rice removes the outer bran, which holds much of the B1. Whole grains, pulses and nuts help prevent beriberi.
fact: In the 1890s a doctor named Christiaan Eijkman noticed chickens fed polished rice became sick and recovered on unpolished rice. This helped lead to the discovery of vitamins.

clues: It usually has lots of salt, sugar or oil but very little fibre, vitamins or protein.
It often comes in shiny packets and fizzy cans and tastes great, but does little to nourish your body.
Doctors say it is fine as a rare treat, not as your daily meals.
explain: Junk food gives plenty of energy from fat, sugar and salt but few of the nutrients your body needs to grow and stay healthy. Eating a lot of it can lead to tooth decay, weight gain and tiredness. Eating it now and then is fine if most meals are balanced.

clues: It gives your body carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water in the right amounts.
A thali with roti, dal, sabzi, salad and curd is a good example.
Eating this way means no single food group takes over your meals.
explain: A balanced diet contains all the nutrients your body needs, in the right amounts. Grains give energy, dal, eggs or milk give protein, fruit and vegetables give vitamins, minerals and fibre, and a little fat helps absorb some vitamins. Different foods do different jobs, so mixing food groups covers them all.

clues: Gram for gram, this nutrient gives more than twice the energy of sugar.
A layer of it under your skin keeps you warm and cushions your organs.
Nuts, cream and fried snacks are rich in this nutrient, and bile breaks it into tiny droplets.
explain: Fat is a nutrient that stores a lot of energy: about 9 calories per gram, compared with about 4 for sugar or protein. It also keeps you warm, protects organs and helps your body absorb vitamins A, D, E and K. You need some fat every day, but large amounts of fried food add more energy than most people use.

clues: Your body needs small amounts of these simple non-living substances, such as zinc and iodine.
Unlike vitamins, they are not made by plants or animals; plants take them up from the soil.
Bones need one of these to be hard, and blood needs another to carry oxygen.
explain: Minerals are simple substances from the earth, such as calcium, iron, iodine and zinc. Plants take them up from the soil, and we get them by eating plants and animals. Calcium builds bones and teeth, iron helps blood carry oxygen, and iodine is needed for the thyroid gland. Vitamins are different: living things make them.

clues: This chemical helper arrives in the small intestine in juice from a gland behind the stomach.
It works best after bile has broken big greasy blobs into tiny droplets.
It splits the main nutrient in ghee and butter into smaller pieces the body can absorb.
explain: Lipase is the enzyme that digests fats. Most of it comes from the pancreas in pancreatic juice. Bile first breaks fat into tiny droplets, giving lipase more surface to work on. Lipase then splits fats into fatty acids and glycerol, which are small enough to be absorbed.

clues: This short, muscular part of the gut comes right after the colon.
It holds waste until it is a good time to go to the toilet.
When it stretches, it sends a message to your brain that you will need the toilet soon.
explain: The rectum is the last part of the large intestine. It holds stool until you are ready to go to the toilet. When it fills and stretches, nerves send a signal to the brain. Ring-shaped muscles keep it closed until you choose to let the waste out through the anus.

clues: Enzymes, acid and bile all play a part in this process.
It turns big molecules like starch into small ones like glucose, small enough to enter the blood.
This is what happens to your lunch between swallowing it and its nutrients reaching your cells.
explain: Digestion is the process of breaking food into molecules small enough to pass into the blood. Chewing and churning break food physically, while enzymes, acid and bile break it chemically. Starch becomes glucose, protein becomes amino acids, and fat becomes fatty acids and glycerol.

clues: It is acidic and contains partly digested protein.
It leaves the J-shaped organ in small squirts through a ring of muscle into the small intestine.
This thick, creamy mush is what food becomes after a few hours of mixing with gastric juice.
explain: Chyme is the thick, acidic liquid that food turns into inside the stomach. The stomach walls mix the food with gastric juice for a few hours. A ring of muscle at the stomach's exit then lets chyme into the small intestine a little at a time, so it is not overloaded.

clues: Dentists sometimes use a pink tablet to make it show up.
Germs living in it feed on sugar and make acid that can eat into enamel.
This soft, pale film builds up along your gum line every day and can harden if it is left there.
explain: Plaque is a soft film of bacteria that forms on teeth every day. When you eat sugar, these bacteria make acid that slowly dissolves enamel and causes cavities. Plaque also irritates the gums. Brushing twice a day and flossing remove it before it hardens into tartar, which only a dentist can remove.

scenario: Anika is running a long cross-country race tomorrow. Her coach tells her to eat foods like rice, roti and bananas, which give the body its main quick fuel. Which nutrient are these foods rich in?
optionNotes: Helps digestion but gives little energy
Broken down to glucose, the body's main fuel
explain: Carbohydrates such as starch and sugar are broken down into glucose, which muscles and the brain use as their main fuel. Athletes often eat extra carbohydrate before a long race so their muscles have stored fuel to draw on. Fibre, calcium and vitamin A are all needed, but they do not supply much energy.

scenario: A woman had her gall bladder removed. She worries that her body can no longer make bile to help digest fat. Which organ still makes bile for her?
explain: The liver makes bile; the gall bladder only stores it and releases it at mealtimes. After the gall bladder is removed, the liver keeps making bile, which now trickles straight into the small intestine. Most people digest food normally afterwards, though some feel better eating smaller, less oily meals.

scenario: In a food lab, a few drops of brown iodine solution are added to a slice of raw potato. The drops turn blue-black. Which nutrient does this show is present?
optionNotes: Leaves a see-through greasy spot on paper
explain: Iodine solution is brown, but it turns blue-black when it touches starch. This is a simple test for starch, a carbohydrate stored in potatoes, rice and wheat. Fat is tested by rubbing food on paper and looking for a greasy patch that lets light through.

scenario: Rohan chews a plain salted cracker for two whole minutes without swallowing. It starts to taste slightly sweet. What is happening in his mouth?
options: Saliva is turning starch into sugar
The salt is changing into sugar
His tongue is melting the cracker
answer: Saliva is turning starch into sugar
optionNotes: Amylase in saliva breaks starch down
The tongue mixes and tastes; it does not digest
explain: Saliva contains an enzyme called amylase. It starts breaking starch, a long chain of sugar units, into smaller sugars. Starch itself has no sweet taste, but those smaller sugars do. This shows digestion begins in the mouth.

scenario: A dentist checks a 5-year-old girl who still has all her milk teeth and has not lost any yet. How many teeth should the dentist count?
optionNotes: Full adult set, with wisdom teeth
Too few for a full set
explain: Children have 20 milk teeth, also called baby teeth. From about age 6 they start falling out one by one as adult teeth push up from below. A full set of adult teeth has 32, including four wisdom teeth at the back. Milk teeth matter: they hold space for adult teeth and help with chewing and speaking.

scenario: A 19-year-old already has 28 adult teeth. Now four new teeth are starting to push through, right at the very back of his mouth. What are they?
optionNotes: Flat cutting teeth at the front
Last molars, at the very back
explain: Wisdom teeth are the third and last set of molars. They usually come through between the late teens and mid-twenties, at the very back of each jaw. Some people never get them, and if there is not enough space a dentist may need to remove them.

scenario: A vegetarian family wants more protein in their everyday meals. Which meal gives the most protein?
options: Dal, rice and a bowl of curd
answer: Dal, rice and a bowl of curd
optionNotes: Dal and curd are good protein sources
explain: Vegetarians get protein from pulses like dal, from milk foods like curd and paneer, and from nuts and soya. Dal eaten with rice gives a better mix of protein building blocks than either food alone. Rice, potato, bread, jam and juice are mostly carbohydrate, so they add energy but little protein.

scenario: The stomach makes acid strong enough to help break down meat, yet the stomach wall itself is usually not harmed. What protects it?
options: Saliva that cancels all the acid
optionNotes: Works in the small intestine, not the stomach
explain: Cells in the stomach lining make a thick layer of mucus that coats the wall. It traps a less acidic liquid next to the cells, so the acid cannot reach them easily. The lining also replaces its cells every few days. If this protection breaks down, a sore called an ulcer can form.

scenario: Newborn babies are usually given one injection of a vitamin soon after birth. It helps their blood clot, so they are less likely to bleed. Which vitamin is it?
optionNotes: Helps make red blood cells and nerves
explain: Vitamin K is needed to make proteins that help blood clot. Newborns are born with very little of it, and their gut does not yet have the bacteria that make some vitamin K. A single dose at birth protects them until their diet and gut bacteria can supply it. Green leafy vegetables are a good source later in life.

scenario: A family eats only plant foods, with no milk, curd, eggs, fish or meat. Their doctor advises a supplement for one vitamin that is found naturally almost only in animal foods. Which vitamin?
optionNotes: Plants give beta-carotene, which becomes vitamin A
Made by microbes; plants do not provide it
explain: Vitamin B12 helps make red blood cells and keeps nerves healthy. It is made by microbes, and people usually get it from animal foods such as milk, eggs, fish and meat. Plants do not provide it, so people who eat no animal foods need fortified foods or a supplement advised by a doctor.

scenario: After most nutrients are absorbed, a watery mush of leftovers moves on. In which organ is much of the remaining water taken back, so that stool becomes firm?
optionNotes: Mixes food before it reaches the intestines
Absorbs water and salts from leftovers
explain: The large intestine takes back water and salts from undigested leftovers. As the mush moves slowly along, it dries into firm stool. If it moves too fast, too little water is taken back and stool is loose (diarrhoea). If it moves too slowly, too much is taken back and stool becomes hard.

scenario: Jay's gums look red and puffy and bleed a little when he brushes. He eats plenty of fruit. The dentist sees a soft film along his gum line. What is the most likely problem?
optionNotes: Plaque irritates and swells the gums
Would follow an injury, with pain
Come through much later, at the back
