Cloudy vision in older people is often caused by a cataract, a clouding of the eye's lens, which can be fixed with a short operation.

scenario: A baby gets her measles vaccine. Her older brother asks how a shot today can stop measles years later. What is the best answer?
options: It teaches her immune system to recognise measles and remember it
It kills every germ in her body forever
It is a vitamin that makes her stronger
It only works after she catches measles
answer: It teaches her immune system to recognise measles and remember it
optionNotes: Memory cells stay ready for years
Vaccines target one germ, not all
explain: The vaccine contains a weakened measles virus that cannot cause the real illness. Her immune system makes antibodies and memory cells against it. If real measles ever enters her body, the memory cells recognise it and respond fast. That is why the vaccine protects for many years.

scenario: A newborn is too young for some vaccines. The doctor asks the parents, grandparents and older siblings to make sure their own vaccines are up to date. Why?
options: Their vaccines travel to the baby through the air
Vaccinated family members are less likely to catch germs and pass them to the baby
It makes the baby's blood stronger
Only vaccinated people may legally hold babies
answer: Vaccinated family members are less likely to catch germs and pass them to the baby
optionNotes: Vaccines do not pass through air
Protects the baby by blocking spread
Family vaccines do not change baby's blood
explain: A newborn's immune system is still learning. If the people around the baby are vaccinated, germs have a much harder time reaching the baby. When enough people in a community are vaccinated, a germ cannot spread easily, which also protects those who cannot be vaccinated. This is called herd immunity.

scenario: After eating cut fruit from a roadside stall, a boy's fever rises slowly, day by day, over a week. He has stomach pain and feels very weak. A blood culture grows bacteria. Which disease is most likely?
optionNotes: Bacteria from dirty food; slowly rising fever
explain: Typhoid is caused by bacteria that spread through food or water dirtied with germs. Its fever typically climbs step by step over several days, with stomach pain and weakness. A blood culture, where blood is kept warm in the lab so any bacteria can grow, confirms it, and antibiotics treat it. A typhoid vaccine and safe food and water help prevent it.

scenario: A blood test shows a child has many more white blood cells than normal. She also has a fever and a painful ear. What does the high white cell count most likely suggest?
options: Her body is fighting an infection
She has been sleeping too much
answer: Her body is fighting an infection
optionNotes: White cells multiply to fight germs
Shown by an X-ray, not white cells
explain: When germs invade, the bone marrow makes and releases more white blood cells to fight them. A complete blood count counts the different blood cells, so a high white cell number, together with fever and ear pain, points to an infection such as an ear infection. The doctor then decides on treatment.

notes: Red cells carry the A marker
Red cells carry the B marker
reason: Group C does not exist; the other four are the ABO blood groups.
explain: Your blood group depends on tiny markers, called antigens, on the surface of your red blood cells. In the ABO system, red cells can carry the A marker, the B marker, both (AB) or neither (O). There is no group C, so it is the odd one out.
fact: Blood groups were discovered by the scientist Karl Landsteiner in 1901.

notes: Uses lots of oxygen from blood
Filters a large share of blood
Clear front of the eye, no vessels
reason: The cornea has no blood vessels; the other four are full of them.
explain: Almost every living tissue has capillaries bringing it oxygen and food. The cornea, the clear window at the front of your eye, has no blood vessels, so light can pass through it without anything in the way. It takes oxygen straight from the air and gets food from the fluids around it.

notes: Red cells carry it from the lungs
Done by the gut, not the blood
reason: Digesting food is the job of the digestive system; the other four are jobs of blood.
explain: Blood is the body's delivery and defence system. It carries oxygen, food molecules and hormones, its white cells fight germs, and it spreads heat so your hands and feet stay warm. Breaking food down happens earlier, in the stomach and intestines; blood only collects the small pieces afterwards.

notes: Pumps blood to the whole body
reason: The tricuspid valve is on the right side of the heart; the other four are on the left side.
explain: The heart is really two pumps side by side. The left side receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and pumps it to the body, using the left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle and aortic valve. The tricuspid valve sits on the right side, which handles oxygen-poor blood on its way to the lungs.
fact: 'Tricuspid' means 'three points': this valve has three flaps, while the mitral valve has two.

reason: Haemoglobin is held inside red blood cells; the other four are dissolved in plasma.
explain: Plasma is the pale yellow liquid part of blood. It is mostly water, with salts, glucose and proteins dissolved in it. Haemoglobin is different: it is packed inside red blood cells, which float in the plasma. That is why plasma looks yellow while the cells give blood its red colour.

reason: A dermatologist treats the skin; the other four care for the heart, blood or blood vessels.
explain: Many doctors' titles hint at what they treat. 'Cardio' means heart, 'haemato' means blood and 'vascular' means blood vessels, so these four all care for the circulatory system. 'Derma' means skin, so a dermatologist treats skin, hair and nails.

notes: Leaves blood for cells to use
Leave blood to keep cells healthy
reason: Carbon dioxide moves from body cells into the blood; the other four move from the blood into cells.
explain: Capillaries are where blood trades with body cells. Their walls are only one cell thick, so useful things like oxygen, glucose, vitamins and amino acids (the building blocks of protein) pass out to the cells. Waste carbon dioxide made by the cells moves the other way, into the blood, to be carried to the lungs and breathed out.

reason: Eyesight is tested with a chart; the other four are measured in a blood test.
explain: A blood test takes a small sample, usually from a vein in the arm, and a lab measures what is in it. It can count red cells, white cells and platelets, and measure haemoglobin and sugar. Eyesight cannot be read from blood; it is checked by reading letters on a chart.

reason: Cartilage is a tissue in joints, ears and nose; the other four words come from 'cardio', meaning heart.
explain: Many science words are built from old Greek and Latin parts. 'Cardio' comes from the Greek word for heart, so cardiac, cardiologist, cardiogram and cardiovascular are all about the heart. Cartilage only looks similar; it is the smooth, bendy tissue at the ends of bones and in your ears and nose.

reason: Hepatitis is a liver illness; the other four words come from 'haem', meaning blood.
explain: 'Haem' comes from the Greek word for blood. A haemorrhage is heavy bleeding, a haematologist is a blood doctor, haemoglobin carries oxygen in blood and haemophilia is a condition where blood clots slowly. 'Hepat' means liver, so hepatitis means swelling of the liver.

notes: Pain can travel to arm or jaw
reason: Itchy eyes are not a heart attack sign; the other four are common warning signs.
explain: A heart attack happens when a blood vessel feeding the heart muscle gets blocked, so part of the muscle is short of oxygen. Common warning signs in adults are chest pain or tightness, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, sweating and breathlessness. Anyone with these signs needs an ambulance straight away. Itchy eyes are usually caused by an allergy.

reason: An octopus has blue blood; the other four animals have red blood.
explain: Blood is red when it uses haemoglobin, an iron-containing protein, to carry oxygen. Humans, birds, sharks and snakes all use haemoglobin. An octopus uses a different protein built around copper instead of iron, which makes its blood blue when it carries oxygen.
fact: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through its gills and one pumps it to the rest of the body.

notes: Red cells lost faster than made
Worms feed on blood in the gut
reason: Too much salt raises blood pressure; the other four can cause anaemia.
explain: Anaemia means the blood has too few healthy red cells or too little haemoglobin. It can happen when blood is lost (from an injury, or from hookworms that feed on blood in the gut), when the body lacks iron to make haemoglobin, or when red cells break down too early, as in sickle cell disease. Too much salt does not cause anaemia.
fact: Wearing footwear outdoors helps prevent hookworm, which enters the body through bare feet.

reason: A jellyfish has no heart; the other four animals have one.
explain: Most animals need a heart to push blood around their bodies. A jellyfish has no heart, no blood and no brain. Its body is so thin that oxygen can soak straight in from the seawater around it.

reason: Watching TV gives the heart no workout; the other four are exercise that strengthens it.
explain: Activities that keep you moving and slightly out of breath for a while make your heart pump harder. Over weeks, this kind of exercise makes the heart muscle stronger, so it pumps more blood with each squeeze. Watching TV keeps the body still, so the heart gets no workout.
fact: Doctors suggest children get about an hour of active play every day.

notes: Part of a blood pressure machine
Picks up sounds from the body
reason: An arm cuff belongs to a blood pressure machine; the other four are parts of a stethoscope.
explain: A stethoscope carries sounds from inside the body to the doctor's ears. The chest piece, which often has a flat side and a cup-shaped bell, picks up the sounds; the tubing carries them; and the earpieces fit in the ears. An arm cuff belongs to a blood pressure machine, which squeezes the arm to measure pressure in the arteries.

reason: 190 beats a minute is far too fast for a resting child; the other four are normal resting pulse rates.
explain: For a 10-year-old resting quietly, the heart usually beats about 70 to 110 times a minute. A rate of 190 is far too fast for someone sitting still; a child's heart might reach it only during very hard exercise. As you grow up, your resting pulse slowly drops to about 60 to 100 beats a minute.

clues: Every person has one, and it is set by markers on their red cells.
You inherit it from your parents, and it stays the same all your life.
Yours might be A, B, AB or O.
explain: Your blood group is decided by markers (antigens) on your red blood cells, which you inherit from your parents. The main groups are A, B, AB and O, and each can be positive or negative. Doctors match blood groups before giving blood, because the wrong group can make the body attack the new cells.

clues: It has a Y-shaped tube with a round metal piece at one end.
A nurse presses its cold disc on your chest or back.
It carries the 'lub-dub' sounds inside your body up to the person using it.
explain: A stethoscope is a simple tool that carries sounds from inside the body to a doctor's ears. Doctors use it to hear the heart's valves closing, air moving in the lungs and gurgles in the gut. It was invented in France in 1816; before that, doctors pressed an ear directly on the chest.

clues: This thick sheet of muscle runs down the middle of an organ with four chambers.
It keeps oxygen-rich blood apart from oxygen-poor blood.
Some babies are born with a small hole in it.
explain: The septum is the muscular wall that divides the heart into a left side and a right side. Because of it, oxygen-rich blood from the lungs never mixes with oxygen-poor blood from the body. Your nose also has a septum: the thin wall between your two nostrils.

clues: There are two of these big vessels: an upper one and a lower one.
They carry oxygen-poor blood collected from the whole body.
They empty into the right atrium.
explain: The venae cavae are the body's two largest veins. The upper one brings blood back from the head and arms, and the lower one from the legs and belly. Both pour oxygen-poor blood into the right atrium, so it can be pumped to the lungs to pick up oxygen.

clues: It is an artery, yet the blood inside it is the dark, used kind coming back from the body.
It splits into two branches, one for each breathing organ in your chest.
Blood travels along it on its way to collect fresh air.
explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Most carry oxygen-rich blood, but the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. There the blood picks up oxygen and returns to the heart through the pulmonary veins.

clues: These small vessels run over the outside of the organ that never stops beating.
They feed that pump itself with oxygen-rich blood.
If one gets blocked, part of the pump is starved of oxygen and the person needs an ambulance.
explain: The heart pumps blood to the whole body, but its own muscle also needs a supply. The coronary arteries branch off the aorta and wrap around the outside of the heart, feeding its muscle. Their name comes from the Latin word for crown, because they circle the heart like one.

clues: It is a medical emergency, most common in older adults.
A vessel feeding the body's pump gets clogged, so part of its muscle runs short of oxygen.
Warning signs include a crushing feeling behind the breastbone, sweating and breathlessness.
explain: A heart attack happens when a coronary artery, which feeds the heart muscle, gets blocked, often by a clot on a fatty build-up. The part of the muscle beyond the block runs short of oxygen. Quick hospital treatment reopens the vessel, so calling emergency help at once matters.

clues: A doctor may notice it during a routine check-up of the chest.
It is an extra swishing noise made when blood flows unevenly inside the body's pump.
Many children have a harmless one that fades as they grow.
explain: A healthy heart makes a clean 'lub-dub'. A murmur is an extra swishing noise heard between those beats, caused by blood flowing in a rough or unusual way. Many murmurs in children are harmless, but a doctor may order a scan to check the heart's valves and walls.

clues: It is a soft, jelly-like lump that forms when liquid blood sets.
Sticky cell fragments and a net of threads trap red cells to make it.
Outside the body it plugs a wound; inside a vessel it can block the flow.
explain: When a blood vessel is damaged, platelets stick to the spot and proteins in plasma form threads called fibrin. The threads trap red cells, turning liquid blood into a jelly-like clot that seals the leak. Clots are life-saving at a wound, but a clot inside a vessel can block blood flow, so the body keeps clotting carefully controlled.

clues: It is about the size of a fist and is tucked under the ribs, behind the stomach.
It filters the blood, removing worn-out blood cells and trapping germs.
A person can live without it, because other parts of the body take over its jobs.
explain: The spleen is a soft organ about the size of your fist, tucked behind the stomach under the left ribs. It filters blood, breaks down old red blood cells and stores white blood cells that fight germs. People can live without a spleen if it is damaged, though they become more likely to catch some infections.

clues: Doctors may do this after a big accident or a major operation.
Blood groups are checked carefully before it starts.
Blood from another person flows slowly into a patient's vein through a thin tube.
explain: A blood transfusion puts donated blood, or one part of it such as red cells or platelets, into a patient's vein. It replaces blood lost in an accident or operation, or helps people whose bodies cannot make enough healthy blood. The blood groups of donor and patient must match, so the patient's body does not attack the new cells.

clues: Laid end to end, all of these in an adult would stretch around the Earth more than twice.
They come in three main kinds: big ones leaving the heart, ones going back, and tiny ones in between.
In a healthy body, blood stays inside them as it travels around.
explain: Blood vessels are the tubes that carry blood around your body. Arteries carry it away from the heart, veins bring it back, and tiny capillaries link the two and reach almost every cell. Together they form a closed network, so blood keeps moving in a loop.
fact: An adult's blood vessels, laid end to end, would stretch about 100,000 kilometres.

clues: Bags of blood are kept here at a cool, carefully controlled temperature.
Each bag is labelled with its group and the date it was collected.
Volunteers visit to give blood, which is tested before anyone receives it.
explain: A blood bank collects blood from healthy volunteers, tests it for infections and stores it until a patient needs it. Red cells are kept cool and last about six weeks, while platelets last only a few days. Regular donors keep blood banks supplied for accidents, operations and illnesses.

clues: It forms on the skin a day or so after you get a graze.
It is made of dried blood, platelets and threads that seal the wound.
It is best left alone until it falls off by itself, once new skin has grown underneath.
explain: A scab is a blood clot that has dried and hardened on the surface of the skin. It protects the wound from dirt and germs while new skin grows underneath. Pulling it off early can reopen the wound and slow healing.

clues: This word means the endless journey of a red liquid through your body.
One full round trip, from the pump out to the body and back, takes about a minute at rest.
Cold, pale fingers in winter can mean this is slow in the hands.
explain: Circulation is the movement of blood around the body in a loop: pumped out by the heart through arteries, through capillaries in the organs, and back through veins. It delivers oxygen and food to every cell and carries waste away. Exercise keeps circulation healthy.

clues: Your liver makes this waxy substance, and some also comes from animal foods like butter and egg yolk.
The body needs a little of it to build the outer layer of cells and make some hormones.
Too much of it over many years can build up inside vessels and narrow them.
explain: Cholesterol is a waxy substance the body needs to build cell coverings and some hormones. The liver makes most of what you need. When there is too much in the blood for many years, it can build up in artery walls and narrow them, which is why doctors check it in adults.

clues: This long-term condition often causes no symptoms, so it is checked at regular visits.
It means the push of blood against the walls of the arteries stays too strong.
In adults, readings above about 140 over 90 again and again point to it.
explain: Hypertension is the medical name for high blood pressure. It means blood pushes too hard against artery walls, which over years can strain the heart, kidneys and blood vessels. Eating less salt, staying active, keeping a healthy weight and not smoking all help prevent it.

scenario: A patient with blood group B positive needs red blood cells. The blood bank has only these four kinds in stock. Which one is safe to give him?
optionNotes: A markers clash with his blood
Has A markers too; they clash
No A or B markers; safe for him
A markers clash, though Rh is fine
explain: Group B blood has antibodies that attack red cells carrying the A marker, so A and AB blood cannot be given. Group O red cells have neither the A nor the B marker, so they are safe for group B. As he is Rh positive, he can also receive Rh positive blood, so O positive works.

scenario: A boy's small cuts keep bleeding for a long time, and his knees swell after minor bumps. His uncle had the same problem. Tests show a clotting protein in his blood is missing. What is the condition?
optionNotes: Missing clotting protein, runs in families
Curved red cells, not slow clotting
explain: Haemophilia is passed down in families and mostly affects boys. Their blood is missing or low in one clotting protein, so clots form slowly and bleeding lasts longer, even inside joints. It cannot be caught from others, and treatment replaces the missing protein.

scenario: Your grandfather suddenly has a crushing pain in his chest that spreads to his left arm. He is sweating and short of breath. What should be done first?
options: Ask him to walk it off
optionNotes: Food will not help and wastes time
Moving makes the heart work harder
Fast hospital care saves heart muscle
Delay lets more heart muscle be harmed
explain: Chest pain spreading to the arm, with sweating and breathlessness, can be a heart attack. A heart attack means a vessel feeding the heart muscle is blocked, and the sooner hospital treatment starts, the more heart muscle can be saved. Call emergency services, keep him sitting and resting, and stay with him until help arrives.

scenario: A doctor moves a gel-covered probe over a child's chest. It sends out sound waves too high for us to hear and makes a moving picture of the heart's valves and chambers. What is this test?
optionNotes: Still picture using X-rays, not sound
Measures what is in the blood
explain: An echocardiogram, or 'echo', is an ultrasound scan of the heart. The probe sends out high-pitched sound waves that bounce off the heart, and a computer turns the echoes into a live picture. It is painless and uses no radiation, so it is safe for children.

scenario: An athlete trains for six weeks high in the mountains, where the air is thin. Back home, her blood carries more oxygen than before. What has her body made more of?
optionNotes: Fight germs; do not carry oxygen
explain: Thin mountain air gives less oxygen with each breath. The kidneys sense this and release a hormone that tells the bone marrow to make extra red blood cells. More red cells means more haemoglobin, so her blood carries more oxygen when she returns.

scenario: An older man often feels faint because his heart beats far too slowly. The heart's own timing signal is not working well. Doctors place a small battery device under his skin to keep the beat steady. What is it?
optionNotes: Sends tiny signals to start beats
explain: The heart has its own natural pacemaker, a small patch of cells that sends an electrical signal to start each beat. If it fails, the beat can become too slow. An artificial pacemaker watches the heartbeat and sends a tiny electrical pulse whenever a beat is needed.

scenario: A 12-year-old wants to choose snacks that are good for his heart and blood vessels in the long run. Which choice is best?
optionNotes: Lots of fat and salt if eaten daily
Too much salt raises blood pressure
Lots of sugar and no nutrients
explain: Foods high in salt, sugar and fat, eaten often, can raise blood pressure and cholesterol over the years. Fruit gives fibre and vitamins, and plain nuts give healthy fats. Habits formed in childhood usually continue into adult life, so small daily choices add up.

scenario: Through a stethoscope, a student hears a heart go 'lub-dub, lub-dub'. She asks the cardiologist what actually makes this sound. What is the answer?
optionNotes: Ribs do not make heart sounds
Lung sounds are softer and different
Closing valves make lub and dub
explain: The heart has four valves that act like one-way doors. 'Lub' is the sound of the two valves between the atria and ventricles closing as the ventricles squeeze. 'Dub' is the sound of the valves at the exits to the aorta and pulmonary artery closing just afterwards.

scenario: A healthy 20-year-old has just donated blood for the first time. What should he do next?
optionNotes: Hard exercise may make him faint
Helps the body refill its fluids
His body needs food and fluid
Strain soon after may make him dizzy
explain: A donor gives about 350 to 450 millilitres of blood, a small part of the roughly 5 litres in an adult body. Resting and drinking fluids helps the body replace the lost liquid within a day or two, and new red cells are made over the following weeks. Hard exercise straight after can make a donor feel faint.

scenario: A lab spins a tube of blood very fast in a machine. It separates into a dark red layer at the bottom and a clear, pale yellow liquid on top. What is the yellow liquid?
optionNotes: Liver juice, not part of blood
Fluid in lymph vessels, not this tube
Liquid part of blood, mostly water
Form a thin whitish middle layer
explain: A spinning machine called a centrifuge pushes the heaviest parts of blood to the bottom. Red cells sink to the bottom, a thin whitish layer of white cells and platelets sits in the middle, and plasma stays on top. Plasma makes up about 55% of blood and is mostly water.

scenario: In a woman's heart, the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle does not close properly, so some blood leaks backwards with each beat. Which valve is it?
optionNotes: Exit from left ventricle to aorta
explain: Each heart valve stops blood flowing backwards. The mitral valve, which has two flaps, guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle. On the right side the tricuspid valve does the same job, while the aortic and pulmonary valves guard the exits from the ventricles.

scenario: A man's arm is cut deeply by broken glass. Bright red blood spurts out in pulses, in time with his heartbeat. Which kind of blood vessel has been cut?
optionNotes: High pressure, spurts with each beat
explain: Arteries carry blood straight from the heart under high pressure, so a cut artery spurts with each heartbeat. The blood is bright red because it is full of oxygen. This is an emergency: an adult should press hard on the wound with a cloth and call for help at once.

scenario: Riya scrapes her knee on the playground. Tiny dots of blood slowly ooze from many points on the scraped skin. Which blood vessels have been broken?
optionNotes: Tiny vessels just under the skin
explain: Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, thinner than a hair, and they form a dense net just under the skin. A graze breaks many of them, so blood oozes slowly in tiny dots rather than spurting. Washing it gently with clean water and covering it is usually enough.

scenario: A doctor reads a blood pressure of 120 over 80. A student asks what the top number, 120, measures. What is the right answer?
explain: Blood pressure is written as two numbers. The top number (systolic) is the pressure in the arteries when the ventricles squeeze. The bottom number (diastolic) is the lower pressure while the heart relaxes and refills. 120 over 80 is a healthy reading for an adult.

scenario: Under a microscope, a lab worker looks at a thin smear of a healthy person's blood. Which kind of cell will she see the most of?
optionNotes: Only about 1 for every 600 red cells
explain: Red blood cells far outnumber everything else in blood: a single drop holds millions of them. For every white blood cell there are roughly 600 red cells. Platelets are numerous too, but they are small cell fragments and about 20 times fewer than red cells.

scenario: In humans, blood passes through the heart twice on each complete trip: once to go to the lungs and once to go to the rest of the body. What is this called?
optionNotes: Fish: once through the heart per trip
Not a name for a blood route
explain: Humans have double circulation. The right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; it returns to the left side, which pumps it to the body. Fish have single circulation, with blood passing through their heart once per trip, and insects have open circulation, where blood washes loosely around their organs.

notes: Carries blood away from the heart
Carries blood back to the heart
Carries air down to the lungs
Tiny tube where blood swaps materials
reason: The windpipe carries air; the other four are blood vessels.
explain: Blood travels around your body inside tubes called blood vessels. Arteries (like the aorta) carry blood away from the heart, veins bring it back, and tiny capillaries connect the two. The windpipe is also a tube, but it belongs to the breathing system and carries air, not blood.
fact: An adult body holds about 5 litres of blood.

notes: Green juice from the liver for digestion
Help blood clot at a cut
reason: Bile is a digestive juice; the other four are parts of blood.
explain: Blood has four main parts. Plasma is the liquid that everything floats in, red cells carry oxygen, white cells fight germs, and platelets help seal cuts. Bile is made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It helps break down fat in your food, so it belongs to digestion, not blood.

notes: Top-left room; receives blood from lungs
Top-right room; receives blood from body
Bottom-right room; pumps blood to lungs
Bottom-left room; pumps blood to body
reason: The aorta is a blood vessel; the other four are the heart's chambers.
explain: Your heart has four hollow rooms called chambers. The two on top, the atria, collect blood coming in. The two at the bottom, the ventricles, squeeze hard to push blood out. The aorta is not a chamber. It is the large tube that carries blood out of the left ventricle to the rest of the body.

notes: Takes blood from heart to body
Takes blood from heart to lungs
Takes blood up the neck to the brain
reason: The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood; the other four carry oxygen-rich blood.
explain: Most arteries carry blood full of oxygen. The pulmonary artery is the exception. It takes used, oxygen-poor blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs, where the blood picks up fresh oxygen. So the rule is that arteries always carry blood away from the heart, whether or not that blood is rich in oxygen.
fact: 'Pulmonary' comes from the Latin word for lung.

notes: Less red colour in the blood
Body struggles to get enough oxygen
Clears dust or germs from the nose
reason: Sneezing is not a sign of anaemia; the other four are.
explain: Anaemia means the blood has too little haemoglobin, the red substance that carries oxygen. With less oxygen reaching the muscles and brain, a person feels tired, dizzy and out of breath, and their skin can look pale. Sneezing is the nose clearing dust or germs and has nothing to do with anaemia.

notes: Sits at the centre of haemoglobin
Needed to build healthy red cells
A B-vitamin needed to make red cells
reason: Vitamin K helps blood clot; the other four are needed to make red blood cells.
explain: Your bone marrow makes millions of new red blood cells every second, and it needs raw materials. Iron and protein build haemoglobin, while vitamin B12 and folic acid help the cells grow and divide properly. Vitamin K has a different job: the liver uses it to make clotting proteins that stop bleeding.

notes: Cell pieces that plug a wound
Net that traps cells at a cut
Dried clot that protects healing skin
reason: Haemoglobin carries oxygen; the other four are part of clotting.
explain: When you cut yourself, platelets rush in and stick together to plug the hole. Clotting factors in the plasma then make long fibrin threads that form a net, trapping blood cells into a clot. The clot dries into a scab while new skin grows underneath. Haemoglobin plays no part in this; its job is carrying oxygen.

notes: Artery runs close to the skin here
No large artery to press on
Artery used when measuring blood pressure
Small artery over the foot bones
reason: You cannot feel a pulse at the tip of the nose; you can at the other four places.
explain: A pulse is the throb of an artery stretching each time the heart pushes blood into it. You can feel it wherever a fairly large artery runs close to the skin over something firm, like a bone. The wrist, neck, inner elbow and top of the foot all have such arteries. The tip of the nose has only tiny vessels, so there is no pulse to feel.

notes: Body is resting, needs less oxygen
reason: Deep sleep slows the heart; the other four speed it up.
explain: Your heart speeds up whenever your body needs more oxygen delivered quickly. Exercise makes muscles hungry for oxygen, fear releases a hormone called adrenaline, and a fever makes the body's chemistry run faster. In deep sleep your body needs the least energy, so your heart rate drops.

notes: Has a nucleus; contracts to move you
Has a nucleus; covers the body
reason: A mature human red blood cell has no nucleus; the others do.
explain: The nucleus is the control centre of a cell and holds its DNA. As a human red blood cell matures in the bone marrow, it pushes its nucleus out. That leaves more space for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen. Without a nucleus it cannot repair itself, which is why a red cell lives only about four months.
fact: A red blood cell lives for about 120 days before it is recycled.

notes: Body holds extra water, raising pressure
Heart must push blood through more tissue
Keeps blood vessels healthy and flexible
reason: Daily exercise helps keep blood pressure healthy; the other four raise it.
explain: Blood pressure is how hard blood pushes on the walls of your arteries. Salt makes the body hold extra water, so there is more blood to push. Smoking stiffens vessel walls, and extra body weight and long-term stress make the heart work harder. Regular exercise strengthens the heart and keeps arteries flexible, which helps keep pressure normal.

notes: Valve between right atrium and ventricle
Muscle wall between left and right sides
Valve between left atrium and ventricle
Valve where blood leaves for the body
Valve where blood leaves for the lungs
reason: The septum is a wall; the other four are the heart's valves.
explain: The heart has four valves that act like one-way doors, so blood can only move forward. The tricuspid and mitral valves sit between the upper and lower chambers. The aortic and pulmonary valves sit where blood leaves the heart. The septum is a thick wall of muscle that keeps the left and right sides of the heart apart.

notes: Carried by red cells from lungs
Passes through the gut, never enters blood
Waste gas carried to the lungs
reason: Fibre is never absorbed into the blood; the other four are carried in it.
explain: Blood is the body's delivery service. It carries oxygen from the lungs, sugar from digested food, and hormones from glands to the cells, and takes waste like carbon dioxide away. Fibre from fruits, vegetables and grains is not absorbed at all. It stays in the gut and helps waste move along.

notes: Sound-wave video of the beating heart
Measures how much air you blow out
reason: A spirometer tests the lungs; the other four check the heart and blood vessels.
explain: A heart doctor has several ways to check the heart. A stethoscope lets them hear the valves closing, a cuff measures blood pressure, an ECG records the tiny electrical signals that trigger each beat, and an echocardiogram uses sound waves to show the heart moving. A spirometer measures how much air you can breathe out, so it is a lung test.

reason: A frog's heart has three chambers; the other four animals have four.
explain: A four-chambered heart keeps oxygen-rich blood on the left side and oxygen-poor blood on the right side, so they never mix. Mammals, birds and crocodiles have this design. A frog's heart has two atria but only one ventricle, so some mixing happens. Frogs manage because they also take in oxygen through their moist skin.
fact: A fish heart has just two chambers.

notes: True of veins, especially in legs
True of veins, close to the skin
reason: Thick muscular walls describe arteries; the other four describe veins.
explain: Arteries take the full force of each heartbeat, so they need thick, muscular, stretchy walls. By the time blood reaches the veins, the pressure is low, so vein walls are thinner. To stop blood slipping backwards, veins have valves. Many veins lie near the skin, which is why nurses use them to take blood samples.

notes: Large white cell that cleans up
reason: A platelet is a clotting fragment; the other four are types of white blood cell.
explain: There are several kinds of white blood cells, each with its own way of fighting germs. Neutrophils swallow bacteria, lymphocytes make antibodies, monocytes clean up dead cells and germs, and eosinophils fight parasites. A platelet is not a full cell at all. It is a small piece broken off a bigger cell, and its job is to help blood clot.

clues: This fist-sized organ works every second of your life, even while you sleep.
It has four rooms inside and squeezes to push blood around your body.
A doctor listens to its 'lub-dub' sound with a stethoscope.
explain: The heart is a muscle about the size of your fist that sits in the middle of your chest, tilted a little to the left. Each time it squeezes, it pushes blood through tubes to every part of your body, delivering oxygen and food to cells. The 'lub-dub' sound comes from its valves snapping shut.
fact: An adult's heart beats about 100,000 times a day.

clues: Its walls are thick, stretchy and muscular, so it can handle high pressure.
When you press on one at your wrist, you can feel a steady throb.
This kind of tube carries red liquid away from the main pumping organ out to the body.
explain: Arteries are the tubes that carry blood away from the heart. The heart pushes blood into them with force, so they have thick, muscular, stretchy walls. The throb you feel at your wrist or neck is an artery stretching each time the heart squeezes.

clues: Tiny flaps inside work like one-way doors, so nothing slides backwards.
These thin-walled tubes carry used, oxygen-poor red liquid back to the chest.
A nurse often puts a needle into one on the inside of your elbow to take a sample.
explain: Veins carry blood back to the heart after it has dropped off its oxygen. The pressure inside them is low, so their walls are thinner than artery walls. Valves inside stop blood from flowing backwards, which matters most in your legs, where blood has to travel upwards.
fact: Veins look bluish through your skin, but the blood inside is dark red. Your skin changes how light reaches your eyes.

clues: These are the narrowest tubes in your circulation; red cells pass through in single file.
Their walls are only one cell thick, so oxygen and food slip through to nearby cells.
They form a net that links the smallest arteries to the smallest veins.
explain: Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, finer than a hair. Their walls are just one cell thick, so oxygen and nutrients can pass out into the body's cells, and waste can pass in. Every cell in your body is close to a capillary. They are where the real delivery work of the blood happens.

clues: These are not whole cells but small pieces broken off bigger cells in the bone marrow.
At a wound, they become sticky and clump together like a plug.
They help stop the bleeding after you scrape your knee.
explain: Platelets are tiny cell fragments that float in your blood. When a vessel is damaged, they stick to the edges and to each other, forming a plug. They also release chemicals that help build a net of fibrin threads, which traps red cells into a clot. The clot later dries into a scab.

clues: It makes up a little more than half of what flows in your arteries and veins.
It carries dissolved sugar, salts, hormones and waste around the body.
When a sample is spun fast in a machine, it is the pale, straw-coloured layer on top.
explain: Plasma is the liquid part of blood, and it is mostly water. Red cells, white cells and platelets float in it, along with dissolved food, salts, hormones and wastes. When blood is spun in a machine, the heavy cells sink and the pale plasma stays on top.

clues: Without enough of it, a person may feel tired and look pale.
It is packed inside certain cells and gives them their colour.
It grabs a gas in the lungs and lets go of it in the muscles.
explain: Haemoglobin is a protein packed inside red blood cells. Each molecule has iron at its centre, which grabs oxygen in the lungs and releases it where cells need it. Haemoglobin is what makes blood red. When there is too little of it, a person has anaemia.

clues: A doctor counts it for 15 seconds and multiplies by four.
It gets faster when you run and slower when you rest.
You feel it as a gentle throb when you press two fingers just below the thumb side of your palm.
explain: Your pulse is the throb you feel each time your heart pushes a wave of blood through your arteries. Counting it tells you how many times your heart beats in a minute. For a resting child it is usually somewhere around 70 to 110, and it rises with exercise, excitement or fever.

clues: It can stay too high for years without any warning signs, so adults should get it checked.
It is written as two numbers, such as 120 over 80.
A band wrapped round your upper arm fills with air to measure it.
explain: Blood pressure is how hard blood presses on the walls of your arteries. The top number is the pressure while the heart squeezes, and the bottom number is the pressure while it relaxes between beats. If it stays high for a long time, it strains the heart and blood vessels, so doctors check it regularly in adults.

clues: Many girls and women in India have this condition.
It means there is not enough haemoglobin to carry oxygen around the body.
People with it feel weak and breathless on stairs; spinach, lentils and eggs can help.
explain: Anaemia means the blood has too little haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches the body's cells. The most common cause is not getting enough iron, which the body needs to make haemoglobin. Girls and women need more iron because they lose some blood each month during periods. Iron-rich foods, and iron tablets when a doctor prescribes them, help.

clues: Veins in your legs have them too, so blood does not slide back down.
They make sure blood moves only one way through the heart.
The heart has four of them, and their snapping shut makes the 'lub-dub' sound.
explain: A valve is a set of thin flaps that lets blood pass in one direction and then shuts to stop it flowing back. The heart has four valves. A doctor can hear them through a stethoscope: 'lub' is the sound of two valves shutting, and 'dub' is the other two.

clues: The one on the left has the thickest, strongest muscle wall in the heart.
The heart has two of these, one on each side, below the two collecting rooms.
They squeeze hard to push blood out into the arteries.
explain: The ventricles are the two lower chambers of the heart and do the hard pushing. The right ventricle sends blood a short distance to the lungs. The left ventricle sends blood all the way to your head and toes, so its wall is much thicker and stronger.

clues: It curves over like the handle of a walking stick, then runs down through the chest and belly.
Every drop of oxygen-rich blood leaving the left ventricle passes through it first.
It is the largest of the tubes that carry blood away from the chest's main pumping organ.
explain: The aorta is the body's main artery. It leaves the left ventricle, curves over the top of the heart, and runs down in front of the backbone. Smaller arteries branch off it to carry oxygen-rich blood to the head, arms, organs and legs. In an adult it is about as wide as a garden hose.

clues: Its name comes from a Latin word for an entrance hall.
The heart has two of these, and each one collects blood coming in from veins.
They sit above the two bigger, stronger squeezing rooms of the heart.
explain: The two atria are the upper chambers of the heart. The right one receives oxygen-poor blood from the body, and the left one receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs. Their walls are thin because they only need to push blood a short way down into the ventricles.

clues: Over a week or two it may turn green and then yellow as your body cleans it up.
It forms when tiny tubes break and leak under the surface after a bump.
You might get one on your leg after banging it on a table.
explain: A hard bump can break capillaries under the skin. Blood leaks out and gets trapped, which shows as a dark mark. Over the next days your body breaks down the haemoglobin in that blood into other substances that look green and then yellow, and finally clears it away. A cold pack wrapped in cloth soon after the bump can reduce swelling.

clues: Your bone marrow makes about two million of these every second.
When fully grown they have no nucleus, which leaves more room for their cargo.
Shaped like a doughnut without a hole, they carry the gas you breathe in to every cell.
explain: Red blood cells are the most common cells in your blood. They are packed with haemoglobin, which picks up oxygen in the lungs and drops it off around the body. Their dented shape gives them a large surface for taking in oxygen, and they are bendy enough to squeeze through narrow capillaries.
fact: Each red blood cell lives about 120 days.

clues: Healthy adults can do this every few months, and the body soon replaces what was taken.
Camps for it are often held in offices, colleges and community halls.
One person doing this can help save lives after accidents and operations.
explain: In blood donation, a healthy adult lets a trained worker collect a unit of their blood, which is stored in a blood bank. It is later given to patients who have lost blood or cannot make enough. The donor's body replaces the liquid part within a day or two and the red cells over the next few weeks.

scenario: A 13-year-old girl feels tired all the time, gets breathless climbing stairs and looks pale. Her blood test shows low haemoglobin. What is the most likely problem?
optionNotes: Too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen
A virus causing runny nose and sneezing
Usually causes no symptoms at all
explain: Low haemoglobin is the key clue. Haemoglobin carries oxygen, so when there is too little, muscles and the brain get less oxygen. That causes tiredness, breathlessness and pale skin. A doctor will look for the cause, which is often too little iron in the diet.

scenario: Your friend cuts his hand on a paper cutter and it is bleeding steadily. An adult is on the way. What should you do first?
options: Press firmly on it with a clean cloth
Wave it in the air to dry it
answer: Press firmly on it with a clean cloth
optionNotes: Hot water can make bleeding worse
Toothpaste does not stop bleeding and can irritate
Pressure helps platelets form a clot
explain: Firm, steady pressure with a clean cloth squeezes the cut edges together and slows the blood, giving platelets time to build a clot. Raising the hand above the heart also helps. Keep pressing for several minutes without lifting to peek. An adult or doctor should check whether the cut needs stitches.

scenario: A doctor wraps a band around a man's upper arm and fills it with air. She slowly lets the air out while listening with a stethoscope and reads two numbers. What is she measuring?
optionNotes: Checked with a clip on the finger
Checked with an inflatable arm cuff
explain: The inflated cuff squeezes the main arm artery shut. As the air is let out, blood starts to push through again, and the doctor hears it. The pressure when the sound starts is the top number (while the heart squeezes). The pressure when it stops is the bottom number (while the heart rests).

scenario: After a road accident, a patient has lost a lot of blood and needs red blood cells immediately. There is no time to test his blood group. Which group of red cells is safest to give?
optionNotes: Has A, B and Rh markers; many people react
Has A and Rh markers; many people react
Has the B marker; many people react
No A, B or Rh markers; safest for anyone
explain: Blood groups depend on markers on the surface of red cells. If a patient receives cells with markers their body does not recognise, their immune system attacks them. O negative red cells have no A, B or Rh markers, so they are the safest choice when there is no time to test. Doctors still check the patient's group as soon as they can.
fact: People with O negative blood are often called universal red cell donors.

scenario: A nurse counts 20 pulse beats at a resting boy's wrist in 15 seconds. What is his pulse rate per minute?
explain: A minute has four lots of 15 seconds, so you multiply the count by four: 20 x 4 = 80. That is a normal resting pulse for a child. Counting for a short time and multiplying is quicker, but counting for a full minute is more accurate if the beat is uneven.

scenario: A girl's nose starts bleeding during class. She is not hurt anywhere else. What is the right first aid while the teacher is told?
options: Sit her up, lean forward, pinch soft part of nose
Tilt her head back and wait
Lie her flat on her back
answer: Sit her up, lean forward, pinch soft part of nose
optionNotes: Pressure stops the leak; blood drains out, not down
Blood runs down the throat and is swallowed
Can injure the inside of the nose
explain: Most nosebleeds come from tiny blood vessels near the front of the nose. Pinching the soft part presses on them so a clot can form, and leaning forward lets blood drip out instead of running down the throat. Pinch for about 10 minutes without letting go. If bleeding does not stop after 20 minutes, or followed a hard knock, an adult should get medical help.

scenario: A doctor hears an extra whooshing sound in a baby's chest. A scan shows a small hole in the muscle wall that separates the left side of the heart from the right side. Which part has the hole?
optionNotes: Muscle wall between left and right sides
Tiny blood vessel in body tissues
explain: The septum keeps oxygen-rich blood on the left side of the heart apart from oxygen-poor blood on the right. Some babies are born with a small hole in it, often called a 'hole in the heart'. Blood leaking through the hole makes the whooshing sound, called a murmur. Many small holes close on their own; larger ones can be repaired by doctors.

scenario: A man gets chest pain when he walks fast, and it goes away when he rests. Tests show that the arteries supplying his heart muscle with blood have become narrow. Which arteries are these?
optionNotes: Bring blood from the lungs into the heart
Wrap around and feed the heart muscle
Bring used blood back into the heart
Carry blood up the neck to the brain
explain: The heart muscle needs its own oxygen supply, and it gets it from the coronary arteries that wrap around its surface like a crown. If fatty deposits narrow them, the heart muscle gets too little oxygen when it works hard, which causes chest pain. Healthy food, regular exercise and not smoking help keep these arteries open.
fact: 'Coronary' comes from the Latin word for crown.

scenario: A girl bruises very easily and has tiny red spots on her skin. Her blood test shows that the part of her blood that plugs leaks in vessels is very low. Which part is it?
optionNotes: Carry oxygen; low count causes tiredness
Clump together to seal leaking vessels
explain: Tiny vessels in the body get small leaks all the time, and platelets seal them before we notice. When platelets are low, blood escapes under the skin easily, causing bruises and pinpoint red spots. A pathologist counts platelets with a blood test, and a doctor then looks for the reason they are low.

scenario: A 50-year-old man has high blood pressure. He eats pickles, papads and salty snacks every day. Along with his doctor's treatment, which change will help his blood pressure most?
optionNotes: Can cause dehydration; does not fix pressure
Less salt means less water held in blood
Poor sleep can raise blood pressure
Skipping meals does not lower pressure
explain: Salt makes the body hold on to extra water, which increases the amount of blood in the vessels and raises the pressure. Pickles, papads and packaged snacks contain a lot of salt. Cutting down on them, along with exercise and any medicine the doctor prescribes, helps bring blood pressure down.

scenario: A teenager has anaemia because her body is short of a mineral needed to make haemoglobin. Her nutritionist suggests more green leafy vegetables, lentils and eggs. Which mineral is it?
optionNotes: Found in salt; controls water balance
Sits at the centre of haemoglobin
explain: Every haemoglobin molecule needs iron to hold on to oxygen. Without enough iron, the body makes fewer and paler red blood cells, and the person has anaemia. Leafy greens, lentils, beans and eggs supply iron. Eating them with vitamin C foods like amla, lemon or guava helps the body absorb more of it.

scenario: A shopkeeper who stands all day has swollen, twisted, bluish tubes on the backs of his legs. The one-way flaps inside them have become weak, so blood collects there. Which blood vessels are these?
optionNotes: Too tiny to see bulging like this
explain: Blood in the leg veins has to travel upwards against gravity. Valves inside the veins stop it from sliding back down, and leg muscles squeeze the veins to help. If the valves weaken, blood pools and the veins swell and twist; these are called varicose veins. Walking, raising the legs and not standing still for hours all help.

scenario: During a long school assembly in the heat, a boy says he feels dizzy and then slumps to the floor. He is breathing normally. What should the teacher do first?
options: Lay him on his back and raise his legs
answer: Lay him on his back and raise his legs
optionNotes: Standing can make him faint again
Helps blood flow back to the brain
Food will not help him wake up
Can shock him; does not help blood flow
explain: Standing still for a long time, especially in heat, lets blood pool in the legs. Less blood reaches the brain, and the person faints. Lying flat with the legs raised helps blood return to the heart and brain, and most people wake within a minute. If he does not wake up quickly, the teacher should call for emergency help.

scenario: A student asks which heart chamber pushes oxygen-rich blood out to the whole body, from head to toes. It has the thickest muscle wall of all four. Which chamber is it?
optionNotes: Collects used blood from the body
Collects fresh blood from the lungs
Pushes blood only to the nearby lungs
Pushes blood to the whole body
explain: The left ventricle receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and sends it into the aorta. Because that blood has to reach every part of the body, the left ventricle needs the most force, so its wall is the thickest. The right ventricle only sends blood to the lungs next door, so its wall is thinner.

scenario: A woman donated blood last week. Her body is now making new red blood cells to replace the ones she gave. Where in her body are these new cells made?
optionNotes: Soft tissue inside bones; the blood-cell factory
Pushes blood around; makes no cells
explain: Bone marrow is the soft, spongy tissue inside bones such as the hips, ribs and breastbone. It makes red cells, white cells and platelets. After a donation, a hormone from the kidneys tells the marrow to speed up, and the red cells are fully replaced over the next several weeks.

scenario: A child's red blood cells look stiff and curved like a crescent moon. They get stuck in small vessels and break down early, making the child tired. The condition runs in families. What is it?
optionNotes: Cells are small and pale, not curved
Inherited, but blood does not clot well
Inherited; red cells bend into crescents
Not caused by misshaped red cells
explain: Sickle cell disease is passed from parents to children through genes. It changes haemoglobin so that red cells turn stiff and crescent-shaped. These cells block small vessels, causing pain, and they break down quickly, causing anaemia. It cannot be caught from someone, and treatment helps people with it lead active lives.
fact: India runs a national mission to screen for and reduce sickle cell disease.

notes: Found only in girls and women
Deep in the brain of everyone
reason: Ovaries are found only in females; boys and girls both have the other four glands.
explain: Most endocrine glands are the same in boys and girls: everyone has a thyroid, a pineal gland, a pituitary and two adrenal glands. The sex glands are different. Girls have ovaries, which make eggs and the hormone oestrogen, while boys have testes, which make sperm and testosterone.
fact: Ovaries and testes start out from the same tissue in a very early embryo.

notes: Controlled by nerves in a split second
reason: The knee-jerk reflex is controlled by nerves; the other four are controlled by hormones.
explain: Your body has two messaging systems. Nerves send fast electrical signals, so a reflex like the knee-jerk happens in a fraction of a second. Hormones travel slowly in the blood, so they control long-lasting jobs like growing, puberty, sleep timing and keeping blood sugar steady.

notes: Too little vitamin C in food
Too much growth hormone in childhood
reason: Scurvy is caused by missing vitamin C; the other four happen when a gland makes too much or too little hormone.
explain: Hormone disorders happen when a gland makes the wrong amount of its hormone. Too much growth hormone in childhood makes a person grow extremely tall, and too little or too much thyroxine slows down or speeds up the body. Scurvy is a deficiency disease: it comes from not eating enough vitamin C, found in fruits like amla and oranges.

notes: Hydra grows a bud that breaks off
Body breaks into pieces that regrow
reason: Fertilisation is part of sexual reproduction; the other four are ways of reproducing with just one parent.
explain: In asexual reproduction one parent makes new young on its own, by budding, splitting in two, breaking into pieces or making spores. The young are copies of the parent. In sexual reproduction two parents are needed: a sperm from the male joins an egg from the female in fertilisation, so the young get a mix of features from both.

notes: Male releases sperm over eggs in water
Eggs fertilised outside, in a pond
Sperm meets egg inside her body
Fish eggs fertilised in river water
Fertilised outside the body, in water
reason: In hens, fertilisation happens inside the body; in the other four it happens outside, in water.
explain: Fertilisation is when a sperm joins an egg. In frogs, toads and most fish, the female lays eggs in water and the male releases sperm over them, so fertilisation happens outside the body. In hens, as in humans and cows, the sperm meets the egg inside the female's body, which is called internal fertilisation.
fact: A frog can lay hundreds of eggs at once because many eggs in open water never get fertilised or are eaten.

reason: A cow gives birth to live young; the other four lay eggs.
explain: Animals that lay eggs are called oviparous, and the young develop inside the egg outside the mother's body. Animals like cows, dogs and humans are viviparous: the young grow inside the mother's uterus and are born alive. Most mammals give birth to live young.

notes: Bright light delays the sleep hormone
Bright light delays the sleep hormone
reason: A dark, quiet bedroom helps you fall asleep; the other four delay the sleep hormone melatonin.
explain: Your pineal gland releases melatonin when it gets dark, and this hormone makes you feel sleepy. Bright light, especially from screens, tells the brain it is still daytime, so melatonin is held back and sleep comes later. A dark, quiet room lets melatonin rise at the right time.

reason: White sugar has no iodine; the other four are sources of iodine.
explain: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make its hormone, thyroxine. Iodine comes from food: sea fish, seaweed and eggs contain it, and salt has iodine added to it in India. White sugar gives energy but no iodine, so it cannot help the thyroid.

items: Wrap used pad and bin it
reason: Flushing pads blocks toilets and drains; the other four are good period hygiene habits.
explain: During a period, good hygiene keeps the body comfortable and free of infection. Changing pads every few hours, washing hands and bathing daily stop germs from growing. Used pads should be wrapped in paper and put in a bin, because they soak up water, swell and block pipes if flushed.

reason: Strong thirst is a sign of high blood sugar; the other four are signs of low blood sugar.
explain: Blood sugar can go wrong in two directions in people with diabetes. When it drops too low, the body releases adrenaline, causing shaking, sweating and hunger, and the brain runs short of fuel, causing confusion. When it stays too high, the kidneys pass extra sugar into the urine, which pulls water out of the body and makes the person very thirsty.

notes: Early ball of cells forming body
Baby with all body parts formed
reason: The ovary is an organ; the other four are stages a baby passes through as it develops.
explain: A human life starts as a zygote, a single cell made when a sperm joins an egg. It divides many times to become an embryo, and once its main body parts have formed it is called a foetus. After about nine months in the uterus it is born as a newborn baby. The ovary is the organ where the egg came from in the first place.

notes: Swims with a tail and gills
Has legs and a short tail
Lives on land and in water
reason: A caterpillar is a stage in a butterfly's life; the other four are stages of a frog's life.
explain: Frogs and butterflies both go through metamorphosis, a big change in body shape as they grow. A frog hatches from an egg as a tadpole, grows legs as a froglet and becomes an adult frog. A caterpillar is the young stage of a butterfly or moth, which later forms a pupa.
fact: A tadpole needs the thyroid hormone thyroxine to turn into a frog.

reason: A growth spurt is a physical change; the other four are emotional changes of adolescence.
explain: Puberty brings changes both to the body and to feelings. The physical changes include growing taller quickly and new body hair. Hormones also affect the brain, so teenagers may have quick mood changes, feel shy, want privacy or worry about how they look. All of these are normal, and talking to a trusted adult helps.

notes: Wrong: it is deep in the brain
reason: The pineal gland is deep inside the brain, not in the chest; the other four locations are correct.
explain: Endocrine glands are spread around the body, and the blood carries their hormones everywhere. The pituitary hangs below the brain, the pineal gland sits deep in the middle of the brain, and the thyroid wraps around the front of the windpipe in the neck. The pancreas lies behind the stomach, and an adrenal gland sits on top of each kidney.

reason: Online rumours are often wrong; the other four are reliable ways to get answers about growing up.
explain: It is normal to have questions about the changes of puberty. The best answers come from people and sources that are reliable, such as parents, doctors, counsellors and science books. Rumours from friends or random websites are often untrue and can cause needless worry.

reason: A peaceful nap is a calm moment; the other four are scary or exciting moments that release adrenaline.
explain: When you feel scared, excited or in danger, your adrenal glands quickly release adrenaline. It speeds up your heart and breathing so your muscles get extra fuel to run or react. When you are calm and resting, adrenaline stays low and the body can relax and repair.

reason: Insulin is made by the pancreas; the other four are made by the testes or ovaries.
explain: The testes and ovaries have two jobs. They make sex cells (sperm in testes, eggs in ovaries), and they make sex hormones (testosterone in testes, oestrogen in ovaries) that cause the changes of puberty. Insulin comes from the pancreas and controls blood sugar.

clues: This hormone rises in the evening as daylight fades.
Bright screens and lamps at bedtime can hold it back.
It makes you feel drowsy so your body is ready to rest.
explain: Melatonin is made by the pineal gland, a tiny gland deep in the brain. Its level rises when it gets dark and falls in the morning light, which helps set your body clock. That is why bright screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep.

clues: This hormone works as the opposite partner of another hormone made in the same organ.
When you have not eaten for hours, it stops the glucose in your blood from falling too low.
It tells the body to break down its stored glucose and send it into the blood.
explain: Glucagon and insulin both come from the pancreas and work as a pair. After a meal, insulin lowers blood glucose by moving it into cells and storage. Between meals, glucagon tells the liver to release stored glucose so the level does not drop too far.

clues: Girls have two of these, one on each side of the lower belly.
After puberty, about once a month, one of them lets go of a tiny cell.
It stores the cells that can grow into a baby if one joins with a sperm.
explain: The ovaries are the two female sex glands. They store egg cells and, after puberty, usually release one each month. They also make the hormone oestrogen, which brings about the body changes of puberty in girls.

clues: These two glands hang outside the lower body in a pouch of skin called the scrotum.
Sitting outside keeps them slightly cooler, which they need to work well.
From puberty they make millions of tiny swimming cells every day, plus the hormone that deepens the voice.
explain: The testes are the two male sex glands. From puberty they make sperm, the male sex cells. They also make testosterone, the hormone behind a deeper voice, facial hair and bigger muscles in teenage boys.

clues: Its outer layer and its inner core make different hormones.
It makes the hormone that sets your heart pounding in a scary moment.
There are two of them, sitting like little caps on top of the organs that make urine.
explain: You have two adrenal glands, one on top of each kidney. The inner part releases adrenaline in an emergency, preparing the body to fight or run. The outer part makes other hormones, including cortisol, which helps the body cope with long-lasting pressure.

clues: It is about the size of a grain of rice and sits deep in the middle of the head.
It helps set your body clock by responding to light and darkness.
It releases the hormone that makes you drowsy after the sun goes down.
explain: The pineal gland is a tiny endocrine gland deep inside the brain, named for its pine-cone shape. When the eyes sense darkness, it releases melatonin, which makes you sleepy. This helps your body keep a regular daily rhythm.

clues: Using this every day in the kitchen helps prevent a swelling at the front of the neck.
It is an everyday seasoning with a tiny amount of an important mineral added.
The packet says it has a mineral added to protect the hormone gland in your neck.
explain: The thyroid needs iodine to make thyroxine, and many soils and foods in India have little iodine. Adding a small amount of iodine to ordinary salt is a simple way to make sure almost everyone gets enough. It has greatly reduced goitre, a swelling of the thyroid.

clues: It is the largest cell in the human body, just about visible without a microscope.
After puberty one is usually released each month in a girl's body.
If a male sex cell joins it, it becomes a zygote.
explain: An ovum is a female sex cell, often called an egg cell. It is made and stored in the ovaries, and after puberty usually one is released each month. If a sperm joins it, fertilisation happens and a zygote forms, the first cell of a new baby.

clues: It is one of the smallest cells in the human body.
It swims by moving a long, whip-like part from side to side.
Millions are made every day in a teenage boy's body, and one may join an ovum to start a baby.
explain: A sperm is the male sex cell. It has a head that carries the father's genes and a long tail for swimming. Sperm are made in the testes from puberty onwards, and if one joins an egg cell, a new life begins.

clues: It is the very first cell of a new living thing.
It holds one set of genes from the mother and one set from the father.
It forms when an ovum and a male sex cell join, then divides again and again.
explain: When a sperm and an egg fuse during fertilisation, they form a single new cell called a zygote. It carries genes from both parents. The zygote divides many times to form an embryo, which grows into a baby.

clues: It is an early stage of a growing human, when body parts are only just starting to form.
It grows from a single cell that divides again and again.
Once its main body parts have formed, around the eighth week in the womb, it gets a new name.
explain: After fertilisation, the zygote divides many times and becomes a ball of cells that attaches to the wall of the uterus. This early stage, while organs are starting to form, is called an embryo. Once the main body parts can be seen, it is called a foetus until birth.

clues: A young animal's body is rebuilt into a very different adult shape.
In frogs, the thyroid hormone controls when this process happens.
A wriggly larva becomes a pupa and then a winged insect.
explain: Metamorphosis is a big change in body form as an animal grows up. A tadpole loses its tail and grows legs to become a frog, and a caterpillar turns into a butterfly inside a pupa. In frogs this is controlled by thyroxine, a hormone that needs iodine.

clues: It is a group of cells whose job is to make and release a useful substance.
Some send their substance out through tubes; others pour it straight into the blood.
Examples sit in your neck, on top of your kidneys and just below your brain.
explain: A gland is an organ or group of cells that makes and releases a substance the body needs. Exocrine glands, like salivary and sweat glands, use tubes called ducts. Endocrine glands, like the thyroid and adrenals, have no ducts and release hormones directly into the blood.

clues: Your trousers suddenly look short even though they fitted last year.
It usually comes a little earlier in girls than in boys.
Your body shoots up a lot in a short time during the early teenage years.
explain: During puberty, growth hormone and sex hormones work together to make bones grow quickly for a year or two. This is called a growth spurt. Girls often start theirs around 10 to 12 and boys a little later, so classmates can be very different heights for a while.

clues: This small device shows a number on its screen within seconds.
A tiny prick gives a drop that goes onto a thin test strip.
People whose bodies cannot control glucose well use it several times a day.
explain: A glucose meter measures how much glucose (sugar) is in the blood. People with diabetes use it to check whether their level is too high or too low. The reading helps them decide on food, exercise and how much insulin to take.

clues: Its level is usually highest soon after you wake up and lowest around midnight.
Worry that goes on for weeks keeps it high, which can disturb sleep and weaken defences against germs.
It is made by the same small glands that make the fight-or-flight hormone.
explain: Cortisol is a hormone made by the outer layer of the adrenal glands. It helps the body wake up, keep blood sugar steady and cope with pressure. If worry goes on for a long time, cortisol stays high, which can affect sleep, appetite and the immune system.

clues: It happens roughly halfway through each menstrual cycle.
It is the moment a ripe ovum bursts out of its tiny pouch.
Afterwards the ovum travels down the oviduct towards the uterus.
explain: Ovulation is when an ovary releases a ripe egg cell. In a typical cycle it happens about two weeks before the next period. The egg then moves along the oviduct, and if it is not fertilised, the lining of the uterus is shed as a period.

scenario: A girl with type 1 diabetes asks why she must inject insulin instead of swallowing it as a tablet like other medicines. What is the best answer?
options: Tablets are too big to swallow
Insulin only works in the arm
Insulin would be digested in the stomach
answer: Insulin would be digested in the stomach
optionNotes: It works all over the body
It is a protein, broken down like food
explain: Insulin is a protein, just like the protein in dal or eggs. If swallowed, the stomach and intestine would digest it into small pieces before it could work. Injecting it under the skin lets it enter the blood whole, ready to move sugar into cells.

scenario: An adult's yearly check-up shows his blood sugar is slowly rising, though he does not have diabetes yet. He drinks several sugary drinks daily and rarely exercises. What is the best advice?
options: Exercise daily and cut sugary drinks
answer: Exercise daily and cut sugary drinks
optionNotes: Helps insulin work and lowers sugar
explain: Type 2 diabetes develops slowly when the body stops responding well to insulin. Regular exercise helps muscles take up sugar, and cutting sugary drinks reduces the load on the body. Healthy habits at this stage can delay or even prevent diabetes.

scenario: A student has felt anxious about board exams for many weeks. She sleeps badly and catches colds often. Her doctor explains that one hormone stays high when worry lasts a long time. Which hormone?
explain: Adrenaline handles sudden shocks, but cortisol from the adrenal glands rises when pressure lasts for days or weeks. High cortisol for a long time can upset sleep and weaken the immune system. Sleep, exercise, breaks and talking to someone help bring it down.

scenario: In a school experiment, tadpoles kept in water with no iodine stay as tadpoles, while those with iodine become frogs. Which hormone could they not make?
explain: The thyroid gland uses iodine to make thyroxine. In frogs, thyroxine controls metamorphosis, the change from tadpole to frog. Without iodine, the tadpoles cannot make enough thyroxine, so they stay tadpoles.

scenario: A pregnant woman asks how her growing baby gets food and oxygen while inside her uterus. Through which part does it reach the baby?
explain: Inside the uterus, a baby cannot eat or breathe air. The umbilical cord connects the baby to the placenta, which is attached to the mother's uterus. Food and oxygen pass from the mother's blood to the baby through the cord, and waste passes back. The belly button is where the cord was attached.

scenario: A pregnant woman wants to see how her growing baby is doing. The doctor wants a safe test that uses sound waves, not radiation. Which test is best?
optionNotes: Sound waves make a moving picture
explain: An ultrasound scan sends high-pitched sound waves into the body and turns the echoes into a picture on a screen. It uses no radiation, so it is safe for a growing baby. Doctors use it to check the baby's growth, heartbeat and position.

scenario: A 13-year-old has mild cramps in her lower tummy on the first day of her period. She is otherwise well. What is the best advice?
options: Run hard to stop the pain
A warm water bag and rest
answer: A warm water bag and rest
optionNotes: Hard exercise will not stop cramps
explain: Period cramps happen because the muscles of the uterus squeeze to shed its lining. Warmth on the tummy, rest and gentle movement often ease mild cramps. If the pain is very bad or stops her from going to school, a parent should take her to a doctor.

scenario: A 12-year-old boy notices his underarms now smell after games, which never happened before. He is healthy. What is the best advice?
options: Use the same shirt all week
optionNotes: Lets bacteria and smell build up
explain: At puberty, hormones switch on new sweat glands in the underarms. Their sweat has no smell at first, but bacteria on the skin break it down and make body odour. Bathing every day and wearing clean clothes removes the sweat and bacteria.

scenario: A 10-year-old is growing far taller than anyone in his family, and his hands and feet are very large. Tests show a gland below his brain is making too much growth hormone. Which gland is it?
optionNotes: Makes growth hormone; below the brain
explain: The pituitary gland, about the size of a pea, sits just below the brain. It makes growth hormone, which tells bones and muscles to grow. If it makes far too much during childhood, a child can grow extremely tall, a condition called gigantism, which doctors can treat.

scenario: A man with diabetes has a small cut on his foot that is healing very slowly. He did not even feel it happen. What should he do?
options: Show it to a doctor soon
Put ice on it for an hour
answer: Show it to a doctor soon
optionNotes: Raises the risk of new cuts
explain: Years of high blood sugar can damage nerves and blood vessels, especially in the feet. People with diabetes may not feel small cuts, and wounds heal slowly and can become infected. Checking the feet every day and showing any wound to a doctor early prevents serious problems.

scenario: Expecting parents ask what decides whether their baby will be a boy or a girl. What is the correct answer?
options: The sperm's X or Y chromosome
answer: The sperm's X or Y chromosome
optionNotes: Birth month does not decide this
X makes a girl; Y makes a boy
explain: Every egg cell carries an X chromosome. A sperm carries either an X or a Y. If an X sperm joins the egg, the baby is XX, a girl; if a Y sperm joins, the baby is XY, a boy. So it is decided at fertilisation, and the mother's diet has nothing to do with it.

scenario: A 15-year-old boy's voice is deeper, his muscles are bigger and a moustache is starting. Which organs make the hormone that causes these changes?
explain: In boys, puberty begins when the pituitary gland signals the testes to make more testosterone. Testosterone makes the voice box grow, builds muscle and causes facial and body hair. In girls, the ovaries make oestrogen, which brings about their puberty changes.

scenario: A 9-year-old with type 1 diabetes has a long football match after school. What should she do before the match?
optionNotes: Could make sugar drop too low
Raises the risk of low sugar
explain: Exercise makes muscles use up glucose from the blood, so blood sugar can fall during a long game. Children with diabetes can play every sport, but they check their level first and keep a snack ready. This prevents shaking and confusion from low blood sugar.

scenario: Twins are born: one is a boy and one is a girl. A student asks how they formed. What is the correct answer?
optionNotes: Makes identical twins of one sex
A sperm can join only one egg
Only one sperm can enter an egg
explain: Sometimes the ovaries release two eggs at once. If each is fertilised by a different sperm, two zygotes form and grow into non-identical twins. Since each sperm can carry X or Y, these twins can be a boy and a girl, and they are no more alike than ordinary brothers and sisters.

scenario: A couple cannot have a baby because the woman's oviducts are blocked. Doctors join her eggs with sperm in a lab dish, then place the early embryo in her uterus. What is this method called?
optionNotes: Body change in frogs and insects
Splitting in two, as in amoeba
explain: Normally a sperm meets the egg in the oviduct. If the oviducts are blocked, doctors can bring egg and sperm together in a lab dish; 'in vitro' means 'in glass'. The embryo is then placed in the uterus to grow, and babies born this way are sometimes called test-tube babies.

scenario: A 13-year-old feels happy one moment and irritable the next, without a clear reason. She is healthy and growing well. What is the best explanation?
