Small objects breathed in by mistake often lodge in a bronchus, more often the right one, which is wider and runs more steeply downwards. Doctors can remove the object with a thin tube and camera. Keeping beads, coins and small toys away from young children prevents this.

notes: Catch dust before it gets in
Stop sweat running into the eyes
Senses light at the back of the eye
Close to shield and wipe the eye
reason: The retina senses light; the other four protect the eye.
explain: Your eyes are delicate, so the body surrounds them with guards. Eyebrows steer sweat and rain away, eyelashes catch dust, eyelids blink to wipe and shut the eye, and tears wash it clean. The retina has a different job: it lines the back of the eye and turns light into nerve signals for the brain.

notes: High sound but within our range
reason: A bat's ultrasound call is too high-pitched for humans; we can hear the other four.
explain: Pitch depends on how many times a sound wave vibrates each second. Young people can hear from about 20 to about 20,000 vibrations per second. Sounds higher than that are called ultrasound. Many bats use ultrasound calls to find insects in the dark by listening for the echoes, but our ears cannot pick them up.
fact: Dogs can hear much higher sounds than people, which is how dog whistles work.

notes: Correct: honey is full of sugars
Correct: sea water is full of salt
reason: Sugar tastes sweet, not sour; the other four pairs are correct.
explain: Your tongue can sense five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Each taste comes from a type of chemical in food. Sugars give sweetness, acids like those in lemons give sourness, and salt gives saltiness. Bitterness, like in karela, can warn the body about possible poisons, which is why many children dislike it at first.

notes: Cones work best in bright light
reason: Seeing in dim light is mainly done by rods; the other four rely on cones.
explain: The retina has two kinds of light-sensing cells. Cones work in bright light and give you colour and sharp detail; there are three kinds, for red, green and blue light. Rods are far more sensitive, so they let you see in dim light, but only in shades of grey. That is why colours fade when it gets dark.
fact: Each retina has about 120 million rods but only about 6 million cones.

notes: Breaks skin and lets germs in
Keeps germs out while it heals
reason: Scratching bites can break the skin; the other four keep skin healthy.
explain: Skin is your body's outer barrier against germs, sun and water loss. Washing gently, using sunscreen, moisturising dry patches and covering cuts all help that barrier do its job. Scratching an itchy bite can break the skin, letting germs in and causing an infection. A cool cloth helps the itch instead.

notes: Made mostly of collagen and calcium
Its top cells are filled with keratin
reason: Bone is not made of keratin; the other four are.
explain: Keratin is a tough protein made by skin cells. As cells in the outer skin, hair roots and nail beds fill with keratin, they die and harden into a strong, waterproof material. That is why hair and nails can be cut without pain. Bone is different: it is living tissue made of collagen fibres hardened with calcium.

notes: Loud sound right next to the eardrum
Loud noise that goes on and on
reason: Normal chatting is safe for hearing; the other four can damage it.
explain: Very loud sounds, or loud sounds that last a long time, can damage the tiny hair cells in the cochlea that turn sound into nerve signals. Once these cells are destroyed they do not grow back. Keeping a distance from loud noises, turning the volume down and using earplugs protect your hearing for life.

notes: One of the most sensitive spots
Few touch sensors, spread far apart
reason: The middle of the back has few touch sensors; the other four have many.
explain: Touch sensors are not spread evenly over the skin. Fingertips, lips and the tip of the tongue are packed with them, so you can feel tiny details, like the dots of Braille. The middle of the back has far fewer, so two pencil points touching it a few centimetres apart can feel like one. The brain also gives more space to areas with more sensors.

notes: Done by the cornea and lens
reason: Focusing light is done by the cornea and lens; tears do the other four jobs.
explain: Tears are not only for crying. Small glands make a thin layer of tears all the time, and every blink spreads it over the eye. Tears keep the eye moist, wash away dust, help the eyelids slide smoothly and contain substances that kill germs. The focusing of light is done by the clear cornea and the lens.

reason: A red blood cell carries oxygen; the other four are sense receptor cells.
explain: Every sense starts with special receptor cells that detect one kind of change. Rods and cones in the eye detect light, hair cells in the ear detect vibrations, and taste cells on the tongue detect chemicals. Each turns what it detects into a nerve signal for the brain. Red blood cells have a different job: carrying oxygen.

notes: Clear watery fluid at the front
reason: The iris is coloured and blocks light; the other four are clear so light can pass.
explain: Light has to travel through the eye to reach the retina, so everything along its path must be see-through. It passes the clear cornea, the watery aqueous fluid, the lens and the clear vitreous jelly that fills the eyeball. The iris is different: it is coloured and blocks light, and its muscles change the size of the pupil to control how much gets in.

notes: Carries signals from eye to brain
Light tool for looking inside the ear
reason: An otoscope is for the ear; the other four are about the eyes.
explain: Many body words come from Greek. "Opt" and "ophthalm" are linked to the eye and seeing, so opticians, optometrists, ophthalmologists and the optic nerve all deal with vision. "Oto" means ear, so an otoscope is the small light a doctor uses to look down your ear canal at the eardrum.

notes: Pupils widen to let in light
Pupils shrink to block bright light
reason: On a sunny beach the pupils get smaller; in the other four they get bigger.
explain: The pupil works like a camera opening. In dim places, muscles in the iris pull it wider so more light reaches the retina. In bright light, other iris muscles squeeze it small to protect the retina from too much light. This happens automatically within seconds.

notes: Checks for a disease called glaucoma
Checks how wide you can see
reason: The beep test checks hearing; the other four check the eyes.
explain: An eye check is more than reading letters. A letter chart tests sharpness, a colour dot test checks colour vision, an eye pressure test looks for glaucoma, a disease that can harm the optic nerve, and a side vision test checks how wide your view is. A beep test with headphones checks hearing.

notes: Caused by cold or strong feelings
Extra melanin made because of UV
Skin uses UV to make it
reason: Goosebumps are caused by cold or emotions; UV light causes the other four.
explain: Sunlight carries invisible ultraviolet (UV) rays. A little UV helps the skin make vitamin D for strong bones. UV also makes skin cells produce more melanin, which darkens tans and freckles. Too much UV burns the skin. Goosebumps are caused by tiny muscles pulling hairs upright when you are cold or excited.

notes: Strong smell that warns of fire
reason: Carbon monoxide has no smell; you can smell the other four.
explain: Your nose detects chemicals floating in the air, but only some of them. Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas from burning fuel with too little air, and it has no smell or colour. That is why homes use carbon monoxide alarms. Cooking gas has a strong smell added on purpose so that leaks can be noticed.

notes: Hearing organ in the inner ear
Balance tubes in the inner ear
Tiny bone in the middle ear
reason: The hammer is in the middle ear; the other four are in the inner ear.
explain: The ear has three sections. The outer ear collects sound, the middle ear has the eardrum and three tiny bones, including the hammer, that pass on vibrations, and the inner ear is deep in the skull. The inner ear is filled with fluid and holds the cochlea for hearing and the semicircular canals for balance, both lined with hair cells.

clues: Tiny muscles change its shape, making it fatter for near things and thinner for far things.
With age it can turn cloudy, which is called a cataract.
It sits just behind the pupil and bends light so a sharp picture lands on the retina.
explain: The lens is a clear, bendy disc behind the pupil. It fine-tunes the focus so light lands sharply on the retina. Muscles around it change its shape: fatter for close objects and flatter for distant ones. With age the lens gets stiffer, which is why many older people need reading glasses.

clues: It does more of the light-bending for vision than the lens does.
It has no blood vessels, so it gets oxygen straight from the air and from tears.
This transparent dome covers the iris and pupil.
explain: The cornea is the clear dome at the front of the eye. Because it is curved, it bends incoming light and does about two-thirds of the eye's focusing, with the lens doing the rest. It has no blood vessels, which keeps it perfectly clear. It is also one of the most sensitive parts of the body, which is why a speck of dust hurts.

clues: Each one falls out and is replaced every few months.
Some people put mascara on these to make them look darker.
These short curved strands along the edge of your peepers catch dust before it gets in.
explain: Eyelashes are short, curved hairs along the edges of the eyelids. They catch dust and tiny bits in the air, and when something touches them, the eyelids blink shut by reflex. Like other hairs, each lash grows, falls out and is replaced.

clues: In newborn babies it can look slightly bluish because it is still thin.
Thin red blood vessels can show on it when you are tired or have an infection.
It is the strong, pale part you see around the coloured iris.
explain: The sclera is the white of the eye. It is a tough coat that covers most of the eyeball and keeps its round shape. At the front it joins the clear cornea. The six muscles that move your eye attach to the sclera.

clues: The eyeball is a little too short, so light comes to a focus behind the retina.
Reading a book up close is hard, but faraway trees look sharp.
Glasses with lenses that are thicker in the middle fix it.
explain: Hypermetropia, or long-sightedness, means distant things look clear but close things look blurred. The eyeball is slightly short, or the cornea and lens are too weak, so light would focus behind the retina. Convex lenses, thicker in the middle, bend light inward a little extra so it focuses on the retina.

clues: Instead of being round like a football, the front of the eye is shaped more like a rugby ball.
Straight lines in some directions look sharp, while lines in other directions look smeared.
It is very common and is usually corrected with special glasses or contacts.
explain: In astigmatism the cornea, or sometimes the lens, is shaped more like the back of a spoon stretched one way. Light in one direction focuses at a different point from light in another, so some lines look sharp and others blurred. Glasses or contact lenses shaped to match correct it.

clues: A cat's are shaped like tiny hooks, which is why its lick feels like sandpaper.
Most kinds hold taste receptors, but the most common thread-shaped kind does not.
These tiny raised dots cover the upper surface of the organ you lick with.
explain: Papillae are the small bumps on top of the tongue. Most kinds contain taste buds, which hold the cells that detect taste. The most common kind is thread-shaped and has no taste buds; it helps grip and move food. Together they give the tongue its rough feel.

clues: It is made of bendy cartilage covered in skin, with no bone inside.
Its folds and curves catch sound and guide it inwards.
It is the part of your hearing organ you can see on the side of your head.
explain: The pinna is the outer part of the ear that you can see. It is made of cartilage, which is why it bends. Its curved shape collects sound waves and funnels them into the ear canal, and it also helps the brain tell whether a sound is coming from in front or behind.

clues: A quiet whisper is about 30 of these, and a rock concert can be over 100.
Every 10 more of them means the noise carries ten times more energy.
Long exposure to noise above about 85 of these can harm hearing.
explain: Decibels (dB) measure how loud a sound is. The scale climbs fast: 10 more decibels means ten times more sound energy. Normal talking is about 60 dB. Sounds above about 85 dB can damage the hair cells in the cochlea if you hear them for a long time, and very loud bangs can do it at once.

clues: You have between 2 and 4 million of these tiny coiled tubes.
The soles of your feet, your palms and your forehead have lots of them.
They release watery drops when you run or feel hot, and the drying liquid takes heat away.
explain: Sweat glands are tiny coiled tubes in the dermis that open onto the skin through pores. When you get hot, your brain tells them to release sweat, which is mostly water with some salt. As sweat evaporates it carries heat away and cools you down.

clues: Its top is made of flat, dead cells that flake off all the time.
Its bottom row of cells keeps dividing to replace the ones that are lost.
It is the thin top covering of your body, the part you can touch.
explain: The epidermis is the thin outer layer of skin. New cells form at its base and move upward, filling with tough keratin and dying as they go. The dead top cells form a waterproof barrier and flake off all the time. Below it is the thicker dermis, with blood vessels, nerves, hair roots and sweat glands.
fact: Your outer skin replaces itself roughly every month.

clues: Blocked ones can turn into blackheads.
Oil from the roots of your hairs comes out through these openings.
They are small openings dotted over your body, where salty water comes out on hot days.
explain: Pores are small openings in the skin. Some let out sweat from sweat glands; others are the openings of hair follicles, where natural oil reaches the surface. When oil and dead skin cells block a pore, it can become a blackhead or a pimple. Gentle washing keeps pores clear.

clues: They are flat and harmless, and often run in families, especially in people with red or fair hair.
They have extra melanin pigment and get darker in summer.
They are small light-tan dots, often sprinkled across the nose and cheeks.
explain: Freckles are small flat patches where skin cells make extra melanin, the pigment that colours skin. Sunlight makes them darker, and they often fade in winter. They run in families and are harmless, but they are also a sign that skin is sensitive to the sun.

clues: Guitar players, cricketers and people who walk barefoot often get them.
It forms where something presses or scrapes on the same spot again and again.
It is a tough, yellowish patch on a palm or heel that protects the area underneath.
explain: A callus is an area of skin that has become thick and tough because of repeated pressure or rubbing. The epidermis responds by making extra layers of keratin-filled cells. This protects the tissue underneath. A blister is different: it is a sudden bubble of fluid from fresh rubbing.

clues: The pale half-moon near its base is called the lunula.
It grows from a root under the skin, about 3 millimetres a month.
It is the hard plate that protects the tip of each digit on your hands and feet.
explain: Nails are plates of hard keratin that grow from a root under the skin at their base. They protect the tips of fingers and toes and help you pick up small things. The nail itself has no nerves, so cutting it does not hurt, but the skin beneath it is very sensitive.
fact: Fingernails grow faster than toenails.

clues: When you are surprised, these shoot upwards.
They help stop sweat and rain running down into your vision.
They are two curved strips of short strands that help show feelings on your face.
explain: Eyebrows are the strips of hair above the eyes. Their shape and the way the hairs point steer sweat and rain to the sides, away from the eyes. They also help people show and read feelings such as surprise, worry or anger.

clues: Unlike an implant, it needs no operation and simply slips on.
A small microphone picks up noises and a speaker plays them back more strongly.
People with weak hearing wear one, and modern ones run on tiny batteries.
explain: A hearing aid is a small device for people with hearing loss. A microphone picks up sound, a tiny computer makes the important parts stronger, and a speaker sends it into the ear canal. A cochlear implant is different: it is placed by an operation and sends electrical signals straight to the hearing nerve.

scenario: A classmate's eye is pink, itchy and sticky in the morning. The doctor says it is conjunctivitis, which can spread to others. What should she do while it heals?
options: Wash hands; use her own towel
Rub her eye to clean it
answer: Wash hands; use her own towel
optionNotes: Spreads germs from eye to eye
Irritates the eye and spreads germs
explain: Conjunctivitis, often called pink eye, is swelling of the thin clear layer covering the white of the eye. Germs or allergies can cause it. The infectious kind spreads through hands, towels and pillows, so washing hands and not sharing are the most important steps. A doctor decides if drops are needed.

scenario: When a boy cries hard, his nose starts to run too, even though he does not have a cold. Why does this happen?
options: His nose makes its own tears
Water comes up from his stomach
optionNotes: The nose makes mucus, not tears
Tears come from glands near the eye
The tear duct links eye and nose
explain: Tears are made by glands above the outer corner of each eye. After washing over the eye, they drain through tiny holes in the inner corner of the eyelids, down a tear duct into the nose. Usually the amount is small. When you cry, there are so many tears that your nose starts to run.

scenario: A 50-year-old woman now holds her phone at arm's length to read it, though her distance vision is fine. Her eye lens has become stiffer with age. What will help her read?
optionNotes: Add extra focusing power for close work
explain: To focus on close things, the lens must become fatter. With age, usually from the mid-forties, the lens gets stiffer and cannot change shape as much, so close reading becomes blurry. This is called presbyopia. Reading glasses with convex lenses give the extra focusing power needed.

scenario: After a heavy cold, a 5-year-old has earache and a fever. The doctor finds infection behind his eardrum, in the middle ear. Germs reached it through a tube from the back of his throat. Which tube?
optionNotes: Links the middle ear to the throat
explain: The Eustachian tube links the middle ear to the back of the nose and throat. It lets air in and out to keep pressure equal on both sides of the eardrum. In young children it is short and level, so germs from a cold can travel up it easily. That is why middle ear infections are common in small children.

scenario: A boy walks from a sunny street into a dark cinema. At first he sees nothing, but after a few minutes he can find his seat, though colours look dull. Which retina cells are now doing most of the work?
optionNotes: The lens is not part of the retina
Sensitive cells that work in dim light
Carry oxygen, do not sense light
explain: Rods are very sensitive to light, but they take several minutes to adjust after bright sunlight. As they do, you start to see shapes in the dark. Rods cannot tell colours apart, so dim scenes look grey and dull. Cones, which give colour, need brighter light.

scenario: A 14-year-old has pimples on his face and back. He wants to squeeze them. What should the dermatologist advise?
options: Scrub hard with a rough cloth
optionNotes: Keeps pores clear and avoids scars
Irritates skin and makes it worse
Pushes germs deeper and can scar
Lets oil and dirt build up
explain: During puberty, oil glands in the skin become more active. Oil and dead skin cells can block pores, and bacteria grow inside, making red, swollen pimples. This is acne. Gentle washing helps, while squeezing pushes germs deeper and can leave scars. A dermatologist can suggest creams if acne is bad.

scenario: After standing next to huge speakers at a concert, a teenager hears ringing in his ears and sounds seem muffled for a day. Which part was strained by the noise?
optionNotes: Only collect sound, not harmed by it
explain: Inside the cochlea, thousands of tiny hair cells bend with sound vibrations and send signals to the brain. Very loud noise over-bends and tires them, causing muffled hearing and ringing, called tinnitus. Usually it settles in a day, but repeated loud noise can kill hair cells, and they do not grow back. Earplugs and keeping a distance from speakers protect them.

scenario: In hot, humid weather, a baby gets tiny itchy red bumps on her neck and back where sweat gets trapped. What helps most?
options: Keep her cool in loose cotton clothes
Keep her in the hot sun
answer: Keep her cool in loose cotton clothes
optionNotes: Lets sweat dry and skin breathe
Can block sweat pores even more
explain: This is heat rash, also called prickly heat. When sweat ducts get blocked, sweat leaks under the skin and causes small itchy bumps. Keeping the skin cool and dry, with loose cotton clothes and a fan or shade, lets the ducts clear. It usually fades in a few days.

scenario: When a girl enters a room where incense is burning, the smell is strong. After ten minutes she hardly notices it, though it is still there. Why?
options: Her senses tune out a steady smell
answer: Her senses tune out a steady smell
optionNotes: Her sense of smell is fine
The smell is still in the room
The tongue does not block smells
explain: Your senses are built to notice changes. When a smell stays the same, the smell receptors and the brain gradually respond less to it. This is called sensory adaptation, and it frees your attention for new smells, like smoke. The same thing happens when you stop feeling the clothes on your skin.

scenario: A book says the tip of the tongue tastes only sweet and the back tastes only bitter. A girl tests this with sugar and lemon on different parts of her tongue. What will she find?
options: All areas can sense every basic taste
answer: All areas can sense every basic taste
optionNotes: Taste buds everywhere sense all five
explain: The "tongue map" with separate zones for each taste is a myth based on a misread old study. Taste buds on all parts of the tongue can detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Some areas may be slightly more sensitive to a taste, but every area can sense all five.

scenario: A boy closes one eye and tries to catch a ball. He keeps misjudging how far away it is. Why does he catch better with both eyes open?
options: Two views let the brain judge distance
Closing an eye makes the ball faster
Two eyes make the ball bigger
answer: Two views let the brain judge distance
optionNotes: The ball speed does not change
explain: Your two eyes are a few centimetres apart, so each sees a slightly different picture. The brain compares the two views to work out how far away things are. This is called depth perception. With one eye shut, the brain has fewer clues, so judging distance is harder.

scenario: A 5-year-old's left eye sees poorly, though it is healthy, because her brain has been relying on the stronger right eye. The doctor wants the weaker eye to work harder. What treatment is common?
optionNotes: Lets the weak eye rest, so no help
Glasses may be part of treatment
Makes the brain use the weaker eye
explain: This is a lazy eye, or amblyopia. If one eye sends a blurrier picture in early childhood, the brain starts ignoring it. Covering the stronger eye forces the brain to use and train the weaker one. Treatment works best in young children, while the brain's vision pathways are still developing, so early eye checks matter.

scenario: After football, a boy's armpits smell, though fresh sweat has almost no smell. What causes the odour?
explain: Sweat itself is almost odourless. Armpits have special sweat glands that become active at puberty, and bacteria living on the skin feed on their sweat. The waste the bacteria make has a strong smell. Washing daily, drying well and wearing clean clothes keep bacteria numbers down.

scenario: A paper scratch scrapes away a thin flake of skin. It stings slightly but does not bleed. A deeper cut does bleed. Why?
options: Paper seals the wound at once
Top skin layer has no blood vessels
answer: Top skin layer has no blood vessels
optionNotes: Blood vessels start in the dermis
The dermis has many blood vessels
explain: Skin has two main layers. The epidermis on top has no blood vessels; it gets food and oxygen from the dermis below. A very shallow scratch only removes epidermis, so it does not bleed. A cut that reaches the dermis breaks tiny blood vessels and bleeds.

scenario: A girl who hears with only one ear finds it hard to tell where a car horn is coming from. Why do two ears help locate sounds?
options: One ear hears and the other balances
The brain compares sound at each ear
answer: The brain compares sound at each ear
optionNotes: Both ears hear and both help balance
explain: A sound from your left reaches your left ear a tiny fraction of a second sooner, and a little louder, than your right ear. The brain compares these small differences to work out direction. With only one working ear, these clues are missing, so finding where a sound is coming from is harder.

scenario: A boy bites into a very hot green chilli and his mouth burns. Gulping water barely helps. Which drink usually soothes the burn better?
optionNotes: Milk helps wash the chilli chemical away
The chemical does not mix well with water
Heat makes the burn feel worse
explain: The heat of chilli comes from a chemical called capsaicin. It does not have a taste; it switches on the same sensors in your mouth that detect heat and pain, so your brain thinks your mouth is burning. Capsaicin does not mix well with water, but milk helps wash it away. The burning fades as the sensors settle.

notes: Snail-shaped hearing organ in the ear
Light-sensing layer at the back of the eye
Black hole that lets light in
Clear front window of the eye
reason: The cochlea is part of the ear; the rest are parts of the eye.
explain: Light enters the eye through the clear cornea, then passes through the pupil, a hole whose size is set by the coloured iris. The lens focuses the light onto the retina at the back, which turns it into nerve signals for the brain. The cochlea is a snail-shaped tube deep in the ear that turns sound into nerve signals.

notes: Thin skin that vibrates with sound
One of three tiny ear bones
reason: The iris is part of the eye; the rest are parts of the ear.
explain: Sound waves travel down the ear canal and make the eardrum vibrate. Three tiny bones, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, pass the vibrations to the cochlea in the inner ear. Tiny hair cells there turn the vibrations into nerve signals that the brain hears as sound. The iris is the coloured ring in your eye.

reason: The lungs are for breathing; the others are sense organs.
explain: Sense organs have special cells called receptors that detect something from the world around you: light for the eyes, sound for the ears, chemicals for the nose and tongue, and touch, heat and pain for the skin. They send signals to the brain, which makes sense of them. The lungs take in air for breathing; they do not send sense information about the outside world.

notes: Savoury taste of tomato or mushrooms
Felt by pain and heat sensors
reason: Spicy heat is detected by pain and heat sensors; the others are basic tastes.
explain: Taste buds detect five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami (a savoury taste). The burning feeling of chilli is not a taste. A chemical in chillies triggers the same sensors in your mouth that detect heat and pain, which is why spicy food feels hot.
fact: Every part of your tongue with taste buds can sense all five tastes. The old 'tongue map' with separate zones is a myth.

notes: Pit in the skin where hair grows
Tiny coiled tube in the skin
reason: Enamel covers teeth; the others are layers or parts of the skin.
explain: Skin has layers. The epidermis on top is a waterproof shield that keeps renewing itself. The dermis below holds blood vessels, nerve endings, sweat glands and hair follicles, the tiny pits that hairs grow from. Under that, a fat layer keeps you warm. Enamel is the hard coating on your teeth.
fact: Skin is the body's largest organ.

reason: Pumping blood is the heart's job; the others are jobs of the skin.
explain: Skin does much more than cover you. It is a barrier that keeps germs out and water in. Nerve endings let you feel touch, heat and pain. It helps control body temperature by sweating and changing blood flow. When sunlight falls on it, skin makes vitamin D, which helps build strong bones. Pumping blood is the heart's job.

notes: Lets heat escape from the skin
Blood vessels widen to lose heat
Muscle twitches make heat to warm up
reason: Shivering warms the body up; the others help cool it down.
explain: Your body tries to stay near 37°C. When you are hot, sweat comes out onto the skin and takes heat with it as it evaporates. Blood vessels near the skin widen, so more heat escapes and you look flushed. Shade and lighter clothes help too. Shivering does the opposite: fast muscle twitches make heat to warm you when you are cold.

notes: Vibrates with sound; used for hearing
Tell the brain where your limbs are
Fluid-filled loops that sense head turns
reason: The eardrum is used for hearing; the others all help you balance.
explain: Balance uses teamwork. The semicircular canals in the inner ear are three fluid-filled loops that sense when your head turns or tilts. Your eyes show which way is up, and sensors in muscles and joints report where your body parts are. The cerebellum combines all this and adjusts your muscles. The eardrum vibrates with sound and is used for hearing, not balance.

notes: Rest eyes that focus close for long
Stop flying bits hitting the eye
Less strain on the eye muscles
Can scratch the eye and spread germs
reason: Rubbing eyes hard can harm them; the others protect your eyes.
explain: The front of the eye is delicate. Sunglasses that block ultraviolet (UV) light protect it from sun damage, and goggles stop flying bits during sports or science. Good light and screen breaks reduce strain on the small muscles that focus the eye. Rubbing hard can scratch the clear cornea and carry germs from your hands into the eye.

items: Cotton buds deep in the ear
answer: Cotton buds deep in the ear
notes: Cut the sound reaching the ear
Pushes wax in and can hurt eardrum
Gives the inner ear time to recover
reason: Pushing cotton buds into the ear can harm it; the others protect hearing.
explain: Inside the cochlea are thousands of tiny hair cells that sense sound. Very loud or long-lasting noise can damage them, and they do not grow back, so turning volume down and wearing earplugs at loud places protects hearing. Ears clean themselves: wax slowly moves outwards on its own. Pushing cotton buds inside can pack wax deeper or hurt the eardrum.

notes: Ringing or buzzing heard in the ears
reason: Tinnitus is an ear problem; the others are eye problems.
explain: Myopia, hypermetropia and astigmatism happen when the eye does not focus light exactly on the retina, so things look blurry. Glasses or contact lenses usually correct them. A cataract is when the lens inside the eye turns cloudy. Tinnitus is a ringing or buzzing sound in the ears that no one else can hear, sometimes after loud noise.

notes: Sensed by taste buds on the tongue
reason: Taste is sensed by the tongue; skin has receptors for the other four.
explain: Your skin has different kinds of receptors spread through it. Some respond to light touch and pressure, some to warmth, some to cold, and some to pain, which warns you of damage. Fingertips and lips have many receptors, which is why they are so sensitive. Taste is detected by taste buds, mostly on the tongue.

notes: Smell adds most of the flavour
Done by cone cells in the eyes
reason: Seeing colours uses the eyes; your sense of smell helps with the other four.
explain: High inside your nose are smell receptors that detect tiny chemicals floating in the air. Smell warns you about danger like smoke or food gone bad. It also gives food much of its flavour, which is why food tastes bland when your nose is blocked. Colour is seen by cone cells in the retina of the eye.

notes: Blocks much of the UV light
Gives little or no UV protection
reason: Tanning oil does not protect against sunburn; the others do.
explain: Sunburn is skin damage caused by ultraviolet (UV) rays from the sun. Sunscreen, hats, clothing and shade all reduce the UV reaching your skin. UV is strongest around the middle of the day, so shade matters most then. Tanning oil gives little or no protection and is used to make skin darken faster.

notes: Last bone; pushes on the inner ear
First to vibrate when sound arrives
First tiny bone in the chain
reason: The semicircular canals are for balance; the others pass sound vibrations along.
explain: Sound travels as vibrations. The eardrum vibrates first, then the three tiny bones of the middle ear, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, pass the vibrations to the cochlea, making them stronger along the way. The semicircular canals sit next to the cochlea in the inner ear, but their job is balance: they sense when your head moves.
fact: The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body, about the size of a grain of rice.

notes: Bubble of fluid from rubbing or burns
reason: A cataract affects the eye; the others are skin problems.
explain: Many problems affect the skin. Eczema makes skin dry, itchy and red. Acne happens when pores get blocked with oil and dead skin. Sunburn is damage from UV rays, and a blister is a bubble of fluid that forms to protect damaged skin underneath. A cataract is a clouding of the lens inside the eye, and it is more common in older people.

notes: Made by sweat glands to cool you
Made by glands in the mouth
Grows from follicles in the skin
reason: Saliva is made in the mouth; the others are made in the skin.
explain: Skin is a busy organ. Sweat glands release sweat to cool you, and oil glands release an oil that keeps skin and hair soft and waterproof. Cells in the epidermis make melanin, the pigment that colours skin and helps block UV. Hair grows from tiny pits in the skin called follicles. Saliva is made by glands around the mouth.

clues: A doctor may shine a small torch to watch it shrink.
It gets bigger in the dark to let in more light, and smaller in bright sunshine.
It is the dark round opening in the middle of the coloured part you look through.
explain: The pupil is the opening in the middle of the iris that lets light into the eye. It looks black because light goes in and does not come back out. The iris muscles make the pupil smaller in bright light to protect the retina, and bigger in dim light to let in more light.

clues: It has a small blind spot where the nerve to the brain leaves it.
It is a thin layer at the very back, about the size of a postage stamp.
It works like the screen in a camera, catching the picture and sending it to the brain.
explain: The retina is a thin layer lining the back of the eye. It holds two kinds of light-sensing cells: rods, which work in dim light, and cones, which see colour and detail. They turn light into nerve signals that travel along the optic nerve to the brain. The picture on the retina is actually upside down, and the brain turns it the right way up.

clues: Its pattern is so unique that some scanners use it to identify people.
It is a muscle that changes the size of the opening in the middle.
It is the part you look at to say whether someone has brown, blue, green or grey peepers.
explain: The iris is the coloured ring of muscle around the pupil. By tightening or relaxing, it makes the pupil smaller or bigger to control how much light gets in. Its colour comes from the pigment melanin: lots of melanin gives brown eyes, and less gives blue or green.

clues: It is a thin, tight sheet of skin, about as thin as a sheet of paper.
It sits at the end of the canal, separating the outer and middle parts of your hearing organ.
When noises hit it, it shakes and passes the shaking to three tiny bones.
explain: The eardrum is a thin membrane stretched across the end of the ear canal. Sound waves make it vibrate, and it passes those vibrations to the tiny bones of the middle ear. Pushing objects into the ear can damage it, which is one reason not to use cotton buds inside your ears.

clues: It is filled with fluid and lined with thousands of tiny hair cells.
It turns vibrations into electrical signals for the brain.
It is a coiled tube deep in the head shaped like a shell with a little animal inside.
explain: The cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear. Vibrations from the middle ear make the fluid move, which bends tiny hair cells. The hair cells turn this into nerve signals that the brain hears as sound. Different parts of the cochlea respond to high and low sounds.

clues: You have thousands of these, and they are replaced every couple of weeks.
They sit in the tiny bumps you can see when you stick out the pink muscle you lick with.
They tell you whether food is sour, salty, bitter or umami.
explain: Taste buds are tiny clusters of sensing cells, mostly on the tongue. Chemicals from food dissolve in saliva and touch the taste cells, which send signals to the brain. They detect five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Taste cells are worn out quickly and are replaced every week or two.

clues: People with albinism make very little of it, so their hair is very pale.
Sunlight makes your body produce more of it, which darkens you after a holiday at the beach.
It is the natural dark substance that sets the shade of a person's complexion, hair and irises, and blocks some UV.
explain: Melanin is a dark pigment made by special cells in the epidermis. It gives colour to skin, hair and eyes, and it absorbs some UV light, protecting skin cells. When skin is exposed to sun, it makes more melanin, which is a tan. A tan is a sign the skin is under UV stress, so it does not replace sunscreen.

clues: Spending more time outdoors in daylight seems to lower the chance of getting it.
The eyeball is a little too long, so light focuses in front of the retina.
A child with it reads a book easily but struggles to see the board from the back of class.
explain: Myopia, or short-sightedness, means near things look clear but distant things look blurry. Usually the eyeball is slightly too long, so light comes to a focus in front of the retina instead of on it. Glasses with concave lenses spread the light out a little so it focuses correctly. Time outdoors in daylight helps protect children's eyes from developing it.

clues: You can get it even on a cloudy day, because UV rays pass through clouds.
It makes skin sore, hot and sometimes peel a few days later.
It happens after spending too long outside in strong daylight without protection.
explain: Sunburn is skin damage from ultraviolet (UV) rays. The rays harm skin cells, so the skin becomes red, sore and hot, and later may peel. Repeated sunburn raises the risk of skin problems later in life. Sunscreen, hats, clothing and shade, especially around midday, protect your skin.

clues: It is common in children and you cannot catch it from someone else.
Harsh soaps, wool or dust can make it flare up.
Rough, red patches appear, often in elbow and knee creases, and it helps to moisturise every day.
explain: Eczema is a common condition in which the skin's protective barrier does not work well. Skin loses water easily and gets dry, red and itchy, often in the creases of elbows and knees. It is not contagious. Moisturising every day, using mild soap and not scratching help, and a doctor can give creams for flare-ups.

clues: A scary film or a favourite song can also cause them.
Tiny muscles at the base of little fibres on your arms pull them upright.
Little raised dots that pop up on your skin when you step out into chilly air.
explain: Goosebumps appear when tiny muscles attached to each hair in the skin tighten and pull the hairs upright, raising little bumps. In furry animals this traps a layer of warm air, and it also makes them look bigger when frightened. Humans have little body hair, so goosebumps do not help much, but the reflex is still there.

clues: Your brain fills in the gap so you never notice it.
There are no rods or cones on this small patch of the retina.
It is the place at the back of each eye where nerve fibres leave for the brain, so it cannot detect light.
explain: The blind spot is a small area on the retina where the optic nerve leaves the eye. There are no light-sensing cells there, so light falling on it is not detected. You do not notice it because your two eyes cover for each other and your brain fills in the gap using what is around it.

clues: It slowly moves outward on its own as you chew and talk.
It is sticky and traps dust and germs before they go too deep.
It is the orange-brown gunk that collects in the canal you hear through.
explain: Earwax is made by glands in the ear canal. It traps dust and germs and keeps the skin of the canal from drying out. Ears clean themselves: wax slowly moves out as you move your jaw. Poking inside with cotton buds can push wax deeper and block hearing, so only the outer ear should be wiped.

clues: Even identical twins do not share the same pattern.
These ridges form before you are born and stay the same all your life.
Detectives dust for the marks your hand leaves on a glass, and phones can use them to unlock.
explain: Fingerprints are the patterns of tiny ridges on your fingertips. They help you grip things and feel textures. Each person's pattern is unique, even between identical twins, and it stays the same for life. That is why fingerprints are used to identify people.

clues: It was invented by a French teenager who had lost his sight as a small child.
Each letter is a pattern made from up to six small raised bumps.
People who cannot see use their fingertips to follow this writing system.
explain: Braille is a writing system of raised dots that people who are blind or have low vision read with their fingertips. Each letter or number is a pattern within a grid of six dots. It works because fingertips have many touch receptors packed close together. Louis Braille created it in France when he was about 15.

clues: They contain a substance that helps kill germs.
Small glands above the outer corner make them all the time, and each blink spreads them.
Drops that roll down your cheeks when you chop onions or feel upset.
explain: Tears are made by tear glands above the outer corner of each eye. Every time you blink, a thin layer spreads over the eye to keep it moist and wash away dust. Tears also contain substances that fight germs. Extra tears flow when something irritates the eye, like onion fumes, or when you feel strong emotions.

clues: It holds about a million fibres bundled together.
Where it leaves the retina, there is a small spot that cannot detect light.
It is the cable that carries signals from the retina to the part of the head where seeing is processed.
explain: The optic nerve is a bundle of about a million nerve fibres that carries signals from the retina to the brain. The brain, mainly the occipital lobe at the back, turns these signals into the pictures you see. Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no light-sensing cells, which creates the blind spot.

scenario: An eye test shows a 12-year-old is short-sighted: light focuses just in front of her retina. Which type of lens in her glasses will help?
optionNotes: Spreads light so it focuses further back
explain: In short-sight, the eye bends light too much, so it focuses in front of the retina and distant things look blurry. A concave lens is thinner in the middle and spreads light out slightly. This moves the focus back onto the retina, so the picture becomes sharp. Long-sight is corrected with convex lenses, which are thicker in the middle.

scenario: A boy spills hot water from a kettle on his hand. The skin is red and painful. An adult is with him. What should they do first?
options: Hold it under cool running water for 20 minutes
answer: Hold it under cool running water for 20 minutes
optionNotes: Traps heat; not a burn treatment
Traps heat and can cause infection
explain: A burn keeps damaging skin while heat stays in it. Cool running water for about 20 minutes draws the heat out, eases pain and limits the damage. Ice is too cold and can harm skin, and butter or toothpaste trap heat and may cause infection. Afterwards, cover it loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth. Large burns, or burns on the face or hands, need a doctor.

scenario: On a windy day, a speck of dust blows into a girl's eye. It feels scratchy and her eye is watering. What should she do first?
options: Poke it out with a fingernail
Keep her eye shut for a week
Blink and rinse with clean water
answer: Blink and rinse with clean water
optionNotes: Can injure the eye and add germs
Not needed and does not remove it
Tears and water wash the speck out
explain: The eye already has a cleaning system: blinking and tears wash small specks away. Rinsing with clean water helps. Rubbing or poking can drag the speck across the clear cornea and scratch it. If the feeling does not go away, or something is stuck, an adult should take her to a doctor.

scenario: A boy's hearing in one ear has become muffled. He has been cleaning deep inside with cotton buds. The doctor sees the ear canal is blocked with packed wax. What is the best next step?
options: Use a hairpin to dig it out
Let the doctor soften and remove it safely
answer: Let the doctor soften and remove it safely
optionNotes: Can hurt the canal or eardrum
Drops soften it; doctor clears it
explain: Earwax protects the ear, and it normally moves out on its own. Cotton buds push it back in and pack it tight, which can block sound from reaching the eardrum. A doctor can use ear drops to soften the wax and then clear it safely. After that, he should only wipe the outer ear.

scenario: A girl feels sick whenever she reads a book in the back seat of a car on winding roads. Which advice helps most?
options: Look out of the front window at the distance
answer: Look out of the front window at the distance
optionNotes: Eyes still see a still page
Eyes and inner ear agree on motion
explain: Motion sickness happens when your senses disagree. The balance organs in your inner ear feel the car turning, but your eyes, fixed on a still page, say you are not moving. The brain gets mixed signals and you feel sick. Looking at the horizon lets your eyes see the same motion your ears feel.

scenario: After spinning round and round in the playground, a boy stops but feels as if the world is still turning. Which part of his ear causes this feeling?
optionNotes: Fluid inside keeps moving after you stop
explain: The semicircular canals in the inner ear are three loops filled with fluid. When you turn, the fluid moves and bends tiny hair cells, telling your brain you are spinning. When you stop suddenly, the fluid keeps swirling for a few seconds, so your brain still thinks you are turning, and you feel dizzy.

scenario: A family is going to the beach for the whole day. What is the best way to protect their skin from sunburn?
options: Only protect skin if it is sunny, not cloudy
Sunscreen every 2 hours and after swimming, plus a hat and shade
answer: Sunscreen every 2 hours and after swimming, plus a hat and shade
optionNotes: Wears off with sweat and water
explain: Sunburn is caused by UV rays, which damage skin cells. Sunscreen wears off with time, sweat and water, so it should be put on again about every 2 hours and after swimming. Hats, clothes and shade add protection, and UV is strongest around midday. UV also passes through clouds, so overcast days still need protection.

scenario: A 9-year-old has dry, itchy, red patches in the creases of her elbows that get worse in winter and after bubble baths. The doctor confirms eczema. Which daily habit helps most?
options: Wear scratchy wool next to the skin
Use mild soap and moisturise every day
answer: Use mild soap and moisturise every day
optionNotes: Repairs the barrier and keeps water in
Hot water dries skin out more
explain: In eczema, the outer skin barrier is weak, so skin loses water and gets irritated easily. Mild soap and daily moisturiser help keep water in and protect the skin. Hot baths, harsh soaps and rough fabrics dry or irritate it more. Scratching damages the skin further, so keeping nails short also helps.

scenario: A boy cannot tell the red and green dots apart in a colour test, though his sight is otherwise sharp. Which cells in his retina work differently?
optionNotes: Work in dim light; do not see colour
explain: The retina has two kinds of light-sensing cells. Rods work in dim light but only see shades of grey. Cones detect colour, and there are three types, sensitive to red, green and blue light. In red-green colour blindness, one type of cone works differently, so those colours look alike. It is usually inherited and is much more common in boys.
fact: About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of colour blindness.

scenario: A girl plays on a tablet for hours. Her eyes feel dry and tired. Which habit helps her eyes most?
options: Every 20 minutes, look at something far away for 20 seconds
answer: Every 20 minutes, look at something far away for 20 seconds
optionNotes: Dark room with bright screen strains eyes
explain: Looking at something close for a long time keeps the small focusing muscles in the eye tight, and people blink less when staring at screens, so eyes dry out. The 20-20-20 rule helps: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. This relaxes the focusing muscles and reminds you to blink.

scenario: A grandmother says her sight has become cloudy, like looking through a foggy window. The eye doctor finds the lens inside her eye has turned cloudy. What is the usual treatment?
options: Replace the cloudy lens with an artificial one
answer: Replace the cloudy lens with an artificial one
optionNotes: Has no effect on the lens
explain: The lens inside the eye focuses light onto the retina, so it needs to stay clear. With age, its proteins can clump and make it cloudy; this is a cataract. Doctors treat it with a short operation that removes the cloudy lens and puts in a clear artificial one, and most people see much better afterwards.

scenario: A boy with a cold and a blocked nose says his favourite curry tastes of almost nothing. His tongue is healthy. Why does food taste bland?
options: His taste buds have fallen out
Blocked smell receptors cannot add flavour
answer: Blocked smell receptors cannot add flavour
optionNotes: Smell gives food most of its flavour
explain: Your tongue senses only five basic tastes. Much of what we call flavour comes from smell: as you chew, smells from food rise up the back of your throat into your nose. When mucus blocks the smell receptors, you lose that part of flavour, so food seems bland until the cold clears.

scenario: A child often asks people to repeat themselves. The doctor wants to measure how well she hears different pitches, using headphones and beeps of different loudness. Which test is this?
explain: Audiometry is a hearing test. Beeps of different pitches are played through headphones, getting quieter, and the child signals each time she hears one. The results show the quietest sound she can hear at each pitch. This tells the doctor whether there is hearing loss and helps find the cause.

scenario: New shoes have rubbed a blister on a girl's heel. It is unbroken and a little sore. How should she care for it?
options: Leave it unbroken and cover it with a plaster
answer: Leave it unbroken and cover it with a plaster
optionNotes: The skin roof protects healing skin
explain: A blister is a bubble of fluid that forms under the top layer of skin after rubbing or a burn. The fluid and the skin on top act like a natural plaster, protecting the new skin growing underneath. Popping it lets germs in. Covering it and avoiding the rubbing lets it heal on its own.

scenario: A runner on a hot day gets wet with sweat. Which body response is cooling her down?
options: Narrowing blood vessels in her skin
optionNotes: Keeps heat in; used when cold
explain: When you get hot, sweat glands in the skin release watery sweat. As the sweat evaporates, it takes heat away from the skin, cooling you. The other three are ways the body keeps warm when it is cold. Drinking water during exercise replaces the water lost in sweat.

scenario: As a plane comes down to land, a boy's ears feel blocked and sore because air pressure is changing. What helps balance the pressure?
options: Press a finger hard into each ear
Hold his breath for a long time
optionNotes: Does not reach the middle ear
Opens the tube from throat to ear
explain: Behind the eardrum is an air-filled space called the middle ear. A narrow tube, the Eustachian tube, connects it to the back of the throat. When the plane descends, outside pressure rises and pushes the eardrum in, which feels blocked. Swallowing, yawning or chewing opens the tube so air can flow in and balance the pressure.
